NHRA and World Wide Technology Raceway announced a sellout crowd for Saturday’s racing at the 15th annual NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals, marking the sixth consecutive Saturday sellout for the St. Louis-area event.
“Today’s sold-out crowd at the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals is another tremendous showcase of the passion and enthusiasm St. Louis fans have for NHRA drag racing,” said NHRA President Glen Cromwell. “The team at World Wide Technology Raceway continues to provide an outstanding experience, and it’s exciting to see another packed house in St. Louis during our 75th anniversary season.”
Saturday’s capacity crowd represents NHRA’s 11th sellout of the 2026 season and its third consecutive Saturday sellout during the NHRA Mission Foods Drag Racing Series Countdown to the Championship.

articles.title_orig: Ax-wielding FlyDubai co-pilot had been flagged over extremism concerns
articles.title_zh: Ax-wielding FlyDubai co-pilot had been flagged over extremism concerns
articles.content_orig:
The co-pilot of a FlyDubai plane who attacked the flight's captain with an axe this week was attempting a terrorist attack, the United Arab Emirates said Saturday.
"The co-pilot began executing his plan during the flight, attacking the captain inside the flight deck using a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft," UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said in a post on X titled: "Planning and attempted terrorist act behind flydubai flight FZ1073 incident."
Anwar Gargash, senior advisor to the UAE's president, said the region's "struggle with extremism persists, and justifying terrorism through hate speech is part of the danger, not its margins."
"The latest terrorist operation is a new warning that the confrontation has not ended," Gargash said in a post on X.
The flight on Sept. 30 from Dubai to Tel Aviv was carrying 172 passengers and crew, according to UAE-based FlyDubai. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said most of those aboard were Israeli citizens, adding that the attacker "tried to crash the plane."
The aircraft landed safely at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia.
Media reports and witness accounts say passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot after he attacked the captain.
The UAE's attorney general's statement was the first time authorities have clarified the weapon the attacker used.
Large aircraft are typically equipped with a so-called crash axe that flight crews can use to break out of their cockpit in emergencies, according to the UK Civil Aviation Authority and the Royal Air Force Museum.
"Investigations are ongoing to establish the full circumstances, motives, and any links related to the incident, as well as to complete technical examinations and analysis of physical and digital evidence," the UAE's Al Shamsi said.
The Associated Press identified the co-pilot as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, citing three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and Western diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
CNBC could not independently verify the co-pilot's identity.
Netanyahu identified the injured pilot as Indian national Smit Machchhar. The Indian embassy in Riyadh said on X that Machchhar was in a hospital in Tabuk and reported to be in stable condition. FlyDubai later said the captain was returned to the UAE.
The Israeli prime minister also identified the passenger who broke into the cockpit as Yaniv Hayun, calling him a "hero" and adding he deserved "a global medal of honor."
Flight data from tracking site FlightRadar24 showed that the plane, a Boeing 737 Max 8, experienced extreme altitude fluctuations before broadcasting a "general emergency" squawk code.
FZ1073 dropped from more than 14,000 feet in just 29 seconds, according to FlightRadar24. Transponder data showed vertical speeds ranging from about -30,000 to +10,000 feet per minute.
Vertical speeds during normal operations rarely exceed plus or minus 4,000 feet per minute,  FlightRadar24 said.

articles.title_orig: Brazil's Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro Wrap up Campaigns Ahead of First-Round Vote
articles.title_zh: Brazil's Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro Wrap up Campaigns Ahead of First-Round Vote
articles.content_orig:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro have wrapped up their election campaigns, each voicing confidence in victory ahead of Sunday’s tightly contested first-round presidential vote.
Lula, 80, closed his re-election bid on Saturday with a march through Sao Paulo, Brazil’s economic powerhouse, drawing what his campaign called a record crowd for a closing rally.
“Tomorrow, we’re going to win the elections in the first round,” he told supporters, describing Sunday’s vote as a choice between “democracy and barbarism” and promising to “defeat the far right”.
He has also framed the election as a test of Brazil’s sovereignty, warning against “meddling” by Washington.
Bolsonaro led a motorcycle caravan through towns in Sao Paulo state, echoing the campaign style of his father, before rallying later in Rio de Janeiro. “I am convinced that everything is in place for us to win this election in the first round,” he said.
The 45-year-old is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of US President Donald Trump. The former leader, 71, is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 election loss to Lula.
The younger Bolsonaro was photographed at his rally holding a portrait of his father.
Trump has not formally endorsed Bolsonaro but has said he is watching the election “very closely”, a level of US interest that has become a flashpoint in the campaign .
Lula’s supporters have seized on it as evidence Washington is trying to meddle in the elections, while some Bolsonaro supporters, frustrated by the cost of living, say they would welcome US pressure if it helped force change at home.
Polls released on Saturday suggested Lula was still ahead but his lead was narrowing, with neither candidate likely to win outright on Sunday. Such a result would send the race to a run-off on October 25 between the two frontrunners, a contest polls suggest would also be close.
It is a far tighter race than Lula’s last victory in 2022, when he beat the elder Bolsonaro by less than two percentage points.
Meanwhile, the Bolsonaro campaign has faced scrutiny over a film-funding scandal. Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation over financing for Dark Horse, a biopic about his father, bankrolled by a jailed banker tied to one of Brazil’s biggest financial scandals.
Brazil’s Supreme Court authorised federal police in April to investigate whether Flavio Bolsonaro made defamatory statements about Lula.
Bolsonaro has pledged to seek his father’s release from prison if elected, and has echoed his father’s unsubstantiated claims questioning the reliability of Brazil’s electronic voting system, which analysts say could be laying the groundwork to contest the result if he loses.
Beyond the presidency, Brazil’s nearly 160 million registered voters will also choose lawmakers, governors and senators on Sunday.
Right-wing candidates have gained ground in Latin America in recent months.

articles.title_orig: The fiscal fallout from China’s property bust
articles.title_zh: The fiscal fallout from China’s property bust
articles.content_orig:
Peer reviewed analysis from world leading experts
Peterson Institute for International Economics
China’s property bust has exposed the fragility of a local government finance model built on land sales and off-budget borrowing. Beijing’s transfers and debt swaps have eased immediate liquidity pressures, but they neither reduce overall liabilities nor restore fiscal support for an economy grappling with deflationary pressures. Stronger central stimulus must be paired with a lasting rebalancing of spending responsibilities, local tax authority and borrowing constraints to prevent costs from falling on firms, workers and growth.
For much of China’s high growth era, land finance provided local governments with resources and discretion that the formal fiscal system did not. After the 1994 tax-sharing reform left local governments responsible for most public services and development, localities increasingly relied on selling land-use rights and borrowing off budget, often using land assets as collateral. The model helped finance infrastructure and accelerate urbanisation, but it tied local budgets to the housing cycle.
Land finance was central to China’s investment-led growth model, in which local officials competed to generate growth. Yet that model was inherently procyclical. At the housing market peak in 2021, broadly defined land revenue — including land sale proceeds and other taxes — accounted for nearly half of local governments’ consolidated revenue, or 10 per cent of GDP. By 2025, it had fallen to around 25 per cent of local revenue, or less than 5 per cent of GDP. That figure likely overstates genuine demand because local government financing vehicles bought many land plots, artificially inflating land-sale revenue.
The revenue collapse exposed how much debt local governments had accumulated during the boom. From 2019 to 2023, debt service on official debt, including principal and interest payments, rose from 8 per cent of local revenue before central transfers to 18 per cent. The debt-servicing burden also grew for off-budget debt , much of which was raised against land collateral during the housing boom and became harder to roll over as land values fell. Some heavily indebted provinces, such as Guizhou, even openly pleaded for Beijing’s help.
The consequences extend well beyond local finances. Localities have delayed payments to contractors and withheld wages or benefits from employees. A February 2025 estimate put local government arrears at 10 trillion RMB (US$1.37 trillion) by the end of 2024, about 7 per cent of GDP. These arrears act like a hidden tax on companies, squeezing profits and depressing investment and employment.
Beijing sought to ease localities’ immediate liquidity constraints through greater transfer payments, refinancing and debt swaps. Central transfers to provinces have exceeded the central government’s own revenue since 2023, requiring Beijing to rely partly on debt issuance to fund them.
Beijing has also allowed localities to issue more long-term, low-interest government bonds to refinance debt and replace off-budget liabilities. These measures have eased immediate cash-flow pressures — from 2019 to 2025 , the average maturity of outstanding local government debt rose from 5.1 to 10.5 years, while the average interest rate declined from 3.6 per cent to 2.8 per cent. Debt service as a share of local revenue started to drop after 2023.
But Beijing’s strategy offers more relief than repair. Debt swaps and transfers buy time, but they do not reduce the overall stock of local government liabilities, which must eventually be reckoned with . Nor can they create a durable post-land-finance fiscal model to replace the one that has failed. They may even reinforce local dependence on Beijing and encourage moral hazard. To the extent that banks are forced to bear the cost of that relief through lower returns, it also puts further pressure on the financial system.
Despite Beijing’s relief measures, fiscal support to the broader economy weakened at precisely the wrong time. Since 2023, more than half of local government bond issuance has gone towards refinancing debt or replacing off-budget liabilities rather than financing new spending. Local government spending has continued to decline as a share of GDP since peaking in 2020, and higher central spending has not entirely offset that retrenchment. The contribution of government spending to aggregate demand has therefore weakened — the opposite of what an economy struggling with persistent deflationary pressures needs.
China needs a more forceful countercyclical fiscal expansion to support domestic demand and break the deflationary cycle. While such an expansion would require Beijing to tolerate a larger fiscal deficit and higher debt in the short run, it has room to do so. The central government still has a relatively strong balance sheet , with its net financial worth among the strongest of any major economy. Once inflation has durably returned to target, Beijing should raise taxes and cut spending to stabilise the debt ratio.
Over the long run, a sustainable post-land-finance fiscal model requires two major changes. The central government should assume more responsibility for nationally important spending, including social protection, which local governments administer almost entirely, while reducing unfunded local mandates. Local governments also need a broader tax base and greater tax authority, combined with further constraints on off-budget borrowing.
The reform blueprint unveiled at the 2024 Third Plenum points in this direction, proposing greater local control over excise tax collection and a local tax surcharge whose rate localities could set within limits. But these incremental measures alone are unlikely to be enough. The plenum omitted a nationwide property tax, likely due to concerns that it could further depress the housing market. Once the market stabilises, a carefully designed property tax should be considered as a more stable local revenue source.
Land finance helped build China’s economic miracle, but left local government finances hostage to the housing cycle. Now that the housing bubble has burst, China needs to recalibrate its fiscal system to fund public services, respond to shocks and support the country’s broader growth model transition without relying on land. That requires Beijing to permanently rebalance spending responsibilities and revenue authority between levels of government. Without that repair, the costs of the old model will continue to fall onto firms, workers and the broader economy.
Tianlei Huang is Senior Fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
His forthcoming book is Detox: China’s Fiscal Reckoning in the Shadow of the Housing Bust (PIIE).

articles.title_orig: Health Policy Watch | COVID-19 drops out of world’s top 10 causes of death for first time since pandemic began
articles.title_zh: Health Policy Watch | COVID-19 drops out of world’s top 10 causes of death for first time since pandemic began
articles.content_orig:
COVID-19 dropped out of the world’s 10 leading causes of death in 2023 for the first time since the pandemic began in 2020, and only two years after it topped the list, according to new World Health Organization estimates released Friday (2 October).
The virus directly killed an estimated 0.9 million people in 2023, ranking 14th, as global life expectancy climbed back to near its pre-pandemic level. WHO declared an end to COVID-19 as a global health emergency in May that year.
Revised figures now rank COVID-19 as the world’s leading cause of death in 2021, with 9.4 million direct deaths. WHO’s earlier estimates had placed it second that year. Together with 5.3 million deaths in 2020, the new figures put the virus’s direct toll in the first two years of the pandemic at 14.7 million.
Source : Health Policy Watch

articles.title_orig: Balloons take flight with several minor crashes on day 1 of Balloon Fiesta
articles.title_zh: Balloons take flight with several minor crashes on day 1 of Balloon Fiesta
articles.content_orig:
It's the first day of the 2026 Albuquerque International Balloon Fiesta.
Officials and pilots are gathering at Balloon Fiesta Park to monitor the weather and prepare for the first mass ascension of the year.
Seven minor balloon crashes took place on Saturday, according to a New Mexico Police spokesperson.  KOAT captured the aftermath from three of those crashes.
One balloon crashed into powerlines south of Balloon Fiesta Park on Saturday morning.
KOAT tower cameras caught the incident soon after it happened.
Action 7 News has been told those who were in the basket are safe and the balloon was removed from the power line.
A second crash happened near the 3700 block of Hawkins Street NE.  The balloon clipped a power line as it was making its landing.  No one was injured.
Another crash occurred near the Cinemark Century Rio Plex and XD Theater on Pan American Freeway NE.  That balloon clipped a light pole as it was making its landing.  There were no injuries.
The cluster balloon, piloted by Jonathan Trappe, took flight shortly before the field was closed for launch in the morning.
Inflation for the balloon began a few hours after midnight on Saturday morning.

articles.title_orig: ‘You’re coming in blind?’ Medical plane flying to Boston from Bermuda goes missing off Nantucket
articles.title_zh: ‘You’re coming in blind?’ Medical plane flying to Boston from Bermuda goes missing off Nantucket
articles.content_orig:
Air traffic controllers in New York struggled to communicate with a twin-engine medical transport jet as it rapidly descended toward the Atlantic Ocean south of Nantucket early Saturday.
“You’re coming in blind? Is that what you said?” a controller asked the pilot at about 12:46 a.m. “Are you declaring an emergency, or no?”
The pilot’s response, according to a recording captured by LiveATC.net, was not audible.
The airplane, a Gulfstream G100 that took off from Bermuda late Friday, was carrying six people bound for Boston: a patient and family member as well as a four-person crew.
As the jet approached Nantucket, its pilot reported electrical failures, according to radio transmissions . Data from the website FlightAware show the plane descended thousands of feet within three minutes.
Shortly afterward, around 1 a.m., it disappeared from radar entirely.
The disappearance prompted a massive US Coast Guard search for the aircraft, involving planes, a helicopter, and two boats. As of Saturday night, the Coast Guard had not updated the status of the mission.
The crew members are Canadian citizens and the patient and family member are Bermudian nationals, according to Clarence Togeretz, operations manager for Latitude Air Ambulance, the company in Ontario that operates the Gulfstream G100.
In a statement, the Bermudian government said it was in touch with the families of the passengers and US search crews.
“We are praying that all six people will be found safe,” said Bermuda Premier David Burt.
The plane left L. F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda for the 800-mile flight to Boston at 11:41 p.m. on Friday, said Ciara Eve, an airport spokesperson. Bermuda, a self-governing British territory, is one hour ahead of Eastern Daylight Time.
As the jet descended toward the Atlantic, air traffic controllers asked to confirm whether they were declaring an emergency.
“You’re coming in a little weak so I didn’t hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not,” the air traffic controller said. He later confirmed the pilot declared an emergency, but struggled to reestablish contact with the aircraft.
The air traffic controller asked the pilot of a second plane whether the Gulfstream G100 aircraft was visible on its anti-collision system. But the second plane was flying at a much higher altitude and couldn’t pick up signs of jet, the pilot said.
For much of the flight, the Gulfstream jet traveled at about 24,000 feet, but at about 1:04 a.m., FlightAware data show the plane descended 13,000 feet within three minutes.
With the plane about 80 miles south of Nantucket at 1:06 a.m., a dispatcher at Logan International Airport directed crews to stage on the runway for the plane. She said it was due to land in 15 minutes and had lost “radio and radar,” according to radio transmissions captured by Broadcastify.
Emergency crews got into position and waited.
At 1:20 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration issued an alert, an agency spokesperson said. The plane wouldn’t land at Logan, and a search and rescue mission had been launched.
On the runway at Logan, the Massport Fire Rescue commander heard a radio transmission reporting that air traffic control said it could no longer see the plane on the radar.
“I don’t know if you monitored the tower radio, but the tower lost radar contact with this aircraft,” the commander radioed at about 1:36 a.m.
“Received, I do have it. I was listening,” the dispatcher said.
Emergency crews on the runway were ordered back to their headquarters. At 2 a.m., the FAA alerted the US Coast Guard of the missing plane.
On Nantucket, police checked the island’s airport for the missing jet but found nothing, said Lieutenant Angus MacVicar.
At sunrise, officers and the harbormaster began combing Nantucket’s southern shoreline aboard ATVs in search of signs of the plane, he said.
Governor Maura Healey said Saturday her “thoughts and prayers go to to all on board and all involved.”
“We’ll do whatever we can as a state to support efforts there and work with the Coast Guard,” Healey said at a labor rally in Dorchester.
Coast Guard airplanes, plus a helicopter, cutter, and life boat circled Nantucket to look for the missing plane. As sunlight faded Saturday, there was no word on its location.
Chris Van Buskirk and John R. Ellement of the Globe staff contributed to this report .

articles.title_zh: China, Africa boost law enforcement ties in crackdown on cross-border cybercrime
articles.content_orig:
Police cooperation allows Beijing to expand its security role without formal alliances or a large military footprint, observers say
From online-gambling rings in eSwatini to SIM swapping in Kenya and cybercrime networks in Zambia, a wave of cross-border fraud is drawing African governments and China into closer security cooperation.
China hosted East African security ministers and police chiefs in Lianyungang, Jiangsu province, on September 10 for talks on terrorism, kidnapping, online fraud and other cross-border threats.
On the same day, China launched the International Alliance Combating Telecoms and Cyber Fraud, with 46 founding countries including Kenya.

articles.title_orig: Trump pledges to send $90 checks to millions of seniors on Medicare
articles.title_zh: Trump pledges to send $90 checks to millions of seniors on Medicare
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump promised on Friday to give $90 rebate checks to offset premiums for millions of U.S. seniors on Medicare, his latest pledge to send money to Americans ahead of the midterm elections.
“I am pleased to announce that my Administration will, immediately, begin sending ‘Checks’ of nearly $100 to over 20 MILLION wonderful Seniors to help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which we have already reduced by significant amounts,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post.
Trump said the money “will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, a pointless ‘Slush Fund’ that has only been used by Dumocrats in Congress to pay for the Waste, Fraud, and Abuse for their Special Interest friends, and drive up Healthcare costs.”
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services affirmed Trump’s plans on Saturday, writing in a fact sheet that 20.8 million Americans are eligible for the $90 premium rebates.
“The Administration is making a $90 Premium Rebate available for Part B premiums to certain Medicare beneficiaries because the best way to improve Medicare is to put healthcare dollars back where they belong — in the hands of our Medicare beneficiaries — and make coverage more affordable,” the CMS fact sheet said.
The agency said that some beneficiaries will receive a direct deposit for a $90 rebate in early October followed by an email or a letter from Trump, while other beneficiaries will receive a $90 paper check from the Treasury Department later this month.
Following that timeline, both payment methods are expected to be received before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The CMS fact sheet claims that Trump is the first president to tap into the Medicare Improvement Fund, which was established by Congress in 2008 to help finance general improvements to the Medicare program.
However, the fact sheet also noted that Congress has withdrawn from the fund on numerous occasions to “‘offset’ new spending.”
Trump wrote in his Truth Social post that the $90 checks are “separate from the equally substantial Refund ‘Checks’ we are sending to One Million Americans who were overcharged for their Unaffordable Care Act plans by Joe Biden.”
Last month, Trump said he would send $500 rebate checks to about 1 million ACA recipients across 30 states. The White House has claimed, without evidence, that the beneficiaries had been overcharged by the Biden administration for exchange fees. The president said Thursday those checks had been sent out to recipients.
These one-time premium rebates are also different from the ACA subsidies, which affected people under the age of 65, that the Republican-controlled Congress allowed to expire last year.
The healthcare-focused checks this week add to the list of payments Trump has promised to give Americans.
In his post on Friday, Trump also again promised a $5,000 dividend payment to all adult U.S. citizens if Republicans win both the House and the Senate in November.
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have expressed skepticism about those “Trump dividend” checks, particularly as the president has neglected to give details on the policy that would be required to back up the promise and get it into Americans’ wallets. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told NBC News last month that the funds would not come from taxpayer dollars.
In February 2025, Trump also pledged a 20% return to American citizens from DOGE savings. Later that year, he said he would give a “dividend of at least $2,000 a person” from revenue brought in by his tariff policies. Neither of those payments went out to American citizens.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Kebinatshipi: ‘This was just the start’
articles.title_zh: Kebinatshipi: ‘This was just the start’
articles.content_orig:
Collen Kebinatshipi at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship ( © Getty Images )
“Trust me,” says Collen Kebinatshipi. “This was just the start of an era of Collen. My plan is just to dominate for the longest period possible.”
Whatever about the future, the 22-year-old Motswana, who blazed to the world 400m title in Tokyo last year in 43.53, has been utterly dominant this year – going six for six at Diamond League meetings and setting a national record of 43.40 at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.
Which brought him to the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest high on confidence, where Kebinatshipi was the overwhelming favourite for the men’s 400m. In many races this year, he had saved his energy for the latter half of the one-lap race but, this time, he changed things up.
“I just decided I should go all out and see where it would end,” he says.
He left the blocks in explosive fashion, ripping through the first 100m in 10.61, reaching 200m in 20.67 and 300m in a blazing 31.37, leaving a slew of global medallists trailing far behind.
43.39, another national record, which handed him the Ultimate trophy and $150,000 in prize money.
Collen Kebinatshipi at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship Budapest 26 (© Getty Images)
Kebinatshipi blacked out not long after the race and had to spend several minutes recuperating in a wheelchair. The 400m can do that, especially when you run it as he did.
“It’s normal,” he says. “I know every time I push my body, it’s like that. The plan was to give everything, leave everything on the track.”
He did just that, crowning a season of consistent excellence. There were his two 9.89-second 100m clockings on home turf in Gaborone back in April, his three national 400m records, and Kebinatshipi also helped Botswana to victory in the men’s 4x400m at the World Athletics Relays in Gaborone, clocking an African record of 2:54.47.
“I need to go home and recover,” he says. “I didn’t want to mess up because this is my last race, I didn’t want to leave anything in the tank and now I have nothing in the tank.
“It’s a special thing to keep the [winning] streak alive until the end of the season. It was such an amazing season and it’s a big boost heading towards next year. I just want to make sure I stay healthy until the World Championships.”
Collen Kebinatshipi (© Monirul Bhuiyan)
It’s been a steep ascent in recent years, but Kebinatshipi’s talent has been clear for a long time. He took up athletics in primary school. “I was just doing it for fun,” he says.
In 2019, he met his current coach, Chilume ‘Chippa’ Ntshwarang, at a competition and they started working together. It’s proven a hugely successful relationship. He trains alongside Lee Eppie, a 44.40 athlete who joined Kebinatshipi on the team that won the men’s 4x400m world title in Tokyo last year.
In 2020, he and his coach decided to focus more on the 400m. “Even though I was scared of it,” says Kebinatshipi, “but coach maybe saw something I didn’t see.”
In 2022, he lowered his PB to 45.40 at the age of 18 and reached the world U20 400m final. In 2023, he won gold at the African U20 Championships in 44.91 and reached the world semi-final in Budapest. In 2024, he became an Olympian in Paris, narrowly missing the 400m final and helping Botswana to Olympic silver in the 4x400m.
But things truly clicked in 2025.
Kebinatshipi overcame a scare in his 400m heat at the World Championships in Tokyo, where he finished only fourth in 44.48, but he blazed to victory in his semi-final in a national record of 43.61. In the final, he ran 43.53 to claim his first global gold.
Collen Kebinatshipi wins the 400m at the World Athletics Championships Tokyo 25 (© Getty Images)
“Last year’s win opened a lot of doors for me but that was just the beginning, because this year was about putting my name up there and showing people who I am and what I’m capable of,” he says. “My coach told me to come here and try a new race plan.”
It might have been a very different approach in Budapest, but it worked as well as ever, Kebinatshipi finishing a whopping 0.76 seconds ahead of runner-up Rai Benjamin. He said the world record was not in his mind at the Ultimate Championship, given the fatigue of the previous day’s semi-final was still in his legs.
“The championship itself deserves such challenges,” he says. “Because it’s big money, and big challenges.”
However, Wayde van Niekerk’s mark of 43.03 is certainly a long-term goal.
“I would be lying if I say no – the world record is obviously always running in my mind. The world record talk will be on the table maybe in LA (at the 2028 Olympics).
“The calculations based on training, we’re always (doing), like if I go 20.9 in the first 200m and then go 22.0 or 22.1, it’s going to give us a 42.9. But it’s not easy. I’m still a bit lighter, I’m not doing a lot of gym but as time goes, when I start engaging the body in more constant work I think I will manage (the world record), but for now, no pressure.”
With his season complete, Kebinatshipi plans to take a long break, which he will spend at home in Botswana, where he breeds boerboel dogs on a 10-acre farm.
“I have eight of them at the moment and I have been missing them since May,” he says. “I am going to go back home, spend all my prize money on them. Unfortunately, they are not as fast as I am – they have big muscles and cannot keep up with me.”
Still only 22, Kebinatshipi believes he has “10, 11 years in this track life” left and all options are on the table about his specialist events.
“If we achieve what we want, maybe run under 43 before the next five years, it’d give us another window to try another event,” he says. “Once I accomplish it, in less than five years, I’m going to move to the 200m and after achieving what I want, I can skip again, go to the 800m.”
Whatever way he goes, the era of Collen Kebinatshipi looks built to last.
Cathal Dennehy for World Athletics

articles.title_orig: Hawaii sea arch collapses into Pacific Ocean 550 years after its formation
articles.title_zh: Hawaii sea arch collapses into Pacific Ocean 550 years after its formation
articles.content_orig:
A scenic cliff on the wave-swept coast of Hawaii's Big Island has collapsed, the National Park Service said.
The Holei Sea Arch, located in the Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, was about 90 feet high before it collapsed sometime between Sept. 23 and Sept. 27, possibly when the park was temporarily closed during Hurricane Nolo .
"The exact time of the collapse is unknown and could have occurred when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo," said the Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park in a social media post.
Nolo — which reached winds of 155 mph — moved past Hawaii's Big Island and brought heavy rain and winds to the state last week. Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said the Trump administration approved an emergency declaration for Hawaii that will provide federal resources and assistance to the state in its recovery from Nolo.
In August, Hawaii was battered by Hurricane Lala, which washed away about 100 homes , triggered landslides and caused widespread power outages as it brushed past Hawaii.
The arch's collapse into the Pacific Ocean was not unexpected, however, it marks "the latest transformation of the park's remote and rugged coastline," the NPS said in a Facebook post.
"This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span," NPS said .
People reacting to the post called it a sign of nature taking its course.
Officials at the park service warned visitors to stay away from the site since it is unstable and presents a serious falling hazard.
"Photos on social media show people entering the closed area near where the sea arch once stood, putting themselves and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning," the NPS said.
The popular tourist site was formed about 550 years ago. The name Holei comes from a small endemic plant in the milkweed family.

articles.title_orig: How can the same El Niño cause drought in one part of the world and floods in another?
articles.title_zh: How can the same El Niño cause drought in one part of the world and floods in another?
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
For decades, scientists have struggled to understand the potential link between global warming and El Niño — and whether human activity is making the already powerful climate phenomenon even more extreme and disruptive.
Evidence of a connection has remained elusive, however, as El Niño  is notoriously variable, making it difficult to distinguish long-term changes from its natural ebb and flow.
But now — as this year’s “super” El Niño gains strength — some researchers say they are getting closer to unraveling the mystery.
A study published recently  in the journal Science examines temperature data from more than 900 years of coral records from the Galápagos and suggests that El Niños have become much stronger since people started warming the planet through fossil fuel emissions.
“Prior to the industrial era, we don’t see evidence for periods where the El Niño system is as strong as it is in the most recent decades,” said Julia Cole, a paleoclimatologist at the University of Michigan and the study’s lead author. The swings between warm and cold conditions that define El Niño “were much stronger in the last 40 to 50 years than they were prior to warming.”
A “super” El Niño is now 95% likely to develop this year as the climate pattern gains dramatic strength in the Pacific Ocean — leaving officials across California and beyond bracing for a wet and potentially destructive winter.
The research arrives as experts and officials warn that the current El Niño, which began forming in June, is shaping up to be the strongest ever experienced by a considerable margin . It is developing faster than the previous historic super El Niños of 1997-98 and 2015-16, and is already on track to far exceed historical temperature thresholds.
On Thursday, the World Meteorological Society issued a new El Niño forecast warning that there is a nearly 100% chance it will continue through February, prolonging its effects.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” read a statement from United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres. “The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather.”
El Niños are periods of temporary warming in the tropical Pacific that develop every two to seven years. When they arrive, they trigger widespread changes in weather and climate around the world, from punishing heat waves to dangerous floods and severe droughts. In Southern California, El Niño is associated with warm and wet conditions.
According to authors of the recent study, modern El Niños are about 36% stronger than they were before the start of the industrial era in the mid-1800s, and show a “striking amplification” of about 16% in the last 40 years. El Niño’s strength is primarily measured by how much warmer the sea surface temperature in the tropical Pacific region is than normal.
To be sure, scientists have not yet conclusively established that humanity’s burning of fossil fuels is increasing or intensifying El Niño.
“This is another piece of evidence in an ongoing scientific debate on the role of climate change in El Niño events,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth who was not involved in the study. “It won’t necessarily settle it, but it’s more weight on the side of the scale for a detectable climate impact.”
The ramifications of a direct connection would be serious. Not only is El Niño a leading driver of climate and weather hazards, but it also imposes “tremendous economic costs, ecological damages, and human suffering globally,” according to the Science study. That includes droughts, floods, infrastructure damage, coral bleaching, wildfires, and agricultural and health effects.
Notably, the study did not find that climate change is worsening the other half of the El Niño Southern Oscillation system — La Niña. If anything, it is making ENSO’s variability “kind of lopsided,” Cole said, meaning that the change in variability leans toward stronger warm events than cold ones.
Uncovering these mechanisms has been a challenge, she said, in part because very few people live in the remote part of the ocean where El Niño forms, and “nobody was out there sticking a thermometer in the water every week” over the centuries to create a historical record. It wasn’t until scientists started receiving satellite data in the 1980s that a complete picture of El Niño began to emerge.
So Cole and her colleagues turned to the coral.
A rare convergence of a powerful El Niño, super king tides and sea level rise spurred by climate change could menace California with record coastal flooding this winter.
Coral can live for decades or centuries, and they form a skeleton of calcium carbonate layers as they grow, kind of like rings on a tree. By measuring aspects of their chemistry — the ratio of strontium to calcium and the relative abundance of rare and common oxygen isotopes — the researchers could determine the ocean temperature in which the coral grew down to a specific month, Cole said.
That allowed them to chart temperature data from the Galápagos dating back almost 1,000 years. The Galápagos sit right where eastern Pacific El Niño events have some of their strongest effects.
Though they didn’t have coral samples for every year of the last millennium, the data they generated “have this really unequivocal signal in them, and we thought it was really important to get them out there,” Cole said.
The findings may not settle the debate once and for all, but they “definitely” show an increase in El Niño’s variance in the modern era, said Art Miller, an oceanographer at Scripps Institution of Oceanography who was not involved with the study.
He said the findings are consistent with the appearance of several unusually large El Niño events in the last three decades — namely, 1997-98, 2015-16 and the one gaining strength now.
They also align with observable warming in the ocean and atmosphere, which are potentially affecting El Niño’s dynamics, he said. In fact, this year’s El Niño is developing against the backdrop of unusually warm ocean temperatures, including a record-breaking marine heat wave in the Pacific Ocean that is providing a hotter baseline for the system.
“Since the equatorial zone of the ocean in the western Pacific was loaded with heat, it was primed for triggering an El Niño,” Miller said. But the connection is something of a two-way street: Although the heat wave helped instigate El Niño in the spring and summer, El Niño is expected to feed warmth back toward the West Coast as it develops, keeping coastal waters warmer than usual in the fall and winter, he said.
Other researchers were more skeptical about the coral study’s findings. University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann noted in a post on Bluesky that other factors, such as volcanic and solar activity, could explain patterns seen in the coral record.
For his part, Hausfather cautioned that there are “pretty big uncertainties when you are working with indirect measurements like coral proxy records,” so comparing historical El Niños with modern ones is inherently hard to do.
What’s more, “even if the authors are correct about the climate change link, that doesn’t mean that every single El Niño event will be a strong one,” he said. “El Niño is still largely driven by natural variability, which means that some individual events will be strong and some weak.”
Cole, the lead researcher, agreed. The findings don’t mean that every El Niño will be stronger than the last in a warming world, she said — nor would that be realistic given how unpredictable El Niño can be.
But even if some are weaker than others, the data indicate they are unlikely to revert to preindustrial levels anytime so

articles.title_orig: RuneScape 4, The Next MMO From Jagex, Announced At RuneFest This Weekend
articles.title_zh: RuneScape 4, The Next MMO From Jagex, Announced At RuneFest This Weekend
articles.content_orig:
RuneFest 2026 is over, and we’ve got a roundup of everything announced at Jagex’s big show celebrating its long-running fantasy MMORPG.
This year saw a number of significant announcements, none bigger than confirmation that a fourth RuneScape MMO is in the works . Jagex hasn’t officially called it RuneScape 4 (RS4 is the working title), but we know it’s built on Unreal Engine and is designed to use the latest technology and design, so it really does sound like a next-gen RuneScape game. There’s no information on when it will be released, but the teaser trailer is below.
Jagex announced a new RuneScape animated adaptation, in partnership with YouTuber Charlie White, aka MoistCr1TiKaL, and production company Lyrical Media. No word on what this is exactly or when it will be released, but it’s happening!
Jagex announced RuneScape Reignited, which launches December 2. Jagex called it a “defining moment” for the 25-year-old game, designed to rekindle interest among lapsed players and get existing players excited. There’s a Remastered Journey and Adventure Guide, a fresh economy, and brand-new hi scores. Players can get full Reignited Access without membership from December 2-12. The long-awaited Plugin API launches this month, with players getting an early hands-on ahead of official release. The debut trailer is below:
We also got what Jagex called “the biggest roadmap in the game’s history.” 2027 content unfolds in three story arcs, all of which tie into long-running storylines. Hoard of Dragons (January) offers a sequel to the popular Dragon Slayer quest, City of Gnomes continues the gnome storyline, and Secrets of Karamja introduces a new endgame raid. Also coming is an Agility skill rework, new skilling and solo bosses, new area expansions, and a new Grandmaster Quest.
Old School RuneScape, meanwhile, got an updated roadmap. The Golden Gates to Menaphos are opening finally after 20 years, alongside a suite of fan-demanded content. The Fractured Archive, a new endgame raid, launches October 20. Hardcore Worlds launches November 4. And next year will also see the continuation of the Fairytale questline, Quest month, Dungeons of Gielinor, a Mining and Smithing rework, Chosen Commander, and the Tower of Xorphoros.
The recently released spinoff, RuneScape: Dragonwilds, saw the announcement of the Blood Crystal Saga and updated plans for 2027. The Luminance update is a prelude to 2027’s Blood Crystal Saga, and launches in December this year. This features the introduction of the Elves into RuneScape: Dragonwilds, new elven-themed customisation options for player characters and buildings alike and the Prayer skill.
The Blood Crystal Saga kicks off in 2027 starting with the Song of Rebellion in early 2027. These updates feature enemies like Moss Giants, Kebbits, and Implings, the Hunter Skill as well as new areas for players to explore, new quests and gear as well new decorations for houses inspired by the classic RuneScape city of Prifddinas.
Expect quarterly updates, which will include new Skills such as Hunter and Slayer, as well as monthly updates featuring side quests, weapons, decorations and quality of life improvements. Official modding arrives on Dragonwilds in 2027 through a new partnership with CurseForge — complete with dedicated creation tools and an in-game mod browser and installer, available across all platforms including console.
Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title_orig: Tennessee Commissioner Resigns After Failed Execution of Christa Pike
articles.title_zh: Tennessee Commissioner Resigns After Failed Execution of Christa Pike
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike, 50, remains in a hospital early Thursday after a botched execution in Tennessee.
Pike, the lone woman on death row, was set to be the first female in more than 200 years the state had put to death, according to historical records .
However, after she was injected twice with a lethal drug, Pike did not die, and she was transferred to an “off-site medical facility,” a spokesperson for the Department of Correction told NBC News. Attorneys for Pike said late Wednesday that she was being treated at a hospital but that they did not know her condition.
Here’s what to know about her case.
In 1995, Knoxville police said Pike and two teenage accomplices had worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, 19.
Police said Pike and the others lured Slemmer, a classmate in their Job Corps training program, to an abandoned steam plant at the nearby University of Tennessee and attacked her.
The case became sensationalized when investigators said it was tied to the occult because someone had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike bragged to another student that she had kept a fragment of the victim’s skull as a “souvenir.”
Pike does not dispute her role in the grisly killing. But details about her upbringing, marked by years of sexual and physical abuse and neglect, were not shared with the jury that sentenced her to death. Her lawyers believe that if such evidence of abuse were presented at a trial now, a death sentence would not be guaranteed.
They had asked the Supreme Court to halt Pike’s execution, saying she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from being molested and raped beginning when she was a toddler. Being held down and strapped to a gurney, they wrote, was likely to create “severe mental suffering and superadded psychological terror under Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol.”
The state has not denied that Pike has suffered from abuse. But in a response filed Monday, the attorney general’s office said a judge already concluded last month that it was “speculative whether Pike would suffer” greater mental harm from how the lethal injection protocol is carried out.
The Supreme Court appeared to be Pike’s remaining chance for a reprieve after Lee said he was upholding her death sentence “after deliberate consideration.” The high court denied her petition Tuesday evening.
Pike’s lawyers said Monday they were “saddened and heartbroken” that the governor would not be granting clemency.
Another woman, Gaile Owens , was on Tennessee’s death row with Pike until 2010, when Gov. Phil Bredesen changed her sentence to life in prison.
Before she learned Monday that Lee would not intervene in her case, Pike wrote in a letter to NBC News, shared by her spiritual adviser, that people have seen a “limited public persona that has been the only narrative” about her. Her lawyers had tried to convince Lee that she was a product of a tumultuous childhood.
“Stepping into the chaos of Christa’s life that led her to that moment will not justify her actions that night,” one of her lawyers, Randall Spivey, said of the time when she committed her crime. “But the chaos will show you that Christa was broken, not evil.”
Pike’s lawyers also pointed to her age and how it led to such a different outcome in her case.
While she faced a death sentence because of her first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder conviction in Slemmer’s death, another conspirator was spared: Pike’s boyfriend, who was 17 at the time.
Tadaryl Shipp was sentenced to life in prison because he was a juvenile and remains eligible for parole. Shipp testified at his post-conviction hearing that he was the one who carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest.
The third accomplice — Shadolla Peterson, then 18 — served as a lookout in the crime and was sentenced to probation in exchange for her cooperation.
Pike told police that she “wasn’t even thinking” when she assaulted Slemmer and that she had been jealous, believing the victim was trying to steal Shipp’s attention.
Pike’s lawyers said her age would have been more of a factor today, given how scientific research has evolved in understanding that young people’s brains are still developing well beyond their teen years.
In addition, her lawyers said her legal representatives at the time could have accepted a deal from prosecutors who were offering a life sentence without parole in return for a guilty plea.
Pike sobbed as the judge told her she would die by electrocution, then the only form of execution in Tennessee before the state moved to lethal injection as its primary method.
She pleaded through tears : “Can I please hug my mom?”
Pike entered prison, where she was placed in solitary confinement for up to 23 hours a day and prescribed Prozac to treat her obsessive-compulsive disorder. Early on, she struggled to express remorse.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in her clemency petition.
Three years ago, Pike’s lawyers asked Bethany Brand, a psychologist specializing in trauma, to assess whether she suffers from psychological disorders and consider whether any contributed to the crime.
She sat with Pike at her Nashville prison and reviewed police reports, past medical examinations and other files in her case detailing physical and sexual abuse.
Brand learned that Pike’s parents were not stable figures in her life. Her mother’s boyfriends and other men had molested her from a young age, the files said. She did poorly in school, living with other family members in West Virginia and North Carolina. At 17 — one year before she would take part in Slemmer’s murder — Pike reported to North Carolina police that she was walking to the store when a man threw her to the ground and raped her. No one was ever arrested.
In her final report, Brand wrote that the adults in Pike’s life failed her. Doctors only diagnosed a bipolar disorder a few years after she was already in prison.
The level of trauma Pike was subjected to “is almost impossible to grasp because it is so severe,” Brand wrote.
She told NBC News that medications in prison have helped Pike tremendously and that she now has “empathy and great regret” for what she did. Pike’s case, she added, is a lesson in the need for greater awareness surrounding women’s mental health and recognizing trauma and untreated mental illness.
“In Christa’s case, nobody was trying to get her help,” Brand said.
May Martinez, the mother of victim Slemmer, is unconvinced that the person responsible for mutilating her daughter’s body and leaving her nude from the waist up could change.
Martinez recalled that, after the investigation ended, she did not realize all of her daughter’s body parts were not buried with her remains, as some had been retained as trial evidence. She had to pick up Slemmer’s skull from the courthouse, and she remembers that the medical examiner’s office mailed her other parts later. (The office said it rarely retains human remains as it did 30 years ago because of better technology, enhanced photography and lab work.)
“We had her buried in a Catholic cemetery,” Martinez said. “And she had to be dug up every time they mailed me body parts.”
Recently, she said, she has refused to communicate with Pike directly. The only way she can get justice now is when she watches Pike be executed.
“I will sit there with her picture in my hand,” Martinez said of her daughter, “and as she gets hooked up to a needle to go to sleep, she can look at the picture.”
Given the rarity of the execution of a female prisoner, Tennessee corrections officials said they would make an effort to fulfill certain requests made by Pike. They included using female guards when she was moved from her all-women’s prison in Nashville to the nearby Riverbend Maximum Security Institution within 24 hours of her planned execution. An all-female execution team may also have been assigned.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Cotton tussle over daylight savings after cell phone number leak
articles.title_zh: Trump, Cotton tussle over daylight savings after cell phone number leak
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Saturday pressured Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, posting the personal cellphone number of the chairman of Senate Intelligence Committee and urging Americans to call it.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate where some Republicans are strongly opposed. Proponents, including the White House, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.
It was a remarkable escalation on Trump's part of a longstanding fixation shared by both men — with Trump supporting making daylight saving time permanent, and Cotton vociferously opposed — at a time just weeks before the midterms, when Republicans would prefer that the president focus on talking about affordability issues and the party's achievements. Cotton is also up for reelection this November, although that race is not expected to be competitive.
Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it — and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill's enactment.
"It's a lot of work for a lot of people, running around for two days, changing all the clocks in the house," Trump told reporters as his left the White House on Saturday for a rally in Vandalia, Ohio. "It discombobulates everybody," he said.
Trump said the time change gives golfers less time on the greens and tennis players less time on the courts. He blamed Cotton for stopping the bill. "So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all," Trump said on social media on Saturday morning, kicking off the fight.
Trump included a phone number with an Arkansas area code. The Associated Press called the number, but no one answered and the voicemail box was full.
Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own Saturday afternoon. He is not the only GOP senator who opposes the policy, though he has been among the most vocal opponents.
"No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton wrote. "Arkansans don't want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I'll always put Arkansas first."
Trump promptly fired back in another post. "If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn't have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so," Trump said, adding that "that is really putting Arkansas FIRST."
As his motorcade was rolling back to the White House from his golf course, Trump added that "a table full of very distinguished people just told me that they HATE, immediately after a mandatory time change, going home at night – and it's DARK."
"It's depressing!" Trump continued. "One of the gentleman stated that, 'I just hate going home in darkness.' It's also, in Crime Ridden Blue States, a lot more dangerous to be walking home in the dark!"
A 2025 poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of U.S. adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to change their clocks twice a year, while 47% oppose it and 40% are neutral.
Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill four years ago to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.
While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Trump as "unfit for office" after Trump denigrated the military service of Sen. John McCain of Arizona. Trump then released Graham's personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones.
Graham later became a close ally of Trump. In contrast, although they share many of the same policy positions, Trump and Cotton are not known to be close.
Cotton, one of the Republican Party's most prominent national security voices, has advocated for a more hawkish approach on Iran, particularly as Trump entertains pauses in military strikes amid the seven-month war. In Trump's first term, Cotton was a critic of the president's attempts at overhauling the nation's sentencing laws, calling the proposal a "jailbreak."
Earlier this year, Cotton had temporarily defied Trump's attempts at stalling the confirmation process for his own nominee for director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton. The president had wanted to ensure his interim pick for the intelligence job, Bill Pulte, would be able to serve in that role at least briefly when the former director, Tulsi Gabbard, left the job.
But the appointment of Pulte, who had no known national security credentials, drew bipartisan condemnation from Capitol Hill and Cotton had tried to expedite Clayton's confirmation process, which could have prevented Pulte from being installed as acting director.
But Trump ultimately ordered Clayton to not appear before Cotton's committee for his confirmation hearing, and Pulte served in the job for several weeks this summer. Clayton was eventually confirmed by the Senate in late July.
Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Avelumab Effective Against Merkel Cell Carcinoma in Real-World Population, Despite Frequent AEs
articles.title_zh: Avelumab Effective Against Merkel Cell Carcinoma in Real-World Population, Despite Frequent AEs
articles.content_orig:
In a real-world cohort of older patients in Austria, avelumab (Bavencio) was determined to be effective for treating Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC), despite frequent adverse events (AEs).
“ Avelumab achieved clinically meaningful outcomes in this older, less-selected routine care cohort,” said first author Magdalena Forstinger, MD, a physician-researcher with Sigmund Freud Privatuniversität and Klinik Hietzing, Vienna. “Adverse events affected treatment in some patients, underscoring the importance of careful monitoring,” she added.
Forstinger presented the findings on October 2 at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) 2026 Congress in Vienna.
In 2017, avelumab, a programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1)-blocking antibody, became the first treatment approved by the FDA for MCC. The study abstract noted, however, that evidence of the drug’s efficacy and safety in a routine clinical care context was limited, particularly among older patients, a population more likely to be immunocompromised and have comorbidities, who are underrepresented in trials.
The nationwide, multicenter, retrospective chart review included patients with inoperable locally advanced or metastatic MCC who had received at least one cycle of avelumab, with no other exclusion criteria applied, Forstinger said. A total of 49 patients were included in the study, with a median age of 81 years (range, 62-96). The most common comorbidities were cardiovascular, metabolic, oncologic, and pulmonary.
The primary endpoint was real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS). Secondary endpoints included real-world overall survival (rwOS), objective response rate (rwORR), duration of response (rwDOR), and time to response (rwTTR), and safety.
At the start of treatment, 42.9% of participants had stage IIIB MCC and 57.1% had stage IV MCC. A total of 16.3% were immunocompromised or immunosuppressed, and 77.6% had an ECOG performance status ≤ 1. Avelumab was administered as first-line monotherapy in 77.6% of cases, with 22.4% also receiving other modalities such as radiotherapy. Median follow-up was 8.9 months (range, 0-73.1).
Nearly half of evaluable patients (n=48) responded to avelumab, Forstinger said, and median rwPFS, the primary endpoint, was 10.1 months (95% CI, 1.8-18.4). The rwORR was 47.9% (95% CI, 34.5-61.7), and median rwOS was 22.9 months (95% CI, 5.0-40.8). Median rwTTR was 3.9 months (range, 1.4-12.7), and median rwDOR among responders was 19.2 months (95% CI, 8.9-29.5).
Forstinger observed that rwPFS and rwOS were in a similar range to those reported in the 2021 phase 2 JAVELIN Merkel 200 trial (which evaluated first-line avelumab in patients with metastatic MCC), although rwORR was lower. JAVELIN did not include immunocompromised patients, she added.
Overall, 71.4% of patients experienced an AE and 53.1% experienced an immune- and/or treatment-related AE, including 24.5% who had a grade ≥ 3 AE. AEs led to treatment interruption or discontinuation in 28.6% of participants, including permanent discontinuation in 12.2% of cases.
Previously reported AEs for avelumab in patients with MCC include fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, infusion-related reactions, rash, nausea, constipation , cough, and diarrhea . Potentially serious immune-mediated adverse reactions include pneumonitis, colitis , hepatitis , endocrinopathies, nephritis with renal dysfunction, and dermatologic reactions.
In a post-hoc analysis, scores of ≤ 1 on the ECOG performance status scale, which describes a patient’s level of function, were associated with lower hazard ratios (HRs) for rwPFS (HR, 0.257; 95% CI, 0.100-0.658; P = .005) and rwOS (HR, 0.157; 95% CI, 0.047-0.521; P = .002). Forstinger said these findings should be interpreted as “hypothesis-generating.”
Forstinger has reported no relevant financial relationships.
Scott Harris has covered dermatology for more than a decade. He lives near Washington, DC.

Investing.com -- The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of a FlyDubai flight to Israel used an onboard crash ax in an attempt to seize control of the aircraft, the United Arab Emirates said Saturday, according to the Wall Street Journal.

UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said the co-pilot began carrying out his plan during Wednesday's Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, attacking the captain inside the flight deck with the ax and attempting to take control of the flight controls.
The disclosure indicates the attacker likely did not need to smuggle a weapon onto the aircraft. Crash axes are carried on commercial aircraft for emergencies such as fighting fires or cutting through metal, and UAE aviation regulations require one to be stored onboard.
Al Shamsi said authorities were continuing to investigate the circumstances and motive behind the attack, including any possible links, and were examining physical and digital evidence.
The WSJ previously identified the co-pilot as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national who had been banned from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views.
Not finding the right stocks? Our AI's list of investor-grade stock picks for October just dropped »
It remains unclear whether Omani authorities communicated those concerns to FlyDubai or UAE officials before the incident.
The captain was injured during the attack, and the aircraft came close to crashing before passengers and crew members overpowered Hammami, according to the Journal's earlier reporting. The flight subsequently made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
UAE authorities are investigating the incident, which officials have described as an act of terrorism. FlyDubai suspended its Dubai-Tel Aviv service following the attack.
The earlier WSJ report said Hammami's previous ban in Oman had raised questions about aviation security procedures and the sharing of information between authorities.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a UAE presidential adviser characterized the attack as terrorism, according to the Journal.

articles.title_orig: Florida’s dengue outbreak reportedly largest US has seen in decades
articles.title_zh: Florida’s dengue outbreak reportedly largest US has seen in decades
articles.content_orig:
CDC says 392 cases of Dengue were reported for the year so far in the state, along with different county-level data
Several Florida counties recently declared a state of local emergency in response to a spate of dengue fever infections.
Hillsborough county, Florida , officials made the declaration on 24 September as health authorities recorded 134 confirmed cases of dengue fever, which is a mosquito-borne sickness typically found in countries outside the US. Officials said that the spread of the illness poses “an immediate and widespread threat to the public health, safety, and welfare of the residents and visitors of Hillsborough county”.
Controlling the tropical disease – often referred to as breakbone fever because it can cause extreme pain – requires “immediate, aggressive, and continuous” measures such as pesticide application, public education and emergency resource planning, officials said.
Dengue cases have become more common in parts of the US. In 2023, Long Beach and Pasadena reported the first ever known locally acquired cases in California.
The spread of dengue mosquitoes outside tropical and subtropical locales has even hit England, with authorities recently announcing that Aedes aegypti had been found in east London homes.
Scientists have said that global warming is poised to intensify climate-related diseases.
Declaring a local state of emergency enables Hillsborough county – whose seat is the city of Tampa – to request “any available and necessary state, federal, and local emergency funds, grants, financial assistance, and mutual aid” in their ongoing fight against mosquitoes carrying dengue. The initial declaration was put into effect for one week, but officials can extend it.
Neighboring Pasco and Pinellas counties have also declared similar states of emergency in relation to dengue reports.
The Florida department of health said in its recent report on mosquito-transmitted viruses that there were 26 cases of international travel-linked dengue reported in the state during a six-day period beginning on 13 September. There have been a total of 212 known travel-related cases in Florida reported so far in 2026.
Over the same period, there were 38 locally contracted dengue cases reported in Florida. They were among 190 cases of locally acquired dengue across Florida, the state’s health department said .
Numbers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) differ slightly. As of Monday, the CDC noted 392 cases of dengue had been reported overall in Florida for the year so far, along with different county-level data.
Dengue is contracted through the bite of some mosquito species, largely Aedes aegypti , as well as Aedes albopictus . Both species are present in Florida.
Symptoms show up between three days and two weeks after a bite from an infected mosquito. Among the symptoms are “sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain … and bleeding. Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases,” Florida’s state health department said.
The symptoms typically span four days to one week. A rarer form of the illness called dengue hemorrhagic fever can be fatal without the administration of proper supportive care, the state health department said.
Hillsborough county authorities have expressed optimism that dengue infections might slow down in the coming weeks, with zero “mosquito test pools” testing positive recently, according to the local Bay News 9 outlet.

articles.title_orig: Yan Leyfman: Real-World Outcomes After First-Line Osimertinib in EGFR-Mutant NSCLC
articles.title_zh: Yan Leyfman: Real-World Outcomes After First-Line Osimertinib in EGFR-Mutant NSCLC
articles.content_orig:
Yan Leyfman , Medical Oncologist, Co-Founder and Executive Director of MedNews Week, shared on LinkedIn :
“What happens to patients with EGFR – mutant lung cancer after first-line osimertinib stops working? The FLAURA2 trial established that adding chemotherapy to osimertinib improves overall survival in metastatic EGFR-mutant NSCLC .
But one important question remains: how much of that benefit is influenced by what happens after first-line therapy?
A retrospective study of 115 patients treated with first-line osimertinib monotherapy at a U.S. academic medical center offers a sobering real-world perspective.
Among the 66 patients who discontinued osimertinib :
The study also highlights the heterogeneity of EGFR-mutant disease.
Median time to treatment failure was:25.3 months overallBut only 15.7 months for patients with TP53-mutant tumors versus 42.2 months for TP53 wild-type disease.
That difference raises an important question about treatment strategy: If a substantial proportion of patients never receive second-line therapy, should we be thinking differently about how much treatment to deliver upfront?
The findings are strikingly similar to the FLAURA2 control arm, where only about 60% of patients received subsequent therapy.
This is an important reminder that overall survival is shaped not only by the efficacy of first-line therapy, but by the entire treatment journey-including whether patients are able to reach and tolerate subsequent lines.
The challenge now is identifying which patients are likely to benefit from treatment intensification upfront versus those who may derive sufficient benefit from osimertinib alone.
Real-world treatment patterns can reveal something clinical trials sometimes cannot: what actually happens between progression and the next treatment.”
You can also read: FLAURA2 Long-Term Safety: Toxicity Peaks Early With Osimertinib Plus Chemotherapy and Declines Over Time .

articles.title_orig: ‘The World Is Yours’: Family shapes barber scholarship in son’s memory
articles.title_zh: ‘The World Is Yours’: Family shapes barber scholarship in son’s memory
articles.content_orig:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (KCTV) - The Youth & Peace Justice Foundation launched a Fall Matching Drive to fund a barber scholarship honoring a Kansas City teen killed in February.
A foundation benefactor will match donations dollar for dollar, according to organizers. The goal is to award the first S.I.G. Legacy-Barber Scholarship to a Kansas City youth this holiday season.
Leaders said the scholarship honors Santino Israel Gonzalez , 17. He died on Feb. 21 in a shooting near College Ave. and 49th St. Five others were also wounded.
Santino dreamed of attending barber school. His family said he kept a barber chair in his room and cut hair for his father, brother and friends.
His family chose the scholarship name. They also chose its motto: “The World Is Yours. Lock In. Leave Your Spark.”
The family is also designing a T-shirt to benefit the fund, according to the Foundation. Proceeds will support the scholarship.
Organizers added that the scholarship will help a young person who wants to pursue barbering but lacks money for school. The foundation seeks individuals, businesses, community groups and sponsors to help.
Kansas City-area barbershops and barbers are especially encouraged to participate.
Donors should designate gifts for the S.I.G. Legacy-Barber Scholarship HERE .
“We can’t change what happened to Santino,” said Daniel Chapin, president of the Youth Peace & Justice Foundation. “But we can help make sure his dream doesn’t end with him. His family helped shape this scholarship around who Santino was and what he wanted to do. Now we want to see the first Kansas City youth receive that opportunity this holiday season.”
“This is about giving a young person a chance to take that first step,” Chapin added. “Santino loved barbering and wanted to make it his career. If we can help another Kansas City youth pursue that path in his memory, that’s something meaningful.”
The foundation hopes the first award starts a continuing scholarship.
The scholarship is part of a broader memorial effort. Leaders said a tree was planted for Santino in Mark Twain National Forest through the Trees for Peace program. His family received a Certificate of Planting.
The foundation also added that it is working with Kansas City on a possible location for an additional community memorial tree.

articles.title_orig: Young GeoPioneers launches in Columbia to teach kids about their world
articles.title_zh: Young GeoPioneers launches in Columbia to teach kids about their world
articles.content_orig:
COLUMBIA — Young GeoPioneers held its first free pilot event Saturday at Stephens Lake Park to teach children how to better understand the world.
The group is for ages 4 to 10 and focuses on using maps, Geographic Information Systems and satellite data to assess natural resources, the environment, the climate and the planet.
Young GeoPioneers founder Akanksha Balha said while kids are still young, this is the time to teach them answers to real-life questions.
"For example, anything about the environment, like how did the flood happen?" Balha said. "Or where did the flood water go, (or) where a hospital or a park should be located within a city so that it is good for the environment of the surroundings of the city?"
Balha has a doctorate in the application of remote sensing and GIS in urban areas and hydrology, and has been in the research field for 10 years. She said that teaching has always been a part of her work, and she loves teaching kids.
"This was a time when I felt like I want to start something of my own," Balha said. "Where I can teach kids and transfer what I know in this field to them."
Balha cited two main reasons for starting the group. She said geospatial technology is a big part of people's daily lives, and young people should be educated about it because they are the future.
"I do not want them to know about it at a later stage when they go to high school or college, but now, earlier, as they are the future generation of ours and we are in such a technology-driven world," Balha said.
Success! An email has been sent to with a link to confirm list signup.
Error! There was an error processing your request.
She also attributes starting the organization to her curious 17-month-old daughter. When she teaches her daughter about these topics, Balha feels like she pays very close attention.
Balha said she teaches the kids in an understandable and interactive way. On Saturday, the kid's activities were tailored to learn more about geoinformatics, which Balha said consists of remote sensing, satellite data and aerial imagery.
To make this understandable to kids, Balha said she printed out different bird's-eye view photos, and had the children act like birds and imagine how the bird would rise up and tilt to see the specific view.
"When it goes higher up, then how the surface will change in the dimensions, which they pick up like very easily," Balha said. "It was very interesting and easier for them to understand how things change, how the details of the dimensions change when (the) camera moves at a higher elevation, be it for a drone or a satellite."
She also had them read maps for a treasure hunt. Two groups were given a satellite photo of Stephens Lake marked with where the treasure was hidden and they had to use the map to find it.
Balha said she is currently in talks with the Daniel Boone Regional Library to start doing sessions, and she plans to start a paid pilot session at The Children's School at Stephens College.
For more information, visit Young GeoPioneers' Facebook page and Instagram . The group is working on getting a website live in the coming weeks at younggeopioneersllc.com .
