articles.title_orig: CFB World Calls Mike Tomlin for Help as Northwestern's $875M Stadium Turns Nightmare for Media
articles.title_zh: CFB World Calls Mike Tomlin for Help as Northwestern's $875M Stadium Turns Nightmare for Media
articles.content_orig:
Northwestern University finally unlocked the doors to its shiny new $875 million Ryan Field for a marquee Big Ten clash against Penn State. The school expected fans to gush over the most expensive stadium in college football history. Instead, the grand opening turned into a viral meme fest when visiting media members ran into embarrassing press box seating issues, prompting college football fans to ironically call on former NFL head coach Mike Tomlin for an architectural rescue mission.
How did a Super Bowl-winning coach end up in the middle of a college football press box debate? It all kicked off when sports journalist Joel Haas took to X to share a peek behind the scenes. What he showed was a press box crammed tightly into a narrow walkway, leaving reporters struggling to even get a clear view of the field.
"Half the press box is now standing to see the field. Others are sitting on stacks of cardboard boxes. Ugly scene here," his X post stated .
Social media users quickly jumped on the post, pointing out the sheer absurdity of a brand-new $875 million venue leaving journalists hunting for makeshift seats. One user dryly noted that while the night lights looked great, the builders clearly missed out on basic utility. "Look like the did miss on a key feature. Other than that, it looked awesome at night," a fan wrote.
Northwestern's ambitious stadium project is creating unexpected chaos. Subscribe to stay updated on how college football programs navigate infrastructure crises and leadership decisions.
Built as an intimate 35,000-seat stadium, the new Ryan Field is currently the smallest home ground in the Big Ten conference. While Northwestern intentionally cut capacity to bring fans closer to the action, the trade-off seems to have left media infrastructure on the back burner.
So how does an $875 million venue miss the mark on basic media seating? Big Ten conference guidelines require modern press boxes to provide clear sightlines and working desks for over a hundred media members. However, Northwestern's design team built Ryan Field with a primary focus on fan proximity and high-paying luxury suites.
To fit 35,000 seats and a canopy system into a tight suburban footprint, the press area got squeezed into a narrow corridor behind tinted glass. By prioritizing premium fan experience, the university accidentally left visiting journalists sitting on literal stacks of cardboard.
One fan snarkily commented, "Prioritized fans and viewing public over 'press' attendees? Well done NU! This may truly be the perfect stadium."
Amid the online roasting, fans began dropping Mike Tomlin's name. "Embarrassing. Should've had Mike Tomlin design the stadium. IYKYK," one fan wrote, triggering thousands of likes and agreeing comments. The joke took off instantly because sports fans were already obsessed with a wild piece of news Tomlin had dropped just days earlier regarding his personal hobbies.
This X user found hundreds agreeing with the light-hearted joke about Tomlin's Minecraft architectural wonders. One replied with "Unreal comment," while another said "underrated comment lol."
It did not take long for fans to bridge the gap between a college stadium design flaw and an NFL legend. Rather than calling for stadium engineers or university administrators, the internet insisted that Tomlin should take over with a video game controller in hand.
Just recently, the 54-year-old revealed his years-long project. In a 20-minute YouTube video, Tomlin opened up about his love for skyscrapers and urban planning as a preface to the world he built on Minecraft over a decade.
What started as an observation of his children using the unlimited resources to build whatever they wanted in the video game became how the family spends time together. His project started as a small, lively neighborhood of high-rise buildings around a body of water. The internet fell in love with this side of the NFL coach and now jokes about how he could use that $800 million better. Or at least the stadium could've been beta-tested.
"This easily could have been tested in Minecraft beforehand," one wrote. While explaining his project, Tomlin introduced his "boutique hotel," the first building he ever built. He also shared how he was "lighting conscious" during the construction and chose a glass ceiling whenever necessary and appropriate. His endearing attention to detail won hearts, as one commented that Tomlin wouldn't be so careless if he were in charge of the stadium.
"Mike Tomlin would never allow this," the reply said. Because Tomlin's virtual city has every detail to make the timing of this issue even funnier: his carefully planned buildings, aquarium, high-rise residences, green spaces and sports facilities are just too good to ignore. Plus, the press box is just one of the other issues.
The visiting locker room is not up to the standard either. Based on the photos shared online, fans questioned how a stadium this expensive could justify a visitor facility that looked comparatively basic. This stadium's opening is a different ballgame. The school's marching band did not perform its traditional pregame show at the inaugural game. Rather, it appeared at the Great Chicago Food Festival on the stadium grounds. This decision left fans and alumni confused.
The stadium's design was mocked by the Colorado Buffaloes, who called Ryan Field a library during their losing visit. Northwestern silenced them with a 41-7 victory, but the remark does sting, especially when a football coach's unwinding hobby is held in higher regard than your new home ground.

articles.title_orig: Bond yields are hovering near multi-year highs: What it means for your wallet
articles.title_zh: Bond yields are hovering near multi-year highs: What it means for your wallet
articles.content_orig:
Financial influencer Taylor Price joins ‘Varney & Co.’ to break down how shifting your mindset can help Americans grow wealth and achieve the American Dream.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury hit the highest level since 2002 during Thursday's trading session as higher borrowing costs impact the economy of large and impact households.
Yields on longer-dated Treasurys have risen this year amid the geopolitical uncertainty caused by the Iran war and growing federal budget deficits, tighter monetary policy and more competition in the bond market from mounting levels of corporate debt issuance due to the AI buildout.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose as high as 5.34% during Thursday's trading session, the highest level since 2002, before declining later in the day and into Friday.
Brian Therien, senior analyst at Edward Jones, told FOX Business that higher Treasury yields "may be a headwind by increasing borrowing costs for households and business," potentially causing interest rate-sensitive areas of the economy like housing and auto sales to slow despite a solid labor market and resilient consumer spending.
US ECONOMY ADDED 29,000 JOBS IN SEPTEMBER, A SLOWER PACE THAN EXPECTED
Higher Treasury yields can impact consumers through higher interest rates, though they can also boost savers and certain investments. (Getty)
"The most immediate effect is typically through adjustable-rate debt, such as credit cards, home equity lines of credit and adjustable-rate mortgages. Rates on these loans are often tied more closely to short-term benchmark rates than to longer-term rates," Therien explained.
The 10-year Treasury note is a key benchmark for the U.S. economy. Interest rates on 30-year fixed mortgages tend to move in tandem with shifts in the 10-year yield.
It also influences auto loans and fixed-rate student loans through a similar process. Therien said "consumers considering new loans should be prepared for higher rates and payments."
MORTGAGE RATES SURGE TO HIGHEST LEVEL SINCE 2023 AS BOND YIELDS SPIKE
Mortgage rates have trended higher alongside longer-term Treasury debt. (Brett Coomer/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
He added that there are some positives coming from higher interest rates when it comes to saving and investing .
" Savers and fixed-income investors earn more income. High-yield savings accounts, money market funds, CDs and bonds generally offer more attractive yields than they did earlier this year," Therien said.
"For long-term investors, higher starting yields can improve the return potential of bonds, with a larger share of the expected return coming from interest income rather than price appreciation."
FED'S FAVORED INFLATION GAUGE COOLED IN AUGUST BUT REMAINED ELEVATED
Geopolitical uncertainty caused by the Iran war's disruption of oil flows from the Strait of Hormuz has contributed to higher yields. (Giuseppe Cacace/AFP via Getty Images)
Peter C. Earle, senior director of research at the American Institute for Economic Research, told FOX Business "higher long-term yields raise businesses' financing costs as well as putting pressure on stock and existing bond prices. They also affect hiring retirement portfolios."
Earle added that "people buying Treasurys or reinvesting maturing holdings can secure higher yields, which may make it easier to generate income without taking on corporate credit risk.
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE
"But the improvement in purchasing power depends on inflation and taxes. A Treasury bond purchased today can still lose market value if yields rise further and its owner sells before maturity."
FOX Business' Sophia Compton contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Meta is building one of the world's biggest undersea cable networks
articles.title_zh: Meta is building one of the world's biggest undersea cable networks
articles.content_orig:
While data centers dominate headlines amid mounting local opposition over electricity bills, water use, and zoning fights, Meta has been expanding its infrastructure somewhere far less visible: the bottom of the ocean.
On Sept. 21, the company announced Petal , a roughly 4,300-mile subsea cable connecting the U.S. and France. Meta says the cable, expected to enter service in 2029, will be the first to deliver petabit-scale capacity across an ocean. It will carry 1 petabit per second, or about 125,000 gigabytes per second, double what today’s most advanced transoceanic cables can handle.
According to Meta, that’s enough capacity for three-quarters of the world’s population to stream music at the same time. The company says Petal achieves this with two-core fiber, which fits two light paths inside each strand. That lets Meta double capacity without a proportional increase in power or physical infrastructure.
Projects like this rarely make headlines in an industry fixated on AI models and apps, but they’re what make those products run. Meta’s personal AI agent, Muse, launched Sept. 8 and climbed to No. 1 on Apple’s U.S. App Store within two weeks, overtaking ChatGPT. It did so even as critics questioned how much access the agent needs to users’ email, calendars, and payment accounts. Muse is powered by Meta’s Muse Spark models , and products like it depend on moving enormous volumes of data between Meta’s data centers and its users around the world.
Subsea cables aren’t new territory for the company, which is now valued at roughly $1.85 trillion. Meta has spent the past decade building its presence on the seafloor and says it has invested in more than 20 subsea cable projects. Taken together, those projects touch every continent except Antarctica.
The most ambitious is Project Waterworth, announced in February 2025. Meta says the system will stretch more than 31,000 miles, longer than the Earth’s circumference. It will connect the U.S., Brazil, South Africa, India, and other regions across five continents. Some segments will be laid as deep as roughly 4.3 miles below the surface to protect them from ship anchors and other hazards.
Meta’s 2Africa system, whose core was completed last year, circles the African continent and connects to Europe, the Middle East, and South Asia. Meta says it lands in 33 countries and can reach 3 billion people.
Meta hasn’t built all of this alone. Petal is being developed with Japan’s NEC and Sumitomo Electric Industries, and French telecom Orange is handling the landing on France’s Atlantic coast. Meta has even partnered with rivals. The MAREA cable between Virginia and Spain, completed in 2017, is jointly owned with Microsoft and telecom company Telxius. Increasingly, though, Meta is taking the driver’s seat. Waterworth will be wholly owned by Meta, making it only the company’s third solely owned cable, according to telecom research firm TeleGeography.
These projects don’t come cheap. Meta hasn’t disclosed what Petal or Waterworth will cost, but TechCrunch reported before Waterworth’s announcement that the project could top $10 billion. Even so, cables are a small slice of Meta’s overall infrastructure bill. The company expects capital expenditures of $130 billion to $145 billion this year , nearly double the $72.2 billion it spent in 2025.
With 12-figure budgets and record-breaking construction projects, Meta is betting its infrastructure spending will pay off. Whether it does remains to be seen.

articles.title_orig: Clarence Thomas is in the hot seat for Supreme Court’s biggest climate case in years
articles.title_zh: Clarence Thomas is in the hot seat for Supreme Court’s biggest climate case in years
articles.content_orig:
As one of the Supreme Court’s most stalwart conservative and prolific justices, Clarence Thomas’ views on the biggest cases of the day — from guns to race to religion — are rarely in doubt.
Yet when it comes to perhaps the most significant climate change-related case to reach the high court in nearly two decades, environmentalists aren’t yet writing Thomas off, even though he has consistently sided against them.
That’s because Thomas has in recent years staked out positions that align with a Colorado city that is suing Exxon and a Canadian energy company Suncor for damages caused by climate change. The longest-serving current justice has long been skeptical of letting federal law trump state law in other areas, particularly when Congress has not clearly stated its intention to do so.
Alito recuses himself from major Supreme Court climate change case
Lawyers fighting Exxon quoted Thomas and his conservative colleague, Justice Neil Gorsuch, six times in written arguments filed with the justices over the summer. And a series of experts have filed friend-of-the-court briefs debating how Thomas will square the climate case with an opinion he wrote just five months ago rejecting the idea that federal interests could block a lawsuit filed under state law by an Army specialist severely injured in Afghanistan.
“The justices to watch here are very much Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas,” Deepak Gupta, an appellate attorney, said at a recent event hosted by the Supreme Court Institute at Georgetown Law Center. “I think they will find the lack of any textual hook for these arguments troubling.”
The Supreme Court will hear arguments Monday in the case, Suncor Energy v. Boulder, which raises enormous questions about whether big oil can be held accountable by states and cities for planet-warming pollution. Because dozens of other local governments have filed similar suits against energy companies, the court’s decision could have long-term sweeping implications for the oil and gas industry.
Thomas, a former lawyer for the agrochemical industry who was nominated by President George H.W. Bush in 1991, has in recent years opposed federal environmental regulation of wetlands , balked at government efforts to reduce power plant emissions and signed onto a Supreme Court decision that allowed San Francisco to pump more sewage into the Pacific Ocean . But the climate dispute turns on questions about whether state or federal law controls. And on that question, both Thomas and Gorsuch have often been skeptical of letting the feds take charge.
Environmentalists argue that if Thomas embraces a consistent approach, Boulder should win.
“Justices Thomas and Gorsuch have both written opinions that firmly reject the idea that federal law can shove state law out of the way based on hazy arguments about a law’s intentions or policy consequences,” said Kirti Datla, director of strategic legal advocacy at Earthjustice, an environmental group that submitted a brief in the case opposing Suncor and Exxon. “That’s what Suncor’s arguments boil down to in this case, so they should reject this move again here.”
President Donald Trump’s administration is siding with the oil companies in the dispute.
The Supreme Court agreed in February to decide the climate dispute after fossil fuel producers appealed a decision from Colorado’s highest court. The city and county seek billions of dollars in damages for fires and floods they say were caused by rising temperatures. Boulder alleges the oil companies not only contributed to those disasters but misled the public about their role in climate change.
“This litigation is not an attempt to solve climate change; it merely asks that petitioners bear their fair share of local costs incurred in part because of their tortious conduct,” Boulder told the justices.
Exxon and Suncor counter that regulating climate pollution is inherently a federal issue in part because emissions can waft across state lines. They say that intrinsic understanding preempts — or supersedes — state law. And, they argue, allowing every city in the nation to sue oil companies for damages because of climate change would lead to a chaotic patchwork of approaches to greenhouse gas emissions meant to punish companies.
“The intended effect of these lawsuits is to impose an enormous ‘carbon tax,’ in the form of billions of dollars of damages, that could ‘bankrupt’ the energy industry,” the companies allege.
Boulder counters that neither the Constitution nor the federal law make clear that federal interests should preempt state tort claims. And for a conservative Supreme Court that regularly looks to the specific words in a statute or the Constitution to decide cases, that has often been a persuasive argument in other contexts.
It is also a point that Thomas and Gorsuch have frequently made.
Every position staked out at the oral arguments Monday will be watched especially closely because Justice Samuel Alito recused himself from the case, creating the possibility of a 4-4 split. Alito told Bloomberg News in an interview that he felt it was “prudent” to recuse, given his holdings in energy stocks, but not required. The companies Alito holds are not named parties in the dispute.
An even split, a rare outcome , would uphold the decision by Colorado’s Supreme Court that allowed Boulder’s lawsuit to proceed without setting a precedent.
The justices could also find a more limited way to resolve the case by deciding that it isn’t yet fully baked for Supreme Court review. That outcome would send the case back to state courts — likely with a return ticket to the Supreme Court within a few years.
Thomas wrestled with similar themes in an unrelated decision in April.
In that under-the-radar decision, the court sided with an Army specialist who was severely injured by a suicide bomber on Bagram Air Base and was attempting to sue a military contractor for failing to supervise the Afghan employee who carried out the attack. The contractor argued that the state tort claim was preempted by the idea that running a war is an inherently federal endeavor.
Just like in the climate case, the contractor – and the dissenting justices – warned against allowing individual states to “regulate” that federal conduct.
Writing for a 6-3 majority , Thomas shut down that argument.
Trump has stacked up ‘emergency’ wins at the Supreme Court
“There is no federal preemption in vacuo, without a constitutional text or a federal statute to assert it,” the conservative justice wrote, quoting earlier opinions and pressing the Latin term for “in a vacuum” into service. The contractor, Thomas wrote, “has not identified any provision of law expressly preempting” the suit from the soldier, Winston Hencely.
Boulder cites the case four times in its latest brief, including in the second paragraph.
Another cornerstone majority opinion in the case — written by Gorsuch and joined by Thomas — dealt with Virginia’s ban on mining uranium . Minerals companies argued the ban was preempted by the federal Atomic Energy Act, but the Supreme Court rejected that pitch in a 2019 decision.
“Invoking some brooding federal interest or appealing to a judicial policy preference should never be enough to win preemption of a state law,” Gorsuch wrote. “A litigant must point specifically to ‘a constitutional text or a federal statute’ that does the displacing or conflicts with state law.”
John Yoo, a law professor at the University of California, Berkeley, told CNN that the views expressed by Thomas and Gorsuch are “standard preemption doctrine,” because they speak to the idea that for federal law to win out it must be rooted in something .
“The question is how to divine whether the Framers or Congress wanted that preemption to be used over an issue area or in a specific case,” said Yoo, a former Thomas clerk who co-authored a brief in the case supporting Exxon’s position. One of those areas, he noted, has traditionally been understood to include foreign policy

articles.title_orig: Plainville bookstore gets a visit from “Ordinary People Change the World” author
articles.title_zh: Plainville bookstore gets a visit from “Ordinary People Change the World” author
articles.content_orig:
In 2014, bestselling author Brad Meltzer and illustrator Christopher Eliopoulos published the first book in their “Ordinary People Change the World” series, “I Am Amelia Earhart.” That was 12 years ago, and next week, the two will unveil their 40th book in the series, called “We Are the Wright Brothers.” On Tuesday, Oct. 6, they head to the tiny Massachusetts town of Plainville, where there’s a popular bookstore called An Unlikely Story Bookstore and Cafe. Meltzer returned to GBH’s Henry in the Hub . The following interview is slighted editing for clarity.
Henry Santoro: The Wright Brothers captivated your interest a long time ago, right?
Brad Meltzer: These brothers are the reason why we have this series, because when my son was born 24 years ago, my friend Simon Sinek told me this amazing story about the Wright brothers. And every time the Wright brothers would go out to fly their plane, they would bring enough extra materials for multiple crashes. Which means every time they went out, they knew they would fail and they would crash and rebuild and crash and rebuild. And that’s why they took off. And I love that story. I wanted my sons to hear that story. I wanted my daughter to hear that story. I wanted everyone to know if you dream big and you work hard and you have a good side order of stubbornness, you can do anything in this world. And that’s why I started writing these kids’ books. And the Ordinary People Change the World series was built out of that first story. And here we are finally in the 40th book, getting to tell their story.
Santoro: Did you ever fathom 40 books coming out?
Meltzer: The crazy part is, and this will show you what a lunatic I am, yes. Because when I went to sell the books and I went to the publisher, they said, “Oh, how cute, you want to give your kids better heroes to look up to with two books — ”I’m Amelia Earhart“ and ”I’m Abraham Lincoln.“ And I looked them straight in the face in that very first meeting and I said, ”I have no interest in writing just two books. I want to write 100.“ I said, ”I want to build a library so people can teach their kids lessons of kindness and perseverance.“ And to their credit, they didn’t laugh me out of the room. I’m slow, but I’m determined.
Santoro: But you also write everything. You’re writing comic books, you write thrillers, you write college speeches. I mean, you’re just a writing machine.
Meltzer: Well, you know, what I am — I wish I was as fast as I could be, but what I am is I’m a passion machine.
Santoro: The book pub date is Tuesday, Oct. 6 and that’s also the day that you and your illustrator, Christopher Eliopoulos, will be in the little town of Plainville, Massachusetts, at a very popular bookstore called An Unlikely Story Bookstore. And that bookstore is owned by a very dear friend of yours who goes by the name of Jeff Kinney.
Meltzer: Yes. He is my wimpy kid brother. I have to say of all my friends in the entire publishing community, Jeff is my closest friend. And always has been. We’ve traveled to Africa together to find water wells for kids that have no fresh water. My kids have traveled with him. My wife has traveled with him there. I’ve traveled with his whole family there. And for years now, we’ve been to the White House together for the Easter Egg Roll. We’ve been to the White House together for trick-or-treating together when they invited us to read stories. And no one loves giving more than Jeff Kinney and I do. When you come to see us at his beautiful bookstore, which I’ve been to before, you will see us talking. You will see us laughing, but you will also be seeing us try to embarrass each other in a contest of champions.
Santoro: Thank you Brad. For ticket information, visit the website of “An Unlikely Story” in Plainville. I’m Henry in the Hub , and this is GBH.
You are leaving gbh.org and going to a web page that is not owned by GBH. If you are streaming, your experience will be interrupted.

articles.content_orig:
Botanical societies of both countries sign joint plant science cooperation initiative in China’s Taian to tackle pressing global challenges
The joint initiative was signed during a Sino-American botany conference last month in Taian, in China’s eastern Shandong province, which brought together hundreds of experts from institutions in both countries.
The conference, held from September 19 to 23, aimed to “further deepen botanical exchange and cooperation between China and the United States and to establish an international platform that fosters interdisciplinary integration in plant science”, according to the Botanical Society of China.
Topics such as conservation, plant biotechnology, climate change and an international plant megaproject were discussed, the China Science Daily reported.

articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping unwell? Chinese officials sought unusual long breaks during the US visit
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping unwell? Chinese officials sought unusual long breaks during the US visit
articles.content_orig:
By STEPHEN M. LEPORE, US SENIOR REPORTER
Published: 01:42 EDT, 3 October 2026 | Updated: 04:26 EDT, 3 October 2026
Donald Trump went to great lengths to accommodate Chinese leader Xi Jinping due to alleged physical troubles and lack of stamina during his visit to Washington, according to a new report.
The President appeared to get along famously with the Communist Chinese leader during his time in DC , which included a glamorous State Dinner for the leader and his wife, Peng Liyuan.
But it has now emerged that behind the scenes a string of unusual requests by President Xi, 73, drained valuable time from the summit, Wall Street Journal reported.
The accommodations reportedly centered around the premier's need for rest and his physical problems amid rampant speculation about his health .
Those familiar with the planning of the summit said his aides largely built the schedule around how much Xi could physically stand and walk and when he would need breaks.
Chinese officials also reportedly asked for Xi to be given a private 'hold room' in the West Wing for him to take rest breaks between events where only his wife was allowed to stay with him.
The room request was described by former senior China director at the National Security Council Dennis Wilder as 'unusual' and completely unprecedented.
Xi's need for rest forced the cancelation of a working lunch with Trump on September 24 that left them with a five-hour void in his two-day visit.
Donald Trump's White House went to great lengths to accommodate Chinese leader Xi Jinping's alleged physical troubles and lack of stamina during his visit to Washington, according to a new report
The President threw a glamorous State Dinner for the leader and his wife, Peng Liyuan, however it has since emerged Xi had a number of 'unusual' requests during his stay reportedly centered around his health needs
Trump and Xi previously held a similar meeting when the President visited Beijing this past May.
Xi also did nothing outside the working summit on the evening he arrived and zoomed through a trip to the National Archives in ten minutes, despite US officials preparing for a longer stay.
Eagle-eyed viewers watching his descent from his plane on arrival in DC were quick to point out that he appeared to tightly clutch his wife's hand, as if needing extra support on the stairs.
The Daily Mail has reached out to the White House and a spokesperson for President Xi for comment.
It is not the first time the Chinese leader has been dogged by rumors about his health, with many speculating over the years that he has suffered a heart attack, been diagnosed with cancer and survived a stroke .
Last month during the BRICS summit, conspiracy theories spread after a video appeared to show Indian PM Narendra Modi pause a speech to check on the wellbeing of his Chinese counterpart.
The footage shows Modi stopping his opening speech at the BRICS summit and turning towards President Xi after a commotion appeared to catch his attention.
'Is it okay?' Modi repeatedly asks the translator accompanying the Chinese leader, as several people appearing to be aides or members of staff are seen rushing towards him.
Viewers watching his descent from his plane on arrival in DC were quick to point out that he appeared to tightly clutch his wife's hand, as if needing extra support on the stairs
Xi has been fending off speculation about his health since before his presidency
Later in the day, President Xi skipped the gala dinner hosted by Modi for leaders of the BRICS nations – where ally Vladimir Putin was also in attendance – spurring commentary about his ill health.
It later emerged that the exchange at the summit was because Xi's translator earpiece had broken.
However, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal, he skipped the gala because he was unwell, with Foreign Minister Wang Yi attending in his place.
Theories previously reached a peak in 2012, after President Xi mysteriously disappeared for two weeks when he was still the country's vice-president – fueling rumors he had potentially been the subject of an attempted assassination.
In July 2024, a photo of the Chinese leader supposedly wincing in pain went viral on social media, with people claiming that he had suffered a stroke.
It turned out the image was taken from four months before, and the Chinese president was merely reacting to something he had drunk while at the National People's Congress.
In September 2025, a hot mic caught Putin discussing immortality during a summit with President Xi and Kim Jong Un in Beijing to celebrate the 80th anniversary of the end of the Second World War .
The pair were heard chatting about the possibility of achieving immortality with organ transplants and advanced medical procedures.
President Trump and First Lady Melania, welcome China President XI Jinping and his wife, First Lady Peng Liyuan to the White House for an Official State Arrival
Even before Xi became president, his health was a popular topic of speculation in the country, particularly among critics of the communist regime.
This is despite the fact that the high level of internet censorship in China means that anything deemed a criticism of President Xi or the Chinese Communist Party is blocked or immediately removed .
Leaders' health is typically considered a state secret in China.
Trump pulled out all the stops for his visit with Xi as the two spent much of his time discussing the toughest issues facing their nations.
The dramatic spectacle began the moment the Chinese president and his wife touched down at Joint Base Andrews.
As the leaders stood on the tarmac alongside rows of soldiers positioned in front of F-35 fighter jets and Air Force One, a screaming flyover shattered the air overhead.
The deafening roar caught Trump off guard, causing him to visibly wince while a stoic, stone-faced Xi didn't even flinch.
Breaking more than a decade of presidential protocol , the Trumps personally greeted the Chinese delegation on the tarmac – marking the first time a sitting US president has met a foreign leader at an airport in over 11 years.
What do you make of reports that Xi Jinping's schedule was adapted to allow extra rest during his US visit?
Thursday night's lavish black-tie State Dinner in the historic East Room of the White House stands as one of the most star-studded evenings of the administration, offering a glitzy opportunity to smooth over notoriously fierce geopolitical friction with the Asian superpower
Accommodations allegedly included a separate room in the West Wing where Xi could rest which was only accessible to his wife
A grinning Trump also celebrated an immediate PR win when Xi announced Beijing is sending two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, to Zoo Atlanta within days, continuing the famous 'panda diplomacy' tradition sparked by Richard Nixon's 1972 trip.
That was followed by the State Dinner, a lavish black-tie affair in the historic East Room that stands as one of the most star-studded evenings of the administration, offering a glitzy opportunity to smooth over notoriously fierce geopolitical friction with the superpower.
Trump heaped praise on Xi, with whom he says he has developed a 'truly great friendship' over his decade in politics .
However, the two nations remain divided on the war in Iran and are still grappling to find common ground on trade and how to best navigate the jarring advances of artificial intelligence .
Trump had made clear he wanted to impress Xi with the visit.
The Republican President made sure construction of a new helicopter landing pad on the White House’s South Lawn was completed before the visit and he met Xi and his wife on Wednesday evening when they flew into Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.
The Daily Mail contacted Xi's office for comment.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk’s longtime partner Shivon Zilis announces he ended relationship with ‘no warning’
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk’s longtime partner Shivon Zilis announces he ended relationship with ‘no warning’
articles.content_orig:
By DANA KENNEDY, SENIOR INVESTIGATIVE REPORTER and EMILY CRANE
Published: 12:02 EDT, 2 October 2026 | Updated: 04:11 EDT, 3 October 2026
Elon Musk 's longtime love and baby mama Shivon Zilis has revealed the billionaire abruptly ended their relationship 'with no warning' - with the mom-of-four declaring 'it’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week.'
'Hurting' Zilis, an executive at Musk’s brain implant startup Neuralink, poured her heart out in a lengthy X post on Friday - just hours after eagle-eyed social media users noticed the billionaire had stopped following her on the platform he owns.
'I’ve loved him more than life itself and he’s taught me 100 lifetimes of knowledge and made my cup overflow with life meaning, so there is a lot of loss, but luckily we created four beautiful little loves of my life,' Zilis, 40, wrote on X.
'I am so beyond grateful for our children and they make every single day the best day of my life! I do hope and pray he and I can be great friends and coparents.'
Zilis, who is believed to have first embarked on a secret tryst with the Space X founder back in 2016, went on to describe Musk as a 'tortured soul.'
'I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness,' she wrote.
'I loved being that counterbalancing place of safety, sense of calm, and love - and delighted in bringing a smile back to his face when he was down. I will miss him dearly.'
Zilis - the mother of four of Musk's 14 kids - hinted, too, that she was blindsided by the breakup - sharing a screenshot of loved-up text messages the pair had exchanged just last week.
Elon Musk's longtime love and baby mama Shivon Zilis revealed on Friday the billionaire abruptly ended their relationship 'with no warning.' The couple are pictured back in February
Zilis and Musk have four children together, including twins Strider and Azure, who were born by IVF in November 2021
'It was really wonderful to see you for breakfast. Love you very much,' Zilis texted Musk.
'Love you too. I didn't realize that this Xi dinner included significant other (Beijing one did not) or I would have invited you,' he responded on September 24, referencing the White House state dinner for the Chinese president. Zilis replied: 'Aw, that means so much to me. Thank you.'
Musk, 55, hasn't yet commented on the breakup.
Zilis ended her post by saying: 'I’m hurting, but care deeply about E and will always be cheering for his happiness. God speed, Elon, the world is lucky to have you.'
The first apparent sign of trouble in the couple's romance came back on September 28 when Zilis had posted a cryptic message on social media: 'New day, new life.'
Then, earlier on Friday, Big Tech Alert, an account that tracks the online activity of technology figures, flagged that Musk had unfollowed her.
The Tesla founder only follows around 1,400 accounts.
News of the shock split comes just months after Zilis - who is one of four women Musk has children with - took the stand as a key witness in the Space X founder’s case against OpenAI earlier this year.
Should people in high-profile relationships handle breakups privately or share their pain publicly?
Zilis, who is the mother of four of Musk's 14 kids, hinted she was blindsided by the breakup - sharing a screenshot of loved-up text messages the pair had exchanged just last week
Zilis, who is the mother of four of Musk's 14 kids, hinted she was blindsided by the breakup. They are pictured in February last year meeting Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Washington, DC
Zilis and Musk, pictured with their eldest children, embarked on a romantic relationship in 2016. When Zilis decided she wanted to have kids as a single mom, Musk 'offered to make a donation' as a platonic sperm donor towards the end of 2020
It was during her testimony that key details about their once-secret romance were laid bare.
Zilis, who was born in Ontario, Canada and studied at Yale University, had first met Musk through OpenAI - the artificial intelligence lab he co-founded in 2015.
She testified that their relationship began as 'a one-off' at a corporate off-site event - but later turned romantic around 2016.
Zilis told the jury that when she decided to have children as a single mom, Musk 'offered to make a donation' as a platonic sperm donor towards the end of 2020.
Their twins, Strider and Azure, were born by IVF in November 2021. News of their third child, Arcadia, surfaced in June 2024. And their son, Seldon Lycurgus, followed in February 2025.
Zilis testified that she lives in a house in Austin, Texas where Musk often stays when he visits their children.
Zilis and Musk have brought their children to various White House events  in recent years. They are pictured in February 2025
Musk, for his part, called Zilis his 'partner' when it was his turn to testify.
The couple were spotted holding hands as they arrived at the wedding of White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate back in February.
Prior to becoming director of operations and special projects at Neuralink, Zilis had previously worked as a project director on Tesla's Autopilot team from 2017 to 2019.
In the wake of their split, it wasn't immediately clear whether Zilis would keep her roles at Neuralink and Musk's other companies.
The Daily Mail has reached out to Zilis and Musk.

articles.title_orig: Cornell Case Revives Anger About Handling of Campus Sexual Assault Cases
articles.title_zh: Cornell Case Revives Anger About Handling of Campus Sexual Assault Cases
articles.content_orig:
Get the best experience and stay connected to your community with our Spectrum News app. Learn More
An intense, public outcry over a woman's account of being gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity house prompted New York's governor this week to angrily yank control of the investigation away from the local prosecutor who didn't initially see what happened as a crime.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said Cornell police omitted key information that could have affected his decision whether or not to pursue criminal charges.
Now, the task of unraveling the case will fall to the state's attorney general, Letitia James, who was appointed as a special prosecutor .
James, a Democrat best known for tangling with President Donald Trump, suggested at a news conference Friday that her investigation wouldn't be rushed. She described it as a monthslong process, with no predetermined outcome.
Here’s what we know and don’t know about the woman's allegations and the investigations that followed:
The woman sued Cornell and seven former students last month, alleging she was given ketamine and became completely incapacitated while members of the Chi Phi fraternity sexually assaulted her at their campus residence in October 2024.
She reported the alleged assault to campus police about three weeks later, giving investigators a detailed account over two days. She also spoke with Cornell’s disciplinary investigators.
But Van Houten quickly declined to pursue charges or further investigation after reviewing a police summary of her interview.
After the victim filed her civil suit, Van Houten said it contained allegations he had never seen. He contended Cornell’s police had withheld key information, including a transcript of the woman’s interview where she explicitly said she was “100% confident” she was raped.
Van Houten said the materials suggested she had consented to some sex with multiple men, hadn't been forced into other acts, and was intoxicated, but not to the point of helplessness.
Under New York law, being too drunk or high to consent to sex isn’t necessarily enough to support a rape charge. The law distinguishes that from being physically helpless or incapacitated by drugs administered without consent.
Van Houten later reopened the investigation. “Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” he said.
Only a fraction of the evidence collected by the school has become public, but the portions that have provided a fuller — though disputed — timeline of events, as well as a glimpse at how the men responded to being accused.
According to the records, the woman had been invited to the fraternity by a member for whom she had long held strong romantic feelings. Cornell's disciplinary panel found that she initially consented to sex with that man and one of his friends, though she later alleged in her lawsuit that she had been pressured into taking drugs and alcohol and was too intoxicated to consent.
Later, other men started coming into the room, some drawn by a message one of the fraternity brothers sent to a Snapchat group at 1:42 a.m. using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman’s body was freely available.
The woman told investigators that her intoxication had rendered her partly defenseless. She said some of the men inhaled drugs off her unclothed body.
“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in,” she told investigators.
The records also show that she acknowledged that her memory of the night was spotty, due to her extreme inebriation, and had verbally acquiesced to some acts she later felt were sexual abuse.
Some of the accused men disputed her account when speaking to investigators, or said that the drug use and sexual activity were consensual.
Cornell hasn’t detailed the results of its investigation, but said it resulted in some students being expelled. The records show it also cleared at least some of the men of sexual assault allegations.
Hochul said she appointed James because she had lost faith in Van Houten's handling of the case. She said Van Houten should have asked Cornell for more information and interviewed the woman before closing it.
“This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable,” she said. “And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”
Van Houten said he supports James’ appointment but maintains that New York law didn’t allow him to prosecute based solely on the woman’s allegations that she was too incapacitated to consent.
At a Cornell Student Assembly meeting Thursday, students and other members of the university community spent more than 2 1/2 hours discussing the handling of sexual assault allegations. Some expressed fear, anger, and grief — while others shared their own experiences of sexual violence on campus.
Among them was Jane Wang, who said she had reported being sexually assaulted at Cornell a year earlier.
When she filed her Title IX case in the midst of “mental, physical and emotional recovery from the assault,” she said, “I was also met with an abundance of paperwork, very little instruction on how to navigate it and no follow-up from our Title IX office of an outcome.”
The presidents of every fraternity in Cornell’s Interfraternity Council voted unanimously to cancel social events this weekend in response to the allegations, according to The Cornell Daily Sun. Twenty student organizations are also planning a protest Monday calling for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case and changes to its sexual assault policies, the newspaper reported.
The case has also renewed scrutiny of a New York sexual assault law that makes it more difficult to prosecute cases involving people too intoxicated to consent. New York is one of 19 states with such laws .
Hochul said Friday that she supports changing the law.

articles.title_orig: Two Gators Headed to Rotterdam for World Championships
articles.title_zh: Two Gators Headed to Rotterdam for World Championships
articles.content_orig:
Florida will have two athletes representing gymnastics program at the 2026 Artistic Gymnastics World Championships later this month, set for Oct. 17-25 in Rotterdam, Netherlands.
On the five-woman roster for the U.S. World Team is Skye Blakely. Backing her up as the team’s traveling replacement athlete is Florida signee Dulcy Caylor.
Blakely has already seen the world stage three times. Her first appearance in 2022 ended in gold for the U.S. and a fifth place finish for her on the balance beam. In 2023, she saw the same success for the team as a whole, and 2025 led her to fourth place on the uneven bars.
Caylor is in a unique position. She signed for the Gators but deferred her enrollment until fall 2028 to train for the 2028 Olympic Games.
Like Blakely, Caylor has been at the World Championships before this year. In 2025, she competed in all-around, balance beam and floor exercise, placing sixth on floor and eighth on beam.
To get the bid for the World Championships, the U.S. athletes first had to compete in selection events Wednesday and Thursday.
Day one welcomes two athletes to the team based 60% on the selection event and 40% on their combined championships results. These spots were given to Claire Pease and Charleigh Bullock.
Day two fills the leftover three positions. The athletes are allowed to compete in up to two categories for their selection consideration. Blakely competed in bars and beam, earning a 14.40 and 13.25, respectively. Caylor had a 13.25 on beam and a 13.15 on floor.
Gator gymnast Simone Rose was also vying for a spot on the team, but her 12.95 on bars and 13.65 on beam did not get her on the final roster.
The committee named Blakely, Reese Esponda and Hezly Rivera for the remaining spots. Caylor was named traveling alternate and Jade Carey was named non-traveling alternate.
With her bid, Blakely is now the only 2026 team member to have competed at the World Championships as a collegiate athlete twice.
The University of Florida is making history of its own at the competition as well. It is now the only NCAA program with a gymnast on the last three U.S. World Championship teams. Former Gator Leanne Wong competed in 2022, 2023 and 2025, and Kayla DiCello also was a replacement athlete for the 2023 team. Blakely finished the trifecta with her bid this year.
With the roster set, Blakely and the U.S. will open the championships with Women’s Team Qualifications on Oct. 18. The Women’s Team Final follows Oct. 21, with the finals for the individual events set for Oct. 23-25.

articles.title_orig: The Supreme Court faces another term jam-packed with controversy
articles.title_zh: The Supreme Court faces another term jam-packed with controversy
articles.content_orig:
Broadcast journalists work in front of the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 15. The new term begins on Monday. Roberto Schmidt/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The U.S. Supreme Court formally opens a new term on Monday, with big test cases on religion, bans on semi-automatic weapons, climate change, immigration and — waiting in the wings — election law cases.
It used to be that the first Monday in October marked the beginning of a new Supreme Court term. And that's still true, technically. But for all practical purposes, the formerly quiet summer months after the court finishes its opinions in all argued cases no longer exists.
Indeed, as Georgetown University law professor Stephen Vladeck observes, the number of emergency appeals has ballooned during the Trump administration, while at the same time, fully briefed and argued cases have dropped precipitously over the years.
"So now we have twice as many full court rulings on emergency applications as we have on the merits docket," Vladeck observes, adding, "That is a very new phenomenon."
The difference is that decisions on the emergency docket are rendered quickly, with little briefing, no oral arguments, and ultimately little or no explanation of the ruling. In contrast, a decision on the merits is typically worked on for months after full briefing and lengthy oral arguments.
Of late, the court seems to be making an effort to offer some limited explanations of its emergency docket rulings, but lower court judges, both liberal and conservative, complain that isn't enough to provide them with adequate guidance. And the Trump administration often takes what used to be the rare step of getting to the Supreme Court by leapfrogging over lower appellate courts that the administration views as hostile.
With that backdrop, here are the cases the court will be hearing in the coming weeks:
The opening case, to be argued Monday, tests whether state and local governments can sue energy companies for allegedly deceiving the public about the damaging effects of fossil fuels.
"The theory is that the energy company defendants deceived the public for many years," says Deepak Gupta, who teaches at Harvard Law School and practices law in Washington, D.C. What the companies were telling the public for years, he says, is "the opposite of what the company's own scientists knew, and the local cost of that deception."
That said, however, most court observers see the case as an uphill battle for environmentalists.
Perhaps the biggest case of the term so far, in terms of ripple effects, involves religion, a subject on which the court's conservative super majority has dramatically changed its legal doctrine. Indeed for the better part of a century, the Supreme Court emphasized the First Amendment's separation of church and state, with the free exercise of religion playing an important — but secondary — role. Since President Trump's appointment of three new justices, however, things have changed.
"It's literally the opposite of what the law was not that long ago, and it's just a complete shift," observes Michigan State University law professor Frank Ravitch.
The court may, in fact, be on the verge of requiring taxpayers to fund religious schools that refuse to admit LGBTQ students and parents. Last term the justices deadlocked on the issue in a separate case after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself because of a conflict. The 4-4 tie vote automatically left in place an Oklahoma Supreme Court decision that barred overtly religious charter schools from from being funded by the taxpayers. But this year the issue is back in a case from Colorado. The case centers on a state law that provides universal preschool programs that are open to all students, regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation or gender identity.
St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colo., wants the state funding guaranteed in the state's universal pre-k law. But it doesn't want to admit LGBTQ students or students with gay or trans parents. The parish maintains such admissions would violate church's right to the free exercise of religion. The state counters that funding the church school would violate the state's anti-discrimination law.
The court's conservative majority has, in multiple cases, ruled in favor of religious exemptions from generally applicable laws. Until now, however, the court has never said that religious schools are entitled to full taxpayer funding. But given the current court's views, and with Justice Barrett participating in the Colorado case, taxpayers could well end up having to fund religious schools in Colorado and elsewhere.
Bans on semi-automatic weapons
In December the court will hear a case testing whether state and local governments violate the Second Amendment right to bear arms when they ban semi-automatic weapons, like the AR-15.
Former Solicitor General Don Verrilli Jr., articulates two different ways to look at the question.
On the one hand the AR-15 "can deliver upwards of 100 bullets per minute" without any enhancements, and 500 bullets per minute with various enhancements. On the other hand, he notes that millions of Americans own AR-15s, "and it would be quite disruptive to suggest all these Americans ... would be dispossessed of their weapons."
Lawyer Erin Murphy, who has litigated lots of cases on behalf of gun owners, says the "single most important question is who gets to decide what guns you have," and he argues it makes no sense to say, "You've got this right against the government, but the government decides which arms you can get."
The Trump administration has repeatedly taken positions in immigration cases that no other administration has adopted. Most recently, the court announced it would hear arguments and decide a case testing whether the Department of Homeland Security may deport migrants to so-called "third countries," when their countries of origin refuse to accept them. Since Trump began his second term, his administration has deported thousands of people to third world countries where they have no connections, may not speak the language, have often been jailed and allegedly subject to torture. The court has twice blocked lower court decisions that prevented the third country policy, and now the justices have said they will hear arguments about the policy in December.
In a second immigration case, the issue is the Trump administration's policy of detaining undocumented immigrants without a bond hearing, regardless of how long they have been in the U.S.
Possible cases: The 10 commandments and much more
There are many more cases waiting in the wings that the justices may take up. Among them is a case that seeks to reverse a nearly half-century-old Supreme Court precedent; it bars public schools from posting the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms. Now, however, Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana and Alabama have passed laws that conflict with the Supreme Court's 1980 ruling, and the lower courts are split on the question. That split all but guarantees the the Supreme Court will revisit the question.
Another case that could to make it to the court this term tests whether states can regulate Kalshi, the $40 billion prediction market behemoth that has sports fans betting on everything from the next pitch to the point spread or at the other end of the spectrum, betting on the outcome of Supreme Court cases.
And then there are cases that the Trump administration has slow-walked for close to two years, after quickly losing in the lower courts. Prime examples are the administration's attempt to deny medical research grants to Harvard University, and other attempts to deny security clearances to law firms, as well as seeking money damages from law firms Trump views as hostile. Earlier this year the Justice Department told a federal court in Washington that it was dropping the law firm cases. But the next day it went back to court to reverse course.

articles.title_orig: America Wants to Make More Generic Drugs. India Shows Why That’s Hard.
articles.title_zh: America Wants to Make More Generic Drugs. India Shows Why That’s Hard.
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s order to levy 100% tariffs on certain patented pharmaceutical products and ingredients takes effect on Tuesday.
But experts question the extent to which the move will achieve its goal of spurring more drug manufacturing in the US. That’s because the burden will fall most heavily on small and midsize companies that generally don’t have the wherewithal to shift or expand production in America.
Instead, experts say, the tariffs could force these drugmakers to close or merge with larger rivals, which could in turn reduce the number of medications that they provide to patients and could lead to higher prices – which is the last thing Trump says he wants.
What’s more, the tariffs could dampen the discovery of new medicines since these smaller firms tend to be more innovative, some experts argue.
The tariffs were announced in April, but the president had long signaled that he would target the industry, which had largely escaped such levies for decades due to a longstanding international agreement designed to keep essential medicines flowing freely across borders.
However, there are many provisions and exceptions that will limit the tariffs’ impact. Notably, the levies won’t apply to the larger pharma companies that have signed “Most Favored Nation” agreements. These manufacturers have promised to beef up their domestic production, as well as provide their medicines at lower prices to Medicaid and TrumpRx , the administration’s direct-to-consumer clearinghouse. They make the vast majority of brand-name drugs.
Also, generic medications, orphan drugs for rare diseases and certain specialty medicines are largely exempt. Patented pharmaceutical products from the European Union , Switzerland, Japan and South Korea, which have existing bilateral trade deals, will be subject to a 15% tariff rate, while those from the United Kingdom will not be subject to the levies. And companies that have an agreement to produce more in the US will face a 20% tariff.
That leaves a small share of pharmaceutical manufacturers and their products that will be subject to the 100% tariff rate, industry analysts said when the levies were unveiled.
There are more than 100 drugmakers that make at least one drug that is not exempt, according to a preliminary analysis from the Brookings Institution. A majority of these companies do not have any production facilities – instead, they use contract manufacturers to make their medications, said Marta Wosinska, a senior fellow at Brookings.
There is a “crazy level” of competition for contract manufacturing capacity in the US, so it would be very expensive for these drugmakers to make more of their products domestically, she told CNN.
“Their pockets are not as deep,” she said of the smaller companies.
Many may have no choice but to sell themselves to larger players in the industry if they can’t negotiate deals with the White House, Wosinska said.
‘Voters are like, No thanks’: Trump’s tariffs fall flat with the working class
Patients with conditions that aren’t treated by major pharmaceutical manufacturers could feel the biggest impact since they often depend on medications made by smaller companies. The prices of these medicines will likely rise, said Mollie Sitkowski, an international trade lawyer with Faegre Drinker. Plus, she expects there will be fewer new drugs released in coming years.
The Biotechnology Innovation Organization, which represents smaller and mid-sized drugmakers, wrote to the Commerce Department earlier this month warning that “tariffs that punish U.S. innovators are counterproductive and risk slowing the investment and innovation needed to be successful.”
“The reality is that tariffs on America’s medicines will raise costs, impede domestic manufacturing, and divert scarce resources away from research and development critical to maintaining American biotech leadership,” wrote John Crowley, BIO’s CEO.

articles.title_orig: Dad with MS targets half marathon world record
articles.title_zh: Dad with MS targets half marathon world record
articles.content_orig:
A man from Liverpool has set himself the challenge of breaking a Guinness World Record for the fastest half marathon run by a man with multiple sclerosis (MS).
Father-of-two David Price, 42, was diagnosed with MS in 2018 after starting to struggle with his balance and peripheral vision.
Eight years on, Price is preparing to attempt the record at the Manchester Half Marathon, but admits to feeling nervous.
The current record is held by Chris White, who achieved a time of 1 hour 30 minutes and 46 seconds in Brighton in March this year.
"It would mean the world to me to break the record," David said. "I'm not underestimating how much of a challenge it will be, but it would be absolutely fantastic."
David, who works in IT, said his symptoms of MS first became noticeable in the office.
"I was stumbling around the office and knocking things off desks. My peripheral vision and senses had gone a little bit strange and weird," he said, adding that he also "started to get tingling arms and legs."
David described his diagnosis of MS as a "shock to the system", and something that took a long time to come to terms with.
"Me and the wife didn't have a clue what multiple sclerosis was," David recalled.
"It took me about three years to accept I had this long-term disability."
Despite medication, life has its daily challenges.
"You will have times where your cognitive functions aren't quite right or your thought process isn't quite where it should be.
"Like when you try to speak. You know what you want to say, but you struggle to get it out."
In 2021, David started to run and lift weights, something he said brought out a "remarkable" change in him.
"I never looked back from that point," he said. "I changed my mindset."
Training for Sunday's race, David said he has been listening to his body closely.
"I've got to accept that just because it's on the training plan, doesn't mean it has to be done.
"I've got to be big enough to say I'm not capable of doing that today - I need to take a rest day.'"
He said he wanted to attempt the world record to show others that setting high goals is possible.
"I'm not defined by MS," he said.
"And MS doesn't define me."
The Manchester Half Marathon takes place on Sunday 4 October.

articles.title_orig: Google AI Plus and free users are losing access to Gemini models, and it's happening very soon
articles.title_zh: Google AI Plus and free users are losing access to Gemini models, and it's happening very soon
articles.content_orig:
About three months ago, Google offered me a deal on the Plus subscription tier: a ~75% discount for three months. It was a really good deal for more storage, more Gemini usage, and, most importantly for me, access to the Gemini Pro model.
Unfortunately, Google has seemingly decided that the Plus subscription tier is too much of a good thing, as it's losing Pro access later this month alongside a restriction to the free tier.
I first noticed this when I headed over to Google Gemini on the web. A notification popped up, informing me that I was losing access to the Google Gemini Pro model in the coming weeks. Clicking the included link took me to a page titled "Changes to Gemini model access and limits," which detailed what's happening later in October.
On October 9th, free users will lose access to Flash, meaning they'll only have Flash-Lite. Meanwhile, the Google AI Plus subscription tier will lose the Pro model, but they'll still have Flash-Lite and Flash at their disposal. Google says Plus subscribers will receive an email detailing when they'll lose access to Pro. Every other subscription tier will see no changes.
Here's the chart Google supplied to visualize the changes better:
Of course, if you use Google AI Plus, you still keep all the storage benefits and access to Flash, but I must admit that the Pro model was a big reason why I kept my subscription. Maybe it's time I checked out what the rivals are doing .

articles.title_orig: America’s data center fight is a preview of what's to come for the rest of the world
articles.title_zh: America’s data center fight is a preview of what's to come for the rest of the world
articles.content_orig:
As the AI boom becomes a major part of political debate, the public backlash against data centers in the U.S. is spreading to Europe and Asia — raising risks for investors.
Across the Atlantic, negative sentiment is growing in Europe, which has more at stake due to its densely populated countries and higher electricity prices , experts told CNBC.
Similar tensions are emerging in South Korea, with growing opposition to data centers near residential areas and proposals for tighter local restrictions, even as the national government pushes to accelerate development.
Public opposition has already impacted around $42 billion of data center investments in Europe, in account delays and cancellations, according to research from STL Partners. That compares to around $77 billion in the U.S.
The pushback could be the "straw that breaks the camel's back," Olivier Darmouni, associate professor at HEC Paris who specializes in the energy transition, told CNBC.
More than 70 data center projects in Europe were rejected or restricted between January and April — more than in all of 2025, according to the European Data Center Monitor. It found that pushback had snowballed from local town halls to courts, regulators and parliaments.
Scotland has paused planning approvals for new hyperscale data centers after campaigners called on the government to avoid the "cautionary tale" of Ireland, where overwhelming power demand led to a moratorium.
Constraints have been rising in the Nordics, where investors were drawn to large tracts of land and renewable energy. After a surge in power applications , Denmark passed an emergency law that could see data centers at the back of the queue for grid power applications.
Spain also proposed new data center rules this summer, requiring data centers to source 80% of their electricity from renewables. Projects in the U.K. have stalled after pushback from locals.
Much of the concern centers around water usage , power consumption , electricity prices, and the sheer amount of space that some centers require. There is also little agreement on how many permanent jobs the sector creates, and no precedent for projecting a center's economic value per megawatt.
"The gains of AI are very diffused," Darmouni told CNBC.
"There's definitely been more understanding of the scale of the potential AI build-out and its geographical spread, and perhaps ... more information about how much bigger these are, and that they're a little bit more like giant ghost warehouses that consume a lot of resources and can hurt local communities in some ways."
Europe's denser population, and the fact that many data center operators are U.S. companies, might mean that the backlash hits harder, the professor added.
South Korea, home to tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, sits at the heart of the AI supply chain. In June, its government named AI data centers as one of three major investment projects, alongside semiconductors and physical AI.
But its push to build the infrastructure needed is running into resistance at the local level.
In the Geumcheon district of southwestern Seoul, residents have called for authorities to revoke the building permit and halt construction of a data center near their homes, according to the local government.
In July, officials announced plans to require consent from a majority of residents living within 200 meters of proposed data center sites and to introduce a three-stage system for reviewing projects and mediating disputes.
Residents have also gathered outside the local government office on weekday mornings for months to protest against the project. The demonstrations had continued for 172 days as of mid-August, according to local media .
In Gwacheon, a city just south of Seoul, a local council member proposed an ordinance aimed at protecting nearby residents from risks associated with data centers operating around the clock, including potential fires involving backup batteries.
Despite the pusback, the AI boom shows little sign of slowing down.
But a community's ability "to derail a $10 billion [data center] plan is quite powerful," said Asya Walters, managing director at Alvarez & Marsal.
She told CNBC the business-friendly environment in the U.S. has historically made it easier to overcome pushback.
But in Europe and Asia, there's some "hot and coldness" at the country level about where demand is going, Walters said. The "push and pull" between favorable conditions for data centers and more restrictive regulation can be challenging for investment.
Public backlash can also end up raising costs for operators, because even if they pull out of a project before construction starts, money will likely have already been spent.
Though most capex expenditure happens after the permits are in place, operators spend a lot to reach that point, "so there is some loss that could happen there if they never get the permits," Walters said.
"Digital infrastructure is becoming more visible and it's understandable that communities want to understand what's being built near them, why it's needed and how local impacts are being managed," said Eulalia Flo, vice president of growth and emerging markets, EMEA at Equinix , one of the biggest data center operators in Europe.
"We don't see this as a structural constraint on growth, but the policy environment is genuinely tightening in some markets," said Flo.
But the AI buildout has meant "a misunderstanding of the industry in a very broad sense," according to Dominic Ward, CEO of data center operator Verne.
"We used to be a completely unknown part of the economy," Ward told CNBC. "We were just a black box. We were just a building that had stuff that went in that nobody understood. Now we are one of the fundamental layers driving the economy."
He added: "Now everybody knows where they are, so there's kind of no hiding behind this."

articles.title_orig: DA did not review witness statements and other evidence Cornell police collected in alleged gang rape of student
articles.title_zh: DA did not review witness statements and other evidence Cornell police collected in alleged gang rape of student
articles.content_orig:
Cornell University police spoke to witnesses and received anonymous tips about an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house in the first weeks of its investigation two years ago , but the local prosecutor did not review the additional information before deciding not to bring charges.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said he based his decision not to pursue charges on the accuser’s initial six-page statement given to police.
Investigators from the campus police department documented those witness interviews and other steps taken to determine whether Jane Doe, a 20-year-old woman who reported the incident, was the victim of sexual assault during a party at the Chi Phi house from Oct. 19 to 20, 2024, according police records obtained by NBC News.
Documents reviewed by NBC News offer the most thorough look to date at how police handled the allegations from Jane Doe, who last month filed a lawsuit against Cornell University and seven Chi Phi brothers who she alleges sexually assaulted her over the course of hours while she was under the influence of ketamine, alcohol and marijuana.
Van Houten, along with police and university officials, has come under intense fire for their handling of the matter. Jane Doe’s attorney has argued that she was failed by authorities who did not conduct a thorough investigation and who prejudged the events based on her earlier statement that she consented to parts of the night.
Gov. Kathy Hochul on Thursday announced the appointment of Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to consider whether charges are appropriate.
“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript” of the victim’s interview, Hochul asked Friday at a news conference announcing James’s appointment.
On Nov. 25, 2024, a police investigator approached Van Houten’s office to tell them about interviews they’d done.
An investigator in Van Houten’s office, according to the documents, replied that “he and several [attorneys] at the District Attorney’s Office had read [Jane Doe’s] statement … [and] stated that they all agreed that, based on [Jane Doe’s] statement, criminal charges would not be pursued in this case.”
Van Houten defended his decision Monday and said that Jane Doe’s statement did not allege criminality. He also agreed to reopen his inquiry before that role was assigned to the attorney general.
When reached for comment by email Friday, Van Houten argued “there was nothing to review” in that discussion with police because the interviews flagged “were each of the frat members declining to speak on the advice of their attorney.”
Van Houten did not respond to a follow-up request asking whether he was told about interviews with other fraternity members in addition to tips from callers.
The records also show that police received a portion of a larger Snapchat thread where one member of the group announced there was “free p----” in the alumni room of the house, where Jane Doe engaged in what she said was initially a consensual threesome.
“Similarly there was no material obtained by CUPD from Snapchat (what was provided came from a witness),” Van Houten added. “So again nothing to review.”
It was unclear whether Van Houten was aware that on Nov. 26, 2024, police made a request to Snapchat for a more complete data history.
That request was answered on Dec. 23, when police said they obtained 1,665 pieces of data from five Snapchat accounts.
“After reviewing all of the data returned from Snapchat, there appeared to be only 3 snapchats that included [Jane Doe] or mentioned this incident,” a CUPD investigator wrote. “None of these 3 snapchats show anything that can be construed as being criminal in nature. No further action taken.”
Jane Doe was only notified by Cornell police about the district attorney’s Nov. 25 determination not to pursue charges nearly two months later on, Jan. 21, 2025.
Van Houten added that his office had “no part in the timing” of conveying his decision to Jane Doe, who was never interviewed by his office.
Thomas Giuffra, the attorney representing Jane Doe, learned about that delay from NBC News’ request for comment Friday. He said that his client — during that two-month window — believed “they were still investigating.”
“I was unaware that they had made the decision to not prosecute in November,” Giuffra said. “If so, that is worse than I thought.”
On Nov. 7, 2024, two weeks after the incident at Chi Phi, Jane Doe submitted to a sexual assault examination and evidence collection process, according to the police records. She had gone to the university health center shortly after the alleged assault to get treatment for a urinary tract infection, but was not offered a rape kit at the time, Giuffra said. He called it “the first failure post assault when she was trying to get help.” Cornell did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The attorney called it “a code or cry for help to say something bad happened” when Jane Doe told them that she “has a UTI of a traumatic origin.” Giuffra said the medical staff should have asked her: “What kind of trauma do you think caused this UTI?”
He noted that had the health center referred Jane Doe to an outside facility for an examination, there might have been recoverable DNA because she was there within 48 hours.
If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.
Shayna Jacobs is a national reporter for NBC News digital.
Kenzi Abou-Sabe is a reporter and producer in the NBC News Investigative Unit.
