articles.title_zh: Today's NYT Strands Hints (and Answer) for Saturday, October 3, 2026
articles.content_orig:
Tim Mulkerin is a freelance writer, editor, and social media manager who has been working in digital media and the tech world since 2016.
He has a bachelor's degree in art history and is currently pursuing a master's degree in communicative sciences and disorders from New York University. He lives in Brooklyn, New York.
If you’re looking for hints and answers for Strands for Saturday, October 3, 2026, read on—I’ll share some clues and tips, and finally the solution to the puzzle with the theme “A figment of your imagination.”
For an easy way to come back to our Strands hints every day, bookmark this page . You can also find our past hints there as well, in case you want to know what you missed in a previous puzzle. (If you play Wordle or Connections , check out our hints for those games, too.)
Below, I’ll give you some oblique hints at today’s Strands answers. And farther down the page, I’ll reveal the spangram and the answers. Scroll slowly and take just the hints you need!
A type of ghost described as a floating light.
We’re about to give away the answers to today’s Strands puzzle.
Today’s spangram is WILLOTHEWISP.
The theme words today are SPECTER, CHIMERA, MIRAGE, PHANTASM, ILLUSION.
Here’s what the board looks like when the puzzle is solved:
I see SPECTER in the upper left. 🔵 Makes sense: that’s a term for a vision or a ghost.
I see WILLOTHEWISP starting in the bottom left corner. 🟡 It’s the spangram!
CHIMERA is below SPECTER. 🔵 I know that word as a type of mythological beast, but I guess it can also refer to an illusion .
MIRAGE is to the right of CHIMERA. 🔵
ILLUSION is in the bottom right. 🔵
You can find the Strands game on the New York Times website and in the NYT Games app.
When you start playing, you’ll see a game board with an assortment of letters, flanked by a clue that gives a hint at the board’s theme—this will be a phrase, like “Better with age.” Your job is to find the hidden words within the board that reflect the puzzle’s theme.
The most important word to find is the “spangram,” a word that more explicitly states the puzzle’s theme. (For example, the spangram for the puzzle with the theme "Better with age" is FERMENTED, which describes products that are, you guessed it, better with age.) The spangram will span the entire game board, either from left to right or top to bottom (hence the name). When you find the spangram, it will be highlighted in yellow. Solving the spangram usually makes the rest of the puzzle much easier to complete.
In Strands, words can travel any direction (up, down, left, right, and diagonal), and you will only use each letter once. There is only one correct solution. When you correctly identify one of the puzzle’s words (for example, KOMBUCHA, MISO, or KIMCHI), it will be highlighted in blue.
If you are struggling to solve the puzzle, you can submit any non-theme words you see (as long as they are four letters or more) to receive credit toward a single hint. If you submit three non-theme words, the “Hint” button will be clickable; if you click it, all of the letters in one of the theme words will be highlighted for you. You will still have to link these highlighted letters in the right order to form one of the theme words. If there is already a hint on the board and you use another hint before solving for that word, that word’s letter order will be revealed.
Unlike Connections and Wordle, you cannot fail Strands. When you submit guesses, you will either correctly identify an answer, receive credit toward a hint, or the text will shake back and forth, indicating that the word you submitted is too short or not valid. You can't run out of guesses, and there is no time limit.
You win when you’ve correctly used all the letters on the board, meaning that you have identified the spangram and all of the theme words. Like other NYT games, upon solving the puzzle, you will see a shareable card that indicates how you performed that day: blue dots 🔵 indicate theme words you found, the yellow dot 🟡 indicates when you found the spangram, and a lightbulb 💡 indicates words that you received a hint for.
Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to Friday's Strands.
Tim Mulkerin is a freelance writer, editor, and social media manager who has been working in digital media and the tech world since 2016.

Search across reports, market insights, and blog stories.
China is unlikely to significantly increase its crude oil imports through the remainder of the year, according to OilPrice, as prices have climbed back above $100 per barrel and independent refiners face difficulty securing cheaper supply following the near-disappearance of Iranian barrels.
September import volumes are expected to be roughly in line with August levels, continuing a pattern of recovering shipments. The cargoes arriving in September were purchased when oil prices were in the $80s, before the latest escalation in early September pushed and held Brent above $100 per barrel.
China's crude oil imports rose for a second straight month in August, as refiners sought additional non-Middle Eastern supply and increased overseas fuel shipments amid eased export restrictions. The August level remained 23.4% below the same month a year earlier, though it marked a clear improvement from the June low of 7.1 million barrels per day.
China cut total crude oil imports to a decade low in June, capping three months of very low import levels driven by high prices and constrained Middle Eastern supply.
The outlook for the rest of the year has weakened as oil trades above $100 per barrel again and a U.S. blockade effectively removes the regular cheap supply that China's independent refiners relied on for years to stay competitive. The teapots could begin reducing refinery processing rates as prices rise and supply from major exporters such as Venezuela and Iran dries up due to U.S. foreign policy decisions.
Chinese state giants are also not rushing to buy much higher crude volumes above $100 a barrel with record-high freight costs, according to analysts. Samuel Kong, senior oil analyst at FGE NexantECA, told Bloomberg that significant upside to China's crude imports is not expected, partly because hefty premiums and expensive freight raise feedstock costs and erode margins.
Analysts at FGE NexantECA and Energy Aspects have revised down their earlier fourth-quarter projections for China's crude oil imports by about 400,000 barrels per day. These consultancies now expect China's crude oil imports to reach 9.2 million to 9.3 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, well below last year's average of 11.6 million barrels per day.

articles.title_orig: Former vendor’s viral post sparks backlash against Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks
articles.title_zh: Former vendor’s viral post sparks backlash against Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks
articles.content_orig:
Nick Neville , Community Correspondent , Orlando, FL
Anthony Guevara , Photojournalist
KISSIMMEE, Fla. – A now former vendor at Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks says she was forced out of the space she rented for about a decade, triggering a viral backlash and calls online for a boycott of the food truck park.
Gabriella Santos, who operated Los Cipotes, posted a video saying she was given just hours to move her food truck after ten years at the location. The post drew millions of views and sparked a heated debate on social media.
Santos told News 6 that her frustration built for years, citing what she describes as safety concerns, rising operating costs, and feeling unsupported.
She also said vendors paid out of pocket for events, absorbed new fees, and saw sales decline as more trucks were added to the park.
“Somebody’s making that extra money, and it’s not us,” Santos said in a Friday interview.
Santos said a lease renewal meeting this week became a boiling point. She claims a manager asked for access to her point-of-sale system, which she believes was framed as a way to determine rent.
“She said wanted access to the POS, and I said ‘Why do you need access to that?’” Santos said. “’Oh it’s because that’s how we’re going to balance how much your rent is going to be.’”
Santos also raised concerns about what she says were new lease terms, including language she interpreted as requiring 60 percent if a renewed lease was later broken.
World Food Trucks publicly disputed that claim, saying in a social media response: “That claim is completely false.”
Santos later clarified during the interview that she was describing her perception of what the changes would mean for her business, not alleging a literal demand for 60 percent of sales.
“I never said that,” she said. “What I said was that they wanted 60 percent of my business because that’s how I feel. That’s my personal feeling of what you’re doing to me. You’re taking my profits.”
She told News 6 she understand the terms to mean the food truck park would have wanted 60 percent of the remainder of the lease agreement.
Santos said after refusing to sign the new lease, she was told to leave by midnight on Thursday. Photos obtained by News 6 show her former spot is now surrounded by tables.
In a statement to News 6, World Food Trucks said in part, “We respect every vendor’s right to share their experience. We also believe disagreements deserve respectful conversation and accurate information. Our vendors pay a fixed weekly rent, rather than a percentage of their food sales, and we remain committed to clear communication with our vendor community.
Our focus is on supporting the more than 100 businesses that make World Food Trucks possible. We invite everyone to visit, meet the people behind the food, and support the local entrepreneurs who have helped build this community.”
Santos said she believes the viral reaction resonated because people see small business owners as vulnerable.
She said she is speaking for other vendors who are too afraid to go public.
“I think people don’t want little people to get bullied,” she said.

articles.title_orig: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
articles.title_zh: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
articles.content_orig:
Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’
The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia . Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination” .
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates , where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

Trump stumped for Republican candidates tonight in Mobile as part of his midterm elections blitz to 17 states.
The Trump administration has responded to CNN, MS NOW and Politico's request for Judge Timothy Kelly to issue a longer-term injunction that would allow the news organizations to maintain access to the White House complex.
Daniel Heuer / Bloomberg via Getty
The administration writes that regardless of the temporary restraining order put in place Sept. 24 that prevents the White House from barring the organizations from the grounds , the news outlets did not respond by the administrationâs deadline to provide reasoning for why the White House should provide them access.
Because of that missed deadline, the organizations "have received adequate notice of the relevant conduct before-hand and have now had the opportunity of post-deprivation process, including the chance to contest the Presidentâs factual findings,â DOJ attorney Michael Velchik writes.
âThey have declined to participate in that process and forfeit any argument that they need additional time to justify their conduct,â Velchik wrote.
In a Sept. 25 letter sent to Velchik by the outletsâ attorney, Ted Boutrous, and provided to NBC News Friday night, Boutrous wrote that âin light of the District Courtâs temporary restraining order,â legal counsel does not believe further response to the White Houseâs letters âis warranted at this time.â
In Friday's response, Velchik wrote that they also believe âthe Presidentâs actions are lawful under the First Amendment.â
âWhile the D.C. Circuit has held that some areas of the White House grounds constitute a nonpublic forum,â Velchik writes, citing a case that found the White House cannot arbitrarily deny press passes to bona-fide journalists, âthat decision is wrong and should be overruled.â
Judge Kelly has scheduled an Oct. 8 hearing where those arguments will be made in an in-person setting. The temporary restraining order allowing the three news organizations access to the White House also expires Oct. 8.
The White House said Friday night that the administration would make a one-time payment of $90 to more than 20 million Medicare Part B enrollees to help pay for premiums.
"I am pleased to announce that my Administration will, immediately, begin sending âChecksâ of nearly $100 to over 20 MILLION wonderful Seniors to help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which we have already reduced by significant amounts," Trump wrote on Truth Social announcing the payments .
The White House said eligible seniors would receive the payments in early October.
Trump said the money would come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, which Congress created in 2008 to make improvements to Medicare Part A and Medicare Part B. In his post, Trump labeled the fund as a "pointless 'Slush Fund' that has only been used by Dumocrats in Congress to pay for the Waste, Fraud, and Abuse for their Special Interest friends, and drive up Healthcare costs."
The announcement comes shortly after Trump said his administration would give each U.S. citizen $5,000 if Republicans retained control of Congress, a move that has drawn criticism from both sides of the aisle , though some Republicans have backed the proposal.
A former Miami congressman and longtime friend of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was sentenced today to 10 years in prison in connection with a secret $50 million lobbying campaign on Venezuelaâs behalf during the first Trump administration .
Republican David Rivera has been jailed since jurors found him guilty in May on all counts, including failing to register as a foreign agent and conspiracy to commit money laundering as part of his work for former Venezuelan President NicolÃ¡s Maduro âs government.
David Rivera. Â Joe Raedle / Getty
Rivera, 61, appeared stone-faced as Judge Melissa Damian denounced him for betraying his lifeâs mission, saying he would surely have been judged harshly his many friends had the millions of dollars come from the Cuban regime instead of its allies in Caracas.
âNobody would accept thatâs OK and I donât think this is different,â the judge said. âThereâs no dispute this money came from the Maduro regime.â
Abdul El-Sayedâs campaign manager says the Michigan Senate Democratic candidateâs ability to use the âattention economyâ to his advantage has kept him in position to prevail in the race.
âAbdul dominates the attention economy and the conversation among the chattering class who just want to talk about the horse race and Twitch streamers. But amidst the noise, whatâs Abdul talking about with Michigan families? Gas. Groceries. Healthcare,â campaign manager Alia Kapasi wrote in a memo , first reported by NBC News. âHow Donald Trump and Mike Rogers are corrupt and selling out Michigan families to make themselves richer.â
El-Sayed, whose primary campaign against moderate Haley Stevens divided Democrats, has sought to saturate the media environment by giving numerous interviews to spread his message, including with a Fox News host openly opposed to his campaign.
The memo touts the progressive candidateâs prospects in the purple state against Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers, claiming that âMike Rogersâ campaign has stalled.â
Kapasi argued that if Rogers could not win in 2024 when Trump was on the ballot, âheâs in an even worse position now.â
The Michigan contest is one of the most competitive Senate races this fall, one that will shape the balance of power in the chamber. El-Sayed leads in most recent polls, often within the margin of error.
Trump has wrapped up his speech in Mobile, Alabama, speaking to the crowd for about an hour and 10 minutes.
The president urged the audience to show up at the polls in November and "pretend I'm on the ballot," a phrase he's repeated during his stump speeches heading into the midterms.
Trump earned three standing ovations from the crowd in Mobile tonight, the second of which was responding to the president's new deal with G7 members on diesel exports.
"Today, I spoke with members of the G7 nations, and Iâm pleased to report that we have reached an agreement for Europe to release massive amounts of diesel fuel from their heavily stocked reserves," Trump said, with the audience standing up and cheering loudly.
Trump said everyone will see the price of diesel âreally come downâ after they finish the war with Iran.
The deal came today after Trump and his administration have pressured European allies to cut into their national emergency stockpiles of diesel fuel as its price has soared in connection with the war in Iran.
The president said tonight that the war in Iran will end "probably right after the election," a claim that he's repeated in recent weeks as more Americans say they disapprove of the war the U.S. and Israel launched in late February.
"Itâs going to end very soon, probably right after the election," Trump told the crowd. "But as soon as it does end, oil prices will come tumbling down."
"Remember about the oil. Theyâre paying a price, but boy, is that a small price than what it would be if these lunatics were allowed to have a nuclear weapon and used it on Mobile, Alabama?" he added, saying the war will be over soon "one way or another."
Trump's remarks come as the average cost for a gallon of gas in the U.S. is currently $4.39, according to data tracked by NBC News.
Trump repeated his claim tonight that "this is the golden age of America" despite the fact that his approval rating continues to slip.
"Itâs a golden age," Trump said. "Our nation is doing better now than ever before."
About 59% of Americans disapprove of Trump, according to NBC News' latest polling. The president's favorability has sunk as voters blame Trump for rising prices as the war in Iran continues, NBC News' polling found.

articles.title_orig: Israeli air attack on Gaza City apartment kills at least five
articles.title_zh: Israeli air attack on Gaza City apartment kills at least five
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli air attack on a residential apartment in western Gaza City has killed at least five people and severely wounded at least six others, according to medical staff at al-Shifa Hospital.
The strike hit the al-Asala building in the Remal neighbourhood early on Saturday without prior warning, according to Al Jazeera’s Hani al-Shaer, reporting from Khan Younis.
Remal is one of Gaza City’s most crowded residential areas, home to thousands of displaced people sheltering in makeshift camps across the neighbourhood.
Al-Shaer said the attack came in the middle of the night, when residents were asleep.
“We heard fighter jets getting louder, then three strikes followed, hitting the apartment and killing those inside,” he said.
The strike penetrated the targeted apartment and tore through the floors below, causing further destruction throughout the multi-storey building.
Fires burned for at least an hour before Palestinian Civil Defence crews managed to put them out.
Al-Shaer described the scene as “horrific”, with people buried under the rubble as they slept.
Civil defence crews were still searching the site for missing people and bodies, he said, as Israeli drones continued flying over the area and fighter jets were heard flying low across the Strip.
Al-Shifa Hospital said the dead included four women, among them an elderly Christian woman and her daughter.
The six wounded were taken to al-Shifa Hospital for treatment.

articles.title_orig: What to know about the Cornell University rape allegations
articles.title_zh: What to know about the Cornell University rape allegations
articles.content_orig:
Albany, NY (WRGB) — On Friday, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said the State is taking on a greater role i n the investigation of an alleged gang rape at a fraternity at Cornell University from 2024. The investigation was reopened by Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten earlier this week, but the Governor appointing Attorney General Letitia James as Special Prosecutor in the case.
The Governor also pushing for the legislature to act, imploring State lawmakers to pass legislation which they say would close a gap in the State's sexual assault law, in that a person's voluntary intoxication would not be used when determining if they were able to consent.
“If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol,” Hochul said Friday. “Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period.”
The legislation has passed the NYS Senate unanimously in recent years, but failed to gain traction in the State Assembly.
Assembly Speaker Heastie releasing a statement in response on Friday, saying:
"As I have said, I am very troubled by what happened at Cornell. The Assembly Majority conferenced this bill twice. We did not have enough votes within the Majority conference to pass the bill. That is why I have convened the working group to resolve the issues with this bill and to look for additional ways to strengthen New York’s sexual assault laws."
Albany Assemblymember Gabriella Romero (D) is on the working group, and is also a former public defender. She spoke with CBS6 about her role.
"So, as a lawyer, I approach this type of working group from lived experience of being in the courtroom, being a defense attorney, having trials and hearings, etc. I am looking forward to reviewing all the state laws that exist right now, in addition to case law, and reviewing that with my colleagues to see what we can do, whether it's codifying case law or reviewing bills to change our current procedure law and penal law," she said. "Frankly, I've had clients that were convicted based off of a voluntary intoxication from the survivor. But the reality is that if people are coming to us with bill language or proposals, we need to review it. We will be reviewing it in this working group, and I hope to propose to the majority something that is simple and something that centers survivors."
The full working group includes Assemblymembers::

articles.title_orig: The Archeparchy attends a World Affairs Council of Philadelphia Event
articles.title_zh: The Archeparchy attends a World Affairs Council of Philadelphia Event
articles.content_orig:
On Thursday, October 1st, representatives of the Ukrainian Catholic Archeparchy of Philadelphia attended “An Evening with Evan Gershkovich” hosted by the World Affairs Council of Philadelphia (WAC).
In March 2023 shortly after the one-year anniversary of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Evan Gershkovich, an American reporter for the Wall Street Journal , was arrested and charged with espionage by FSB agents in Russia. After a sham trial, he was sentenced to 16 years in a Russian prison only to be released after 16 months as part of a prisoner exchange.
During a fireside chat, WAC President & CEO Lauren Swartz engaged Gershkovich in conversation about his newly released book This Cursed Beautiful Land , a memoir of his unlawful imprisonment. Gershkovich spoke about how he admittedly misread all the signals and was lured into a trap at the time of his arrest. He discussed at length how he understood from the beginning that he was part of Russia’s plan to ‘beef-up its negotiating leverage’. He understood that he would be treated with a certain privilege. Almost immediately Gershkovich realized that he wouldn’t be tortured or interrogated in the same manner as other journalists, siting the barbaric and inhumane torture of Victoria Roshchyna, a Ukrainian journalist who was arrested around the same time as Gershkovich.
The Ukrainian Catholic Archeparchy is a non-profit member of the World Affairs Council of Philadelphia and was a promotional partner for this event.

articles.title_orig: World Forest Week: FAO urges greater investment and action for the world's dryland forests
articles.title_zh: World Forest Week: FAO urges greater investment and action for the world's dryland forests
articles.content_orig:
FAO’s Call to Action on Dryland Forests emphasizes that proven solutions for reviving drylands already exist, and the priority is to create the conditions to implement them at scale
Dryland forests provide vital ecosystems, resources and livelihoods for communities around the world.
Rome – Forests and trees in the world's drylands sustain the livelihoods, food security and cultural identity of more than two billion people, yet they remain insufficiently recognized in global climate, biodiversity and land agendas, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
FAO’s Call to Action on Dryland Forests was launched today during a High-level dialogue on Dryland forests for food, nutrition and resilience held as part of the 10th World Forest Week, running alongside the 28th Session of the FAO Committee on Forestry (COFO) at FAO headquarters in Rome.
The call urges governments, donors and partners to strengthen the sustainable management, restoration and governance of drylands forests; better integrate them into national climate, biodiversity and land priorities; and significantly increase investment in their conservation and sustainable use. It also proposes a new Dryland Forest Support Accelerator as an enabling platform to speed up implementation, mobilize finance, and strengthen country-driven action at scale.
“Dryland forests are central to our lives, and that of future generations,” said FAO Director-General QU Dongyu in a video message. “Yet dryland forests are often underrecognized, under-monitored and under-financed. This must change.”
Drylands - which are characterized by water scarcity - host forests, woodlands and trees outside forests and cover roughly 41 percent of the Earth's land surface. They also account for 27 percent of global forest area.
Drylands produce high-demand wood and non-wood products, buffer people against drought, and provide one of the most accessible safety nets for the world's poorest households – from fuelwood and fodder to wild foods and medicinal plants. They also underpin the resilience of agrifood systems by supporting livestock, protecting soils and water resources, and providing food and income when crops fail.
But around 25 percent of dryland forest ecosystems are already degraded, driven largely by land-use change including agricultural expansion, urbanization and unsustainable resource extraction. Climate change is compounding these pressures, with longer droughts intensifying water stress and increasing fire risk. These impacts fall heavily on smallholders, Indigenous Peoples, pastoralists and local communities, as well as women and youth.
Dryland Forest Support Accelerator
The Call to Action emphasizes that proven solutions for reviving drylands already exist, and the priority is to create the conditions to implement them at scale.
At the centre of the call is the Dryland Forest Support Accelerator – an FAO-anchored, country-driven platform to help move action beyond fragmented projects. It would support countries in integrating dryland forests into national planning processes – including nationally determined contributions and land degradation neutrality targets – accessing long-term finance, strengthening monitoring, and improving coordination across sectors.
Building on FAO’s experience on drylands, notably through the GEF-7 Dryland Sustainable Landscapes Impact Program and the COFO Working Group on Dryland Forests and Agrosilvopastoral Systems, the Accelerator would organize support around three objectives:  gathering evidence and identifying country needs; supporting the implementation and scaling of proven approaches; and capturing results and lessons to inform future action.
The Call to Action further advises that governments, donors and the Rio Conventions give greater political and financial priority to dryland forests across global environmental processes, including through formal recognition of dryland forests as a priority ecosystem under the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD).

articles.title_orig: Can the AM Radio Car Mandate Beat the Congressional Clock?
articles.title_zh: Can the AM Radio Car Mandate Beat the Congressional Clock?
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Business and Law
As the U.S. Senate adjourns until after the November midterm elections, a familiar concern for backers of the AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act has surfaced: Will time run out?
The next step for the legislation, as we’ve covered, is for it to move through the Senate. There was palpable momentum after the bill cleared the house in September . And previously, Sens. Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas) secured filibuster-proof majority with 61 senators supporting it.
Most observers believe it will pass in the Senate, and President Donald Trump has expressed his support for the legislation previously. The president would then need to simply sign the bill for the mandate to take effect.
But the bill has to reach the Senate floor for a vote first, and there’s a scant few days left in this current congressional cycle. The 2023 version failed to pass in the Senate after efforts that December fell short .
The AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act’s advocates eyed getting the Senate version of the bill on the floor before the senior chamber cleared for its midterm election recess. That did not happen, and the Senate will not return to the Capitol until the week of Nov. 9, according to The Hill .
If the clock runs out at the end of the year, the process completely resets . Any legislation that fails to pass before the current Congress officially ends on Jan. 3 dies, forcing supporters to reintroduce the bill from scratch next year.
And when the Senate returns from hiatus, it will face a logjam of legislative priorities.
As The Hill noted, the return begins a lame-duck session. When asked about pushing so much work into November and December, Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) sarcastically called the upcoming scramble their “golden era.”
The Senate has only eight working days scheduled for November and 14 for December, including Fridays, which are rarely used for floor action.
But the National Association of Broadcasters continues to express optimism. “We’re on the one-yard line, and the momentum behind the AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act remains incredibly strong,” NAB Vice President of Communications Carrie Healey told Inside Radio .
As we’ve reported, the bill requires the DOT to issue a rule within one year requiring AM radio capabilities to be standard in all new passenger vehicles sold in the United States.
The U.S. Congressional Budget Office reported the bill would impact roughly 2 to 2.5 million vehicles every year for models currently manufactured or planned without built-in AM receiving capability, according to its March cost estimate.
CBO estimates that implementing the bill will cost the federal government a total of $1 million over a five-year period.

articles.title_orig: Saudis plan major offensive against the Houthis, but U.S. won't join for now
articles.title_zh: Saudis plan major offensive against the Houthis, but U.S. won't join for now
articles.content_orig:
Akhtar is a foreign correspondent for The Telegraph based in London
Saudi Arabia is believed to be planning a military offensive to drive Houthi rebels from Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
The operation, expected within weeks, would be fought by Yemeni ground forces under Saudi command and backed by Saudi air strikes, with US intelligence support but no allied combat role.
The Saudis are considering either a narrow push around the Bab el-Mandeb strait or a broader assault across several fronts, and could mobilise more than 100,000 troops, according to regional and Western officials who spoke to the Reuters news agency. The Telegraph could not independently verify the plans.
The Houthis, in the space of a week last month, seized the port of Mokha , took Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and struck deep inside Saudi Arabia.
Bab el-Mandeb, the southern mouth of the Red Sea, has taken on outsized importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz , the key oil-transit route that has been effectively closed by the Iran war.
Washington has declined Saudi requests for direct strikes on the Houthis, while Turkey and Pakistan have supplied drones and equipment, and France is sending defensive systems to guard the port of Yanbu.
The Houthis’ advance was the first real test of the Mecca joint defence agreement , signed in August by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, under which an armed attack on any member is considered an attack on all, in language modelled on Nato’s Article 5.
On the ground this week, the Houthis launched a series of intense attacks across the Taiz governorate in Yemen, trying to extend the lightning advance that handed them the Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces say they have held the line, reporting more than 400 air, drone and artillery strikes against Houthi positions in a 24-hour period.
Analysts say rugged terrain and heavier firepower have blunted the push. Having taken the coast, the Houthis still need the high ground overlooking the strait to secure it, which they have so far failed to seize.
The rebels have also sought to project their momentum and mock their enemies. In nearly an hour-long video last week, the Houthis showed newly captured areas and their operations.
In one sequence, a fighter, his cheek bulging with khat – the mild narcotic leaf chewed across much of Yemen – picks through a position abandoned by the Saudi-backed forces and holds up bottles of Label 5, a cheap blended Scotch whisky.
He turns the liquor to the camera as if to display the decadence and disarray of the men who fled.
The Houthis, a hardline rebel group that bans alcohol across the territory it controls, have long painted Yemen’s internationally recognised government as corrupt and un-Islamic, and such finds – weapons, cash and alcohol left behind in the retreat – are a staple of their battlefield propaganda.
The fighting is exacting a brutal toll on civilians, with the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) warning that hunger is “accelerating before our eyes”. About 74 per cent of households in accessible areas are now unable to meet their basic food needs, the highest proportion recorded this year.
“The latest flare-up threatens to be absolutely devastating,” said Matthew Hollingworth, a senior WFP official, adding that Yemen imports roughly 90 per cent of its food.
Displaced families are reaching the outskirts of Aden and Taiz with nothing, some surviving on bread and soup made from leaves and grass.
Across Yemen, 18.3 million people face severe food insecurity, including 2.2 million acutely malnourished children under five.
More than 149,000 people had been uprooted by the latest fighting, the International Organisation for Migration said, and more than 3,700 had fled across the strait to Djibouti.
Any Saudi assault would come up against a group that has defied far larger campaigns.
Saudi Arabia led an Arab coalition into Yemen in 2015 and fought the Houthis to a bloody stalemate. The US and Israel have repeatedly bombed the group, yet it still controls much of the country and now the strait itself.

articles.title_orig: Amazon vows $1 billion for data center towns, warning U.S. "can't afford to lose" AI race
articles.title_zh: Amazon vows $1 billion for data center towns, warning U.S. "can't afford to lose" AI race
articles.content_orig:
Amazon's cloud computing division on Friday announced a new effort to temper opposition to data centers in some U.S. communities, while saying the U.S. "can't afford to lose" the race to dominate artificial intelligence globally.
The tech giant pledged to invest an additional $1 billion over five years in the communities where it builds data centers, the facilities that power AI, on top of existing commitments. Amazon said the money will go toward education, job training, energy affordability, and water and energy preservation, and also fund other local priorities.
"There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren't the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run," Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said in a blog post . "The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation's focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so."
A recent CBS News poll found that more Americans oppose than favor data centers in their areas, largely because they perceive the facilities as harming the environment and draining local resources.
A report from Schneider Electric, a company specializing in digital automation and energy management, projects that U.S. electricity demand will i ncrease by 16% by 2029, mainly due to the proliferation of data centers. AI searches use 10 times more electricity than normal internet searches, according to a study from the Electric Power Research Institute, a nonprofit organization.
According to a group called Data Center Watch, which tracks opposition to data centers across the U.S., 30  states have introduced or adopted legislation or taken other actions to address some of these concerns. Some communities also imposed preemptive moratoriums on data center construction even before builders planned sites, the group notes.
The number of data centers in the U.S. nearly doubled between 2021 and 2024, according to a report from Environment America, a network of environmental groups. Grassroots efforts to block data center development have thwarted at least 45 developments across 27 states, valued at $68 billion, according to the group.
Amazon's Garman said such disruption is dangerous, claiming that the data center buildout is so geopolitically important that foreign nations could be "intentionally seeding misinformation in the U.S. about data centers to trick us into slowing down."

Meta’s Muse, a personal AI agent that books travel, fills out forms, and shops on a user’s behalf, has already proven popular with the masses, but a new side project could be particularly alluring to tinkerers and hackers.
On Friday, the company introduced Muse Gadgets , an open-source project that lets developers build their own hardware that connects to Muse.
Meta is providing open-source firmware (the low-level software that runs a device), and a Linux software development kit (SDK), along with a few project ideas to get users started. These include giving Muse a color e-ink display or loading it onto a stick that plugs into a TV’s HDMI port.
There don’t appear to be many limits, either. Users can set up a low-cost hobbyist computer like a Raspberry Pi or an off-the-shelf ESP32 board, and then connect Muse “to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench,” Meta notes.
The company has also set up a Discord channel to support users.
Meta has already tried the code itself, naturally. Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, said in a post on X that the company built a gadget called Muse Home Link. The USB-C-powered device lets Muse connect to a home network and talk to the smart devices on it, including speakers and smart TVs.
Meta made 5,000 of these Home Links, in fact, and is giving them away for free to Muse subscribers while supplies last, according to Friedman. Considering Friedman’s post about Home Link received nearly 30,000 views in a few hours, we’re guessing those freebies have been claimed. Friedman said Home Link would be ready to ship a few weeks.
Muse Gadgets may not have wide appeal, but it fits nicely into Meta’s all-in strategy to make Muse more than a standalone chatbot. Meta isn’t content to push Muse on everyday consumers; it’s also trying to woo small businesses and enterprises.
The company earlier this week introduced Muse for Small Business, which is free with usage limits and connects Muse to tools such as Shopify, Dropbox, and Slack. It has also launched a new business unit, Meta Enterprise Platform, to help it push its AI offerings to businesses and corporate customers.

articles.title_orig: Federal judge halts Big Bend border wall construction in blow to Trump agenda
articles.title_zh: Federal judge halts Big Bend border wall construction in blow to Trump agenda
articles.content_orig:
Plan to install barriers through popular national park sparked outrage from advocates and politicians alike
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from expanding the border wall and other security infrastructure across the Big Bend region of west Texas, where contentious plans to build roads and vehicle barriers through a popular national park have led to furious backlash and public protests.
US district judge Kathleen Cardone’s ruling after a Friday hearing in El Paso deals a major blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to expand the border wall through west Texas at breakneck pace, while riding roughshod over the objections of local business owners, landowners, public land advocates and politicians from both parties.
Plans to mar Big Bend national park with new roads and 6-ft tall vehicle barriers have drawn the most national attention since the Trump administration started advancing the border wall construction earlier this year. Images of bulldozers plowing up ground for new roads at the park in August drew outrage, prompting Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, to temporarily halt construction. Construction resumed in September.
Friday’s ruling came after a hearing in a lawsuit filed by the Friends of the Ruidosa church, the Center for Biological Diversity and river guide Billy Miller seeking to overturn several Department of Homeland Security (DHS) waivers that suspended dozens of environmental and historical protection laws to speed construction.
Cardone blocked the DHS waivers in her ruling, saying that the plaintiffs were likely to win and would suffer irreparable harm if construction moved forward. The ruling bars CBP from border security infrastructure construction or ground disturbance, unless it complies with the federal laws that DHS tried to suspend.
“This is a historic victory for Big Bend and everyone who loves this wild corner of Texas ,” said Laiken Jordahl, a public land advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. “No administration has the right to destroy a crown-jewel national park for political theatre.”
“But this fight is far from over,” he added. “We won’t rest until Big Bend’s environmental protections are fully restored and the illegal waiver that allowed so much destruction is gone for good.”
CBP has already awarded five contracts for Big Bend totaling more than $6bn to expand what the agency calls the “smart wall” – a mix of 30-ft steel bollard fencing, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.
“We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region,” a CBP spokesperson wrote in an email in response to the ruling. “We are working with the Department of Justice on next steps.”
The Republican-dominated Congress included a whopping $46.5bn for border wall construction in last year’s “big, beautiful” spending bill. That massive war chest led CBP to focus much of its efforts on the Big Bend region, which contains the longest unwalled stretch along the US-Mexico border.
The plans have sparked furious responses from landowners and local political leaders, who say that unauthorized crossings are already rare there due to the region’s remoteness, the lack of nearby cities on the Mexican side and prominent cliffs that make it very difficult to cross through many stretches of the border there.

David Robinson, a leader on OpenAI's Safety Systems team, has resigned from the company.
An OpenAI spokesperson told Business Insider on Friday that Robinson left last week, marking yet another moment of upheaval in the company's safety ranks. Robinson had previously led the company's policy planning.
Robinson worked on safety transparency at the company, including helping to develop and share system cards that provide information about its models.
He did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Robinson's departure comes alongside a wave of attention on OpenAI's safety practices and staffing. The company shared on Thursday that it had "parted ways" with three researchers, saying they had violated its policies for sharing sensitive information.
In the aftermath of the high-profile Hugging Face security breach , OpenAI is grappling with a series of other safety incidents in which it said its AI models have misbehaved.
Progress in model capabilities has led researchers and company executives to call for a slowdown in AI development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , at the company's developer conference on Tuesday, said safety and alignment need to stay ahead of model capabilities.
Johannes Heidecke, the company's safety head, also left earlier this year.
Robinson, in early September, wrote on X that he felt people at OpenAI were waking up to the implications of highly capable AI models and also expressed some doubt.

articles.title_orig: Unemployment Rate Ticks Higher as Job Growth Slows
articles.title_zh: Unemployment Rate Ticks Higher as Job Growth Slows
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
U.S. employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, and the unemployment rate rose a tenth of a percentage point to 4.2%, the Labor Department announced Friday. Both results failed to meet expectations, as analysts had projected job growth of about 90,000 and a steady unemployment rate for the month.
Job growth in the previous two months was moved lower, as well, with the numbers for July reduced by 31,000, moving the final tally to a loss of 10,000, and August falling by 29,000 to 133,0000.
The healthcare sector provided the majority of the growth in September, as it has for many months, adding a weaker-than-usual 17,000 jobs. Construction firms created 11,000 jobs, and manufacturers 9,000.
Employment in federal, state and local governments fell by 17,000, while professional and business services firms cut 9,000 jobs.
Wages grew 3.0% on an annual basis, the smallest 12-month gain since May 2021.
What the analysts are saying: Analysts downplayed the miss in the top-line numbers, saying the labor market appears to be holding more or less steady, despite the monthly variations. From July through September, job growth has averaged 51,000 per month, a level many economists see as a stable level in a "low hire, low fire" job market.
"The September employment report came in a little bit softer than expected but overall wasn't too worrying," JPMorgan's Michael Feroli wrote in a note to clients. Feroli pointed out that the unemployment rate rose because 485,000 people entered the workforce, a positive sign about the strength of the economy. And he described the three-month growth average as being "close to most estimates of trend monthly growth in the labor supply, i.e. breakeven job growth."
RSM Chief Economist Joseph Brusuelas said the labor market appears to have settled into a new normal, shaped by political policy and basic demographics. "Growth in the domestic supply of labor will remain soft given the well-known long-term demographic challenges posed by the retirement of baby boomers and restrictive immigration policies," he said in a research note . "Soft readings like September's and an underlying trend of around 50,000 new jobs added monthly will be the norm over the next two years at the least."
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, emphasized the same point. "The September jobs report tells us the 'low hire, low fire' job market is still here," she said on X. "There was hope that hiring was picking up, but it's stabilizing at a low ~50k a month." Long noted that job growth is being driven largely by two sectors: healthcare and the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Long added the latest data confirms the worry that millions of American workers are feeling "financial pain," with the lowest year-over-year wage growth in five years (see her chart below). "Inflation has eaten up all wage gains for the average worker since April," she wrote . "Many people are having to make hard choices about what to buy and what to skimp on right now. Yes, consumption is still strong (mainly due to wealthier Americans and people dipping into savings or credit cards), but a lot of people have to think hard about every dollar they spend."
Fed may sit tight: The soft jobs and wage data indicate that the labor market is not contributing to inflation, reducing pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting at the end of the month.
According to CME's FedWatch tool , traders now assign a 22% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the meeting, a big drop from the 35% reading a week ago.
"This report strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to remain patient," said Adam Schickling, a senior economist at Vanguard, per CNBC. "The labor market has not deteriorated sharply, but there is also little evidence that it has meaningfully strengthened, giving policymakers reason to wait for additional data."

Households in the contiguous United States will pay thousands of dollars more for energy through 2040 because of federal policy changes since President Donald Trump returned to office such as canceling new clean energy projects, according to modeling released Friday by a nonpartisan think tank.
The Energy Innovation analysis found that households will pay an average of $6,500 more for energy, cumulatively through 2040. In five states, households will pay roughly $9,000 more: Oregon , Mississippi, South Dakota, Virginia and Wyoming.
The California-based think tank said there will be more demand for natural gas for electricity because the administration is canceling new wind, solar and hydrogen projects and there will be more gasoline demand for transportation because Trump and Congress are revoking policies that incentivized efficient and lower-emissions vehicles. Higher demand increases prices.
Energy prices are elevated in many countries. The International Energy Agency said after Russia invaded Ukraine, record prices were observed between 2022 and 2024 in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Japan and Korea. In many countries, the rise has outpaced income growth and inflation since 2019, including the European Union and the United States.
In some areas of the U.S., demand from data centers is being blamed. The Iran war has sent oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, too. The Energy Information Administration expects residential U.S. customers to pay about 18.6 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2027, compared to 17.3 cents in 2025 and 18.2 cents in 2026.
The independent research firm Rhodium Group has also examined the issue, saying in April the U.S. has entered a new period of rising electricity prices. It cited increasing price volatility in natural gas, which is increasingly used to generate power; needed grid improvements; inflation; storm recovery and wildfire mitigation; and shifting policies.
Absent significant policy action, electricity prices likely will continue their significant rise over the next five years, the firm said.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said Wednesday that lowering electricity prices remains a top priority and Trump is unleashing reliable energy like coal and natural gas to reverse the damage Democrats did to the grid by increasing clean energy. A 2025 Department of Energy report, mandated by Trump, warned of increasing blackouts if the U.S. continued closing coal and natural gas plants.
“Joe Biden created a grid crisis; President Trump is fixing it,” Rogers wrote in an email. “If the Democrats had their way, these costly and unreliable renewable energy projects would still be failing our grid and our communities.”
The Republican president prioritizes fossil fuels to produce electricity, unlike Biden, who saw clean energy as a climate solution. The conservative Institute for Energy Research said in December that blue states have high rates because they have embraced aggressive renewable mandates, 100% carbon-free targets, premature coal and nuclear retirements and restrictions on natural gas infrastructure. It said high electricity prices are not an inevitability; they are a choice.
Analysis examined impact on states solely from federal policy changes
It focused on the sweeping package of tax breaks that slashed funding for clean energy tax credits, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump signed; environmental rollbacks, including clean air and power plant rules and the revocation of a scientific finding that underpinned the U.S. fight against climate change; the loosening of fuel economy standards and blocking of California’s novel rule banning the sale of new gas-powered cars by 2035; and federal actions to stop wind, solar and hydrogen projects.
These changes will result in annual household energy costs rising in every state in the contiguous U.S., plus job losses in 47 of 48 states and losses to the gross domestic product in 46 states, Energy Innovation said. It's projecting 37,000 additional premature deaths from air pollution, $72 billion in additional healthcare costs and more than 9 billion tons of additional carbon pollution because of the environmental rollbacks. The analysis did not include Alaska or Hawaii because key federal data is not available for those two states, said Robbie Orvis, senior director for modeling and analysis.
“Across pretty much every state, things are worse. The outlook now is worse for states and the affordability crisis will be worse because of the combined set of policies,” Orvis said.
Climate Justice Alliance legislative director Mar Zepeda said her Washington, D.C., electric bill increased $200 in the past month. Zepeda blames electricity demands from data centers, and said federal “affordability” policies only exacerbate this.
“They may call it affordability, but affordable for whom and at what cost? Not for regular people,” Zepeda said in an email.
White House says the think tank is partisan
Rogers said it is “irresponsible” to classify Energy Innovation as nonpartisan because its employees have donated to Democrats and worked with Democrats on climate policy.
Spokesman Silvio Marcacci said Energy Innovation works with policymakers who want to cut emissions and lower bills, regardless of party. He said multiple Republican-led states have used their tool designed to model policies affecting energy use and emissions. Much of their data comes from government sources, including the EIA.
Rogers also said states led by Democrats that have embraced aggressive renewable mandates see higher energy costs, notably California and New York. She said this proves Republican policies are working.
However, in the Energy Innovation analysis, three of the five states facing the highest costs have Republican governors. Its research has found that states with high levels of wind and solar generation, including Republican-led Iowa and Oklahoma, have experienced the lowest rate increases.
The average price residential customers pay for electricity increased during Biden's term and has continued to rise under Trump, according to EIA data.
Oregon households’ annual energy spending slated to increase the most
The modeling projects federal policy changes will increase annual energy spending in Oregon by $840 per household in 2035 and $1,200 per household in 2040, with a cumulative $9,300 increase from 2026 to 2040 — the highest of any state.
The Oregon Citizens’ Utility Board advocates for residential utility customers. Executive Director Bob Jenks called those numbers “frightening” because Oregon already has an energy affordability problem. He cited steep rate increases as utilities make upgrades and data centers use more power.
As costs rise, Jenks expects utilities to disconnect more customers who can't afford their bills.
Jenks said wind and solar are essential for affordable electricity, and he wants the federal government to partner with states to develop the energy they need.
“We're trying to optimize among the resource options we have, and they’re trying to take things away and raise the costs,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Shop clerk, son charged with selling illegal kratom amid probe into deaths of 2 Ole Miss students
articles.title_zh: Shop clerk, son charged with selling illegal kratom amid probe into deaths of 2 Ole Miss students
articles.content_orig:
A store clerk and his son have been charged with selling an illegal kratom product as federal authorities investigate the deaths of two University of Mississippi students , prosecutors said Friday.
A drug task force in Mississippi had previously urged people to avoid kratom — an herbal substance that acts as a stimulant at low doses and a sedative at high doses — after authorities found packages of kratom derivatives while investigating the deaths on Sept. 21.
It is still not clear whether those substances contributed to either death, but federal prosecutors said both appear consistent with drug overdoses. Two state agencies were working to expedite toxicology reports for the students, Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves said in a statement last week. Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said Thursday the investigation remained active and additional charges were possible.
Bank records show one of the students, Aidan Hamilton , made multiple purchases in September from a vape, tobacco and beer store in Oxford, Mississippi, where the university is located, according to a federal court filing.
On Sept. 24, an informant sent to the store by investigators purchased kratom-based pills from the clerk, Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, who warned the informant to "be careful taking the pills because people were dying from them," U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration Special Agent Michael Dassance said in an affidavit.
Authorities arrested Mosleh along with his 18-year-old son, Islam Yahya Mosleh, who was working at the store. Each faces one count of possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance, the Justice Department said in a statement Friday.
Scott Davis, an attorney for the elder Mosleh, and A.E. Harlow Jr., an attorney for Islam Mosleh, said in emails that they had no comment. The defendants appeared Thursday before a magistrate judge, who ruled there was sufficient evidence to charge them.
Kratom, which comes from a tree native to Southeast Asia, is legal at the federal level. But some state and local governments have banned it, and federal authorities have issued warnings about its risks.
Proponents say that in its pure, ground-leaf form, kratom is a safe, natural herbal supplement that can help manage pain, anxiety and depression and ease the effects of opioid withdrawal. They say the danger is from kratom derivatives, which are often synthetic and can be highly potent.
Kratom has been linked to deaths in rare cases, though it was typically used with other drugs, making its role in those deaths unclear, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
In August, the DEA banned three kratom-related compounds. In his Sept. 25 affidavit, the DEA agent said one of the banned compounds was listed as an ingredient in products seized from the Oxford store and Hamilton's room.
Hamilton, a freshman from Englewood, Colorado, and the other student who died, Robert Strang , a junior from Atlanta, were found in different locations, one on campus and the other off campus.
Investigators found opened packages of a kratom product labeled "Smax" in both of the students' rooms, according to the Justice Department. Investigators then found a "suspected link" between those packages and the store where the Moslehs worked, the Justice Department said in its Friday statement.
Yahya Mosleh told the informant who went to the store on Sept. 24 to be quiet when other customers came in and pushed the kratom pills out of sight. When the customers left, he completed the sale, according to the affidavit, again telling the informant to be careful.
Eleven states have banned kratom. Others, including Mississippi, have regulated it, in part by requiring people to be 21 or older to buy it. The city of Oxford, additionally, has implemented its own kratom ban.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike unconscious and on a ventilator at Nashville hospital, her lawyers say
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike unconscious and on a ventilator at Nashville hospital, her lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike, the woman who survived an execution attempt in Tennessee earlier this week, remains hospitalized in critical condition, her lawyers said in a new statement Friday.
She is unconscious, intubated and breathing through a ventilator. The death row inmate is also being treated for “significant injuries to both arms” sustained when two lethal injections of pentobarbital failed to kill her.
At one point, Pike said it felt like her arm was exploding, and she could be heard whimpering, according to her legal team.
“We are working closely with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time,” attorney Luke Ihnen said in a statement. “We ask that the public and the media respect that privacy as well.”
The state of Tennessee attempted to put Pike to death Wednesday night by lethal injection for a murder she committed when she was 18.
Pike, now 50, has been on death row for decades and would have been the first woman executed in the state in 200 years.
NBC News earlier reported that there was no emergency medical oxygen in the execution room in case something went wrong. Medical professionals had to retrieve it from elsewhere.
Pike’s attorneys detailed her condition in a new emergency motion filed Friday asking the state to preserve all evidence from the failed execution attempt.
“In the words of one media witness: we have a lot of questions and the Department of Correction has a lot of answers that it needs to provide to the public about what happened here. We agree,” the motion reads.
In their filing, the lawyers described a painful and chaotic scene that unfolded in front of several witnesses, and that they said could have been prevented with the proper care and training.
Medical staff failed to follow basic protocol, like ensuring the needles used were fresh, functional and inserted properly, according to the motion. Further, the state did not heed Pike’s concerns prior to the procedure that preexisting medical conditions could make lethal injection difficult to complete, the motion says.
The motion accuses the department of corrections of “inflicting a cruel and unusual punishment on Ms. Pike through its deliberate indifference to her basic medical needs and reckless disregard of basic medical practices and their own lethal injection protocol.”
The Tennessee Attorney General did not immediately return a request for comment on the new filing. A spokesperson for the state department of corrections said the agency does not comment on pending litigation.
At a news conference Thursday, Stephen Ferrell and another of Pike’s attorneys, Randall Spivey, detailed how the execution attempt went wrong . Spivey, who was in the room, recalled Pike saying she was in pain, and like she felt like her arm was about to “explode.”
“It’s not supposed to be a cruel and an unusual execution,” criminologist Deborah Denno told NBC News. “The goal is to kill somebody, but to kill them within means or in a reasonable way, where there’s not going to be pain and suffering.”
According to Friday’s filing, the execution process lasted longer than two hours. Pike’s legal team filed emergency motions to halt the execution in multiple courts before the prison called an ambulance.
“Even then,” it continues, “attorneys for the State of Tennessee argued that TDOC had no obligation to render life-saving care to Ms. Pike.”
NBC News contributor Dr. Natalie Azar, a rheumatologist, said the pain Pike described could be attributed to pentobarbital flowing into her arm instead of straight into her veins. That would be painful with any medication, Azar said, but the specific properties of pentobarbital would make the experience exceptionally uncomfortable.
The scenario would also result in Pike being administered a less-than-lethal dose. It was enough to suppress her respiratory system but not enough to kill her, Azar explained. The question of how long Pike’s brain was deprived on oxygen will be central to her prognosis.
“There is no reversal of pentobarbital. There is no medicine or antidote,” she said. “You have to basically wait for the liver to metabolize the drug and get it out of your system.”
Pike was convicted in the 1995 murder case. She and two other teenage accomplices worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, Knoxville police said at the time. Pike was sentenced to death. A number of last-minute legal efforts to stop Pike’s execution were unsuccessful.
Jesse Kirsch is a correspondent based in Miami reporting across all NBC News platforms.
Rebecca Cohen is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Abigail Brooks is a producer for NBC News.
Alicia Victoria Lozano is a California-based reporter for NBC News focusing on climate change, wildfires and the changing politics of drug laws.

articles.title_orig: Another disappointing jobs report suggests more challenges for Trump, GOP
articles.title_zh: Another disappointing jobs report suggests more challenges for Trump, GOP
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. economy created far fewer jobs than expected in September, pointing to a surprising soft spot in the labor market and broader economy.
Nonfarm payrolls rose a seasonally adjusted 29,000 for the month while the unemployment rate increased to 4.2%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for job growth of 84,000 and an unemployment rate of 4.1%.
In addition to the weakness in September, the August jobs count was revised lower to reflect a gain of 133,000 while July switched from a gain to a loss as payrolls fell by 10,000. The revisions in total showed 60,000 fewer jobs than previously reported.
Market reaction was swift to the report, with traders interpreting the soft jobs numbers as good news as they likely further cemented the Federal Reserve staying put at its October meeting.
Stock futures rose sharply after the release while Treasury yields slumped after recently rising to levels not seen since the early part of the century. Market-implied odds that the Fed will hold rates steady at its Oct. 27-28 meeting jumped to 82.8%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
"For the Fed, this number should be the nail in the coffin for an October hike," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a note.
"The payroll data surged in August, and we had expected the momentum to continue this month, given the historically low prints on jobless claims in recent weeks," he added. "However, it now appears that the August number was nothing more than a rebound from very weak hiring in June and July."
Fed officials more closely watch the unemployment rate than the headline payrolls numbers.
The household survey, which is used to calculate the jobless level, was considerably better than the establishment survey, which is used to derive the payrolls count.
Household employment rose by 406,000 for the month, while the labor force swelled by 485,000 and the participation rate, which counts those working or actively searching for a job as a share of the total labor force, increased 0.2 percentage point to 61.8%, its highest since May.
An alternative measure of unemployment, which includes discouraged workers and those holding part-time jobs for economic reasons, edged down to 7.6%, its lowest since January 2025.
The report comes with Federal Reserve officials weighing the state of the economy and how it should affect their next interest rate move.
Following statements in recent days from central bank policymakers, markets have recalibrated expectations and now expect the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee to hold off until December for its next hike. The FOMC raised benchmark rates a quarter percentage point in September.
Policymakers largely see inflation as a larger threat to the economy than the labor market, which had shown resilience in recent months. The data has painted a picture of a low-hire, low-fire economy, with weekly jobless claims low and one indicator showing layoffs at their lowest rate in four years.
Inflation, though, has held well above the Fed's 2% target. The most recent indicator of the central bank's preferred gauge showed core inflation at a 3% annual rate.
Wages, though, continued to show signs of disinflation.
Average hourly earnings increased just 0.1% in September, putting the 12-month gain at 3%, the lowest since May 2021. Wall Street had been looking for readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, respectively. The average work week was unchanged at 34.6 hours.
"Americans are frustrated by the lack of opportunities right now," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "Wage growth fell to a new 5-year low and is being wiped out entirely by inflation. That stings heading into the holidays."
However, Long described the labor market as "stable" and said she doesn't think the Fed will be dissuaded from hiking in December.
Most of the monthly job gains came from healthcare, which added 17,000 workers. Construction was up by 11,000, and manufacturing added 9,000.
Government employment fell by 17,000, while temporary help services saw a decline of 11,000, and information services lost 10,000 amid worries over the impact artificial intelligence may have on the jobs picture. Financial activities also saw a drop of 7,000 jobs.
The weak job growth comes despite signs of strength elsewhere.
On a macro level, economic growth has been strong.
Earlier this week, the Commerce Department revised its count of both first- and second-quarter gross domestic product growth, to 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively. The Atlanta Fed is tracking third-quarter GDP at 3.7%.

articles.title_orig: GOP super PAC cancels spending in North Carolina Senate race, shifting money to Kansas
articles.title_zh: GOP super PAC cancels spending in North Carolina Senate race, shifting money to Kansas
articles.content_orig:
A top Republican super PAC is canceling its ad spending in the Senate race in North Carolina and launching a new ad effort in Kansas, the latest sign the fight for the majority is shifting to red states amid an increasingly tough landscape for the GOP.
The new moves from the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, were first reported by Semafor as a “pause” in spending, confirmed by two people with knowledge of the decision.
After the ad-tracking firm AdImpact reported the group was also removing funds from North Carolina, one person familiar with the decision confirmed that the group is canceling the ads planned for October.
Ad spending decisions can provide clear signals about the races parties and outside groups view as the most competitive and further out of reach.
SLF’s move to direct resources to Kansas underscores how Democrats are putting traditionally Republican states in play as they try to net four seats to take control of the Senate. Democrats will need to win multiple states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024, in addition to defending seats in battleground states.
As Election Day draws closer, Democrats are growing more optimistic about their chances as Trump’s approval ratings drop and voters express frustrations with high costs and the Iran war.
The race in Kansas between GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton has become more competitive in the homestretch, even though the state has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.
So far, SLF has reserved more than $8 million in airtime in Kansas, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
SLF had been actively involved in North Carolina, where former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley is facing former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat. In September, the group spent more than $17 million on the race, according to AdImpact.
Trump and Vice President JD Vance also each traveled to the state last month to boost Whatley, whom the president personally encouraged to run for the open seat.
But the decision to pause spending in North Carolina, a perennial battleground, is a sign that the race to replace retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is drifting away from the GOP.
“I am worried about him. I hope he wins,” Trump told reporters Friday of Whatley. “He’s a great man.”
Republicans have been pessimistic for weeks about their prospects in the state, with Cooper leading in recent polling and outspending Whatley.
The party’s level of confidence in their chances of defeating Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia has also been dwindling, but one person familiar with SLF’s spending noted the group has not paused its spending in that race. Trump won Georgia by just 2 points in 2024.
Still, SLF has focused the bulk of its resources on other hotly contested Senate races.
In September, SLF spent $78 million on ads in Texas through an affiliated group, and SLF itself spent nearly $33 million in Ohio. Elsewhere, the group last month spent $16 million in Michigan, $15 million in Iowa, $13 million in Maine, $10 million in Georgia, $8 million in Alaska and $5 million in New Hampshire, according to AdImpact.
In the month of October through the Nov. 3 election, SLF’s Texas group has booked $48 million in ads, while SLF is set to spend $40 million in Ohio, $18 million in Michigan, $17 million in Maine, $16 million in Georgia, nearly $14 million in Iowa, $8 million in New Hampshire and $5 million in Alaska.
Trump carried Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska all by double digits in 2024.
Even as SLF looks to spend its resources elsewhere, the North Carolina Senate candidates are still bracing for a hotly contested race.
Whatley spokesman DJ Griffin said in a statement that Cooper recently noted Democrats are often ahead “until they’re not.”
“Undecided Voters who break late decide the election in North Carolina and the majority of those Late-Breakers typically go Republican,” Griffin said. “We feel confident we have the resources to highlight Career Politician Roy Cooper’s 40 Years of Failures and win in November.”
Cooper campaign manager Jeff Allen also suggested the race is still competitive, noting in a statement that a Democrat has not been elected to the Senate in North Carolina in nearly 20 years and describing North Carolina as “a 50-50 state.”
“We’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them, while Michael Whatley will continue to enrich himself at their expense,” Allen said.
Bridget Bowman is a national political reporter for NBC News.
