articles.title_orig: Community Banks Swing Back at Trump Regulators Over Crypto Charters
articles.title_zh: Community Banks Swing Back at Trump Regulators Over Crypto Charters
articles.content_orig:
Independent Community Bankers of America sued the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency , alleging that the regulator authorized cryptocurrency firms to enter the banking system without being subject to the same scrutiny as community banks, according to a Friday (Oct. 2) press release from the association.
The lawsuit centers on the OCC’s March 2 final rule related to Interpretive Letter No. 1176. The lawsuit says the rule and the guidance attempt to provide the OCC with new powers to charter national banks that are not authorized by the National Bank Act. It asks a federal court to find both the final rule and the letter unlawful, according to the release.
“The OCC’s decision to allow companies to obtain national trust bank charters to conduct substantial non-fiduciary activities exceeds the authority Congress granted the agency,” ICBA President and CEO Rebeca Romero Rainey said in the release. “Congress did not create the national trust charter as a side door into the banking system for crypto firms seeking the credibility of a federal bank charter without the Community Reinvestment Act obligations, consolidated supervision, capital and liquidity standards, and FDIC insurance that apply to insured depository institutions.”

Please add us to your preferred sources list so our news, data and interviews show up in your feed. Thanks!
The OCC did not immediately reply to PYMNTS’ request for comment.
When issuing the National Bank Chartering final rule, the OCC said it clarifies “the longstanding authority of national banks limited to the operations of trust companies and activities related thereto to engage in non-fiduciary activities in addition to their fiduciary activities. The final rule would neither expand nor contract the OCC’s authority to charter a national bank.”
A Bank Policy Institute executive responded to ICBA’s suit against the OCC by saying that novel entities should be subject to the same scrutiny as other chartered institutions.
“As we’ve said in comments filed on numerous national trust bank charter applications, BPI supports efforts to bring innovative new products and services into the regulated banking ecosystem, provided that the entities engaging in those activities are subject to the same rules and responsibilities as every other chartered institution engaging in the same activities,” Paige Pidano Paridon , executive vice president and co-head of regulatory affairs at BPI, said in a Friday statement . “Companies should not receive trust charters unless they plan to limit their operations to genuine trust activities. If they want to engage in traditional banking activities, they should seek full-service banking charters.”
PYMNTS reported March 2 that the OCC said its amendment to the final rule is intended to eliminate potential confusion created by earlier regulatory text and to align its rule more closely with the National Bank Act.
The OCC has long supervised national trust banks, many of which conduct non-fiduciary custody and safekeeping activities in addition to fiduciary services, the report said.
“By explicitly referencing ‘operations of a trust company and activities related thereto,’ the rule confirms that trust-chartered national banks are not confined solely to traditional fiduciary function, which in turn offers a bit of runway for an expanded scope of activities,” the PYMNTS report said.

articles.title_orig: As Trump's proposed arch looms over D.C., protesters pin their hopes on the midterms
articles.title_zh: As Trump's proposed arch looms over D.C., protesters pin their hopes on the midterms
articles.content_orig:
Demonstrators gathered Thursday morning to protest Trump's proposed arch, which would stand in a traffic circle on the bridge connecting the National Mall to Arlington National Cemetery. Saul Loeb/AFP hide caption
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Dozens of activists gathered at Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C., at rush hour Thursday to protest the 250-foot-tall arch that President Trump wants to build there.
Veterans, retirees and lawmakers spoke out — against its scale, its cost, its lack of Congressional approval, its gaudiness, its intrusion on nearby Arlington National Cemetery and more — next to a mockup made of tarp. The real arch, they said, would be 32 times taller.
"It's the wrong monument, in the wrong place, at the wrong time, dedicated to the wrong man," said Jon Gundersen, a retired Army veteran and former Foreign Service officer who is one of the Vietnam War veterans suing the Trump administration over the arch.
Gundersen traveled from South Carolina to speak at Thursday's protest, which was billed as "Vets over Vanity. It was organized in part by Public Citizen, the group leading that lawsuit. He told NPR that it was "heartening" to see so much support for their cause.
"Anyone I talk to, whether Republican or Democrat, they say it's a waste of money and it's not how you honor vets," he said.
Many speakers were especially concerned about the impact of an arch towering over nearby Arlington National Cemetery, and criticized the lack of input from veterans and gold star families in the process.
"I am pissed that the five-time draft dodging coward of a commander-in-chief sitting over there in the White House dares to dishonor the men and women of this country who have put on her collars and sacrificed and served and now lay at rest in the hallowed grounds of Arlington National Cemetery," said Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., who said she and her husband will join them one day.
The White House has told NPR that the arch will "enhance the visitor experience" at the cemetery and serve "as a visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes." But Duckworth and others say a better way to honor veterans would be to spend money on improving services for them, not on a triumphal arch with an observation deck.
Protesters stand Thursday in Memorial Circle near a mockup of Trump's arch, which they say would be 32 times taller. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
"Imagine tourists coming up to this arch looking at the 24 to 27 funerals up there in Arlington," Gundersen said. "It's not only wrong and inappropriate, it's obscene and should never [be] done."
During the half-hour of rapid-fire speeches, the crowd burst into loud applause, sporadic chants of "no arch!" and, at one point, a coordinated rendition of We Shall Overcome . Cyclists and commuters passing by offered supportive waves and honks.
Planes flew overhead every few minutes, a constant reminder that the arch would stand along the approach of one of the nation's busiest airport runways. Several of the speakers addressed the aviation safety concerns raised by the arch and by Trump's recent announcement that the structure will house military drones and snipers .
"Who are the snipers going to shoot — the families at the graves or the tourists at the Lincoln Memorial?" Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., said from the podium. "The real explanation is Trump thinks he's going to lose in court, and maybe if he shouts national security, the Supreme Court will care."
The White House, Department of Interior and Federal Aviation Administration have not responded to NPR's questions about the military complex. The Trump administration has not elaborated publicly on what rebranding the structure could mean for the ongoing federal approval process, despite mounting confusion.
But it did drop hints in a meeting earlier this week.
Administration officials told historic preservation groups in a Tuesday Zoom call that they were unaware of any new submissions and planned to move forward with the original arch proposal, according to a transcript and recording later shared with NPR.
And — despite the public pushback, an ongoing lawsuit and many unanswered questions — that proposal is hurtling towards final federal approval.
The arch is widely expected to come before the National Capital Planning Commission at its next meeting in early November.
As part of the required federal review process, the National Park Service had been in conversation with outside groups to negotiate how to build the arch while doing the least harm to the dozens of nearby protected landmarks . The park service had already dismissed experts' suggestions to build the arch elsewhere.
Then, the last week of September — just days after Trump's military complex announcement — the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation terminated the review process altogether. That was announced in an email to historic preservation groups, reviewed by NPR.
Charles Birnbaum, who participated in the process as the head of The Cultural Landscape Foundation, said he was appalled that the council cut the review short after only two meetings. He recalled this happening only twice in the 15 years he previously spent working for the National Park Service.
"Projects go to the advisory council when there is a stalemate that people have tried to negotiate with state preservation officers, with stakeholders, and there is an authenticity to that process," Birnbaum said.
Instead, the advisory council now says it will give its recommendations directly to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum by Oct. 7.
"They're going to force this upon the process and they're going to nullify outside voices. And what this is symbolic of is where the administration is taking the nation," said Birnbaum, referring to the same council's efforts to roll back protections for historic sites nationwide . Separately, a bipartisan permitting reform bill gaining traction in Congress would also weaken those protections.
Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., speaks to demonstrators at Thursday's event. His efforts to block federal funding for the arch were rejected by a GOP senator earlier in the week. Allison Robbert/AP hide caption
Protesters on Thursday vowed not to let the arch proceed — but braced for the possibility that it might.
"We have to continue to call in to our senators, our congresspeople, and let them say no to this arc," said Julius D. "JD" Spain Sr., a member of the Arlington County Board. "And if it is built, if somehow it is built, I will get my chisel and I'll be right over there with everybody tearing it down."
That prompted some of the loudest applause of the morning. Beyer, whose district includes Arlington, told NPR afterward that there is a "huge body of people ready to protest the moment they see a shovel."
"I don't know how this will play out, whether we end up with tents or hunger strikes, but I know that the American people are ready to protest in any way they can," he said.
There is another possibility, at least in theory: Congress could stop the arch by blocking federal funding from going towards the project. Earlier this week, a single Republican senator blocked Democrats' attempts to stop the construction of the arch as well as the demolition of the Kennedy Center.
"We could stop this today if the Republican majority stepped up and grew a backbone and would oppose Trump," Duckworth told NPR in a phone interview Wednesday.
Next month's midterm elections could change the balance of power in Congress — and, if Democrats prevail, spell bad news for the arch starting in January.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: US FAA says Boeing 737 MAX software glitch poses no safety issue
articles.title_zh: US FAA says Boeing 737 MAX software glitch poses no safety issue
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday that it has determined a new software glitch on some Boeing 737 Max aircraft isn't a flight-safety issue.
The determination paves the way to certification for the last model in the company's best-selling family of airplanes, the 737 Max 10, just as Boeing seeking to sell and deliver more aircraft after years of safety and manufacturing crises.
Boeing flagged the software issue, which could affect certain landing procedures, last month and the FAA on Monday said it was reviewing to determine if it poses a safety of flight issue.
"Following a thorough review, a panel of FAA safety experts on Friday determined a software issue in certain Boeing 737 MAX flight computers is not a safety concern," the FAA said. "The FAA's Corrective Action Review Board made that determination because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous."
Boeing said the issue could arise after a missed approach when pilots alter a preprogrammed flight path, and that pilots must take additional steps to use automated tools on subsequent approaches.
The FAA said on Friday that it will issue a special bulletin to airlines on how to recognize and respond to the issue if it arises.
The agency convened a review board on Friday to assess the issue. Participants included FAA experts on airframes, flight controls, propulsion, flight testing and others.
"As with any situation, the FAA will consider appropriate action if it receives new information about this issue," the agency said.
U.S. airlines said they're not affected by the issue since they could revert to older versions of the software, but the problem raised questions about certification of the Boeing 737 Max 10, which Boeing and airlines expected to come in early fall.
The Max 10 is the largest in the family of airplanes and would be the last of the Max lineup to win government certification to fly. The FAA approved the Max 7 , the smallest in the Max family, in August.
Chief executives of 737 Max 10 customers, Alaska Airlines and Ryanair, earlier this week brushed off concerns about the aircraft's certification delays.

articles.title_orig: As fires rage in Borneo, several of the world’s rarest primates are continually threatened
articles.title_zh: As fires rage in Borneo, several of the world’s rarest primates are continually threatened
articles.content_orig:
A nonprofit environmental group working with primates in Sebangau National Park says the dry peatlands can be a catalyst to more destruction.
(CN) â Since early August, wildfires have devastated the fragile rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra, causing widespread toxic air across Indonesia. Itâs affected most communities in all parts of the region of Kalimantan, a part of the worldâs third largest island under Indonesiaâs governance.
The fires are fueled by shifting El NiÃ±o climate patterns, causing severe drought and extremely dry conditions in the islandâs peatlands, among the planetâs most effective carbon-capturing ecosystems and vital habitat for wildlife found nowhere else in the world.
Sebangau National Park in Central Kalimantan is home to an estimated 6,000 to 9,000 critically endangered Bornean orangutans, one of the islandâs largest populations. The nonprofit Borneo Nature Foundation said a fire crossed the park boundary for the first time in early September.
âOur teams pushed it back, and it was largely confined to sedge and open peat, but some reforestation sites are impacted,â Dr. Susan Cheyne, the Science Director for the Borneo Nature Foundation and the Vice Chair for the International Union for the Conservation of Nature special project group for small apes, said in an email to Courthouse News.
âOur priority is to keep fire out of the forest, because that protects every orangutan in it at once,â she said. Cheyne and her colleagues monitor and document conditions in Borneo, while volunteer firefighting crews work to keep fires out of orangutan habitat and nearby villages. Capturing and removing the apes is âa last resort,â Cheyne said.
Sebangau is also home to several of the worldâs rarest primates, including the largest known population of Bornean white-bearded gibbons, an ape Cheyne has studied for over 20 years.
Gibbons are known for their musical vocalizations, or âsongs.â Males sing alone in the morning before females join them in duets later in the day.
âDuring the 2006 fires I found that gibbons sang less often and sang shorter songs on smoky days. Their song is how they defend territory and keep pair bonds, so this matters,â said Cheyne. âA similar pattern has since been recorded in wild Bornean orangutans exposed to wildfire smoke.â
Gibbons rarely come to the ground, and fire survivors are often left in small, isolated forest patches with little food. Other primates, including red langurs and long-tailed and southern pig-tailed macaques, are found only in Southeast Asia, and each fire further reduces their numbers. Little is known about how fires affect nocturnal slow lorises and western tarsiers, Cheyne said.
The national park includes vast peat swamps, made of partly decomposed plant material accumulated over thousands of years. In parts of Sebangau, the peat dome reaches 12 meters deep.
Peatlands are naturally waterlogged, like giant sponges that do not burn. But in the 1990s and early 2000s, illegal loggers dug hundreds of canals to float timber out of the forest. Those canals continue draining the peat, causing it to dry out and become fuel.
âIn a long dry season like this one, a dried-out peat swamp is a tinderbox,â said Cheyne.
âWhat makes peat fires so hard to fight is that they burn downwards and sideways, not just across the surface. Fire smolders underground through the dry peat, sometimes for weeks, long after the flames above have gone out. These are sometimes called zombie fires.â
Peat fires are particularly dangerous because from the surface, a person may see nothing amiss, perhaps âjust a thin wisp of smoke,â Cheyne said, while a meter below the peat burns and can set nearby tree roots aflame, easily toppling them. And peat fires also produce dense, toxic smoke.
Cheyne said since 2015, the foundation and local crews have built over 1,000 dams to block drainage canals, planted almost a million trees, drilled hundreds of water boreholes and increased support for up to eight fire teams.
âThat preparation is why we are holding,â she said. But itâs still a tenuous situation. For the short-term, Cheyne said, the goal is to keep the firefighting teams in the field fed, equipped and safe, which costs about $100 a day per team. It also means investing in equipment, such as thermal drones that can detect underground peat fires and rewetting the peat, so it doesnât reignite. The foundation, she said, is actively seeking donations from international bodies, advocacy groups and concerned individuals.
While hotspots in Kalimantan have declined since the beginning of the month, according to the foundation, rains are not expected until late October or November.
âWe are not out of this yet,â said Cheyne.
Cheyne said Borneo Nature Foundation Internationalâs co-founder Simon Husson recently passed a troop of monkeys on a river trip and they moved through trees beside mile after mile of burned riverbank.
âThat is the picture,â she said. âLife hanging on right at the edge.â

articles.title_orig: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France
articles.title_zh: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France
articles.content_orig:
Riot police have clashed with protesters as thousands of students demonstrating over education standards disrupted more than 700 schools in France.
Fires have burned in the streets as high school pupils and others objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 1,747 people were arrested on Friday.
The protests began last week in the capital Paris and have spread across the country, with cities including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille affected.
French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said things had "gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public order disturbance".
Darmanin said that 735 of France's 3,700 schools were now affected "one way or another" by the violent protests.
Announcing the arrests late on Friday, Nuñez told France's TF1 television network: "We are sliding into riot and urban violence, and we are using all intermediate means to put an end to it."
Meanwhile, Education Minister Édouard Geffray said the movement had been hijacked by non-students.
He told French broadcaster BFMTV that teachers had said "the people in front of me were not my students".
Earlier on Friday, a 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after protests in Belfort, north-eastern France, where a police officer was targeted.
BBC Verify has now authenticated two videos that show the man, who was later identified as an officer by a minister, being beaten up.
In the graphic footage, a group of young men are seen chasing him. The officer falls to the ground, and is subsequently punched and kicked multiple times in the head.
At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the education ministry said.
In the Paris suburb of Pantin police charged at protesters and made arrests after projectiles where thrown at officers.
Meanwhile, in Strasbourg tear gas was deployed as police feared conditions would become more hostile, according to the Reuters news agency.
Rubbish bins have also been set on fire in Rennes and Paris.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won - our school is closed this morning," Lola, a 16-year-old protester, told the AFP news agency on Friday.
She said police actions had made things worse.
"It makes us even angrier - the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she added.
Police published pictures of some of the items they had seized from demonstrators, including petrol bombs, an axe and so-called mortar fireworks.
"Significant damage" had been done to school facilities, the education ministry said, after attacks on school gates, entrances and fences.
Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes suffered more than €2m (£1.7m) damage, according to the regional government, after fire destroyed its glass entrance and some areas inside the school.
The blockades and protests started last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.
Students say school hours are too long, classrooms too hot and too many members of staff are off work.
It comes at a crucial time for French President Emmanuel Macron, six months before next year's presidential election.
Budget cuts planned, which will impact on education funding, have infuriated the young protesters.
Parents have also been worried that their children have become caught up in a wave of violence and unrest.
At the Claude Monet school in southern Paris, 53-year-old Anya was looking for her son.
"We banned him from coming. I hope he isn't here, but he did leave the house," she told AFP. "We're afraid the situation might escalate."
Darmanin said prosecutors had been asked to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children and "pay for repairs".
Many French unions have given their support to the protesting students.
Education union SNEP-FSU, public services union SNUEP-FSU and Solidaires have all called for members to support them.
Solidaires Trade Union Federation said in a statement: "Let's not let them fire on our children.
"Secondary school pupils have the freedom of assembly, association and demonstration."

articles.title_orig: Hawaii's iconic 500-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch has collapsed into the sea
articles.title_zh: Hawaii's iconic 500-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch has collapsed into the sea
articles.content_orig:
Hawaii's famous Hōlei Sea Arch, a 90-foot-tall (27.4m) lava rock structure that formed about 550 years ago, has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean.
The collapse's exact time is not known. The arch was still projecting into the water from the coast of Volcanoes National Park on 23 September, but was gone by 27 September, the National Park Service (NPS) said.
"The coastline flanking the sea arch has shown signs of instability for years," NPS, which warned in 2021 that the arch would eventually crumble, said in a statement.
Located at the end of Chain of Craters Road on the island of Hawaii, also called "the big island", the formation was a popular - and heavily photographed - tourist destination.
The arch is believed to have fallen when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo last weekend.
The park service said earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcano eruption and summit collapse had damaged the cliffs near the arch.
Its ultimate collapse marks "the latest transformation of the park's remote and rugged coastline".
In January 2020, new cracks and instability in the cliffs led the park to close the original arch viewing area, and a few months later, a new viewing area opened at a safer distance, NPS said.
Waves from a tropical storm later that year broke off a chunk of rock from the bottom of the arch.
"This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span," the park service said in 2021. "The sea arch will eventually crumble into the sea. However, others will replace it as the cliff slowly migrates inland."
Thousands of people have liked and commented on the NPS social media post about the arch's collapse, including sharing their memories of visiting the arch and posting photos of it.
"Nothing and no one is here forever," one Facebook user commented. "Millions of years from now the sun will die. Appreciate the good, the beauty, now."

articles.title_orig: ‘HomePad’ coming: Will Apple hold an October special event?
articles.title_zh: ‘HomePad’ coming: Will Apple hold an October special event?
articles.content_orig:
With Apple reportedly planning to unveil new products on October 13, here’s when the company could announce an event, based on the timing of its previous October announcements.
While Apple’s September event history tends to follow a very predictable pattern, the company’s October event history is much less precise, both in terms of when the events are held and how far in advance they are announced.
Since 2010, Apple has held an October event just 10 times, with the most recent one being the Halloween-themed “Scary Fast” event on the evening of October 30, 2023.
Here’s how far in advance Apple has announced each of its October events since 2010:
That said, Bloomberg recently reported that Apple plans to unveil its long-rumored smart home hub , a new generation of the HomePod mini , and a new Siri AI-powered Apple TV 4K on Tuesday, October 13, though it did not specify whether the company will hold an event to announce the products.
If that turns out to be the case, Apple could potentially announce the event as early as next Monday, October 5, but likely no later than Wednesday, October 7.
It’s worth noting that Apple is also expected to announce an OLED iPad mini , new iMacs , and several new MacBook Pros , including touchscreen models, in 2026. So it remains to be seen whether some of those products would be unveiled at the same event, at a separate event, or through press releases.
Looking back, Apple announced new Macs through press releases over three consecutive days in October 2024, while in October 2025, it unveiled the M5 chip alongside new iPad Pro, MacBook Pro, and Apple Vision Pro models without holding an event.
By contrast, Apple has only held a November event once, in 2020, when its “One More Thing” event introduced the first Macs powered by the M1 Apple silicon chip.
Of course, 2020 was an unusual year for Apple’s event schedule, with the company also holding separate events in September and October after a rare late-June WWDC, as the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted its usual timeline.

articles.title_orig: Amazon’s $1B plan to combat data center backlash draws more backlash
articles.title_zh: Amazon’s $1B plan to combat data center backlash draws more backlash
articles.content_orig:
On Friday, Amazon committed to donating more than $1 billion over the next five years to communities neighboring data centers.
In a press release , Amazon Web Services’ CEO Matt Garman said that communities would decide how to prioritize funds across “education, job training, energy affordability, water, and energy preservation, and local priorities.”
Laying out other community commitments, Amazon also promised to ensure data centers wouldn’t increase power bills or wipe out local water supplies. Regarding the latter, Amazon promised to be “water positive” by 2030, while claiming that 75 percent of projects have already met this goal.
Rolling out these commitments, Amazon seemed bent on convincing Americans that the swelling data center backlash is based on lies. Echoing Donald Trump’s claims that foreign disinformation campaigns are fueling widespread protests, Garman urged that calls for data moratoriums must end or else American frontier AI might fall behind China’s.
According to Garman, US rivals are trying to “trick us into slowing down,” and Amazon’s commitments are meant to reassure Americans that everything’s okay and that we should instead plow ahead, as Trump endlessly advocates.
However, advocates at Stand.Earth—a global nonprofit that’s been fighting for environmental protections in communities hosting data centers—told Ars that Amazon is the one being “misleading” by spreading “corporate propaganda.” Seemingly in crisis mode as billions of dollars in data center projects have been blocked nationwide, Amazon’s promised donations represent “a flailing attempt at damage control for the harm its data center build-out has already caused,” Stand.Earth said.
Most problematic, Stand.Earth suggested, is Amazon’s plan to back a power plant that experts expect will become the largest source of US climate pollution. Glaringly, Amazon’s data center commitments don’t mention the power plant and scarcely address pollution, apart from promising to exclusively rely on back-up generators that use the lowest possible emissions.
“For all the claims Amazon makes about investing in carbon-free energy, it conveniently leaves out that it is constructing the single-largest source of climate emissions in the United States in Pecos, Texas,” Stand.Earth said. “Communities will face 33 million tons of harmful air pollution every year—with the power plant using the same amount of energy needed to run more than 1.9 million homes.”
Additionally, Stand.Earth called out Amazon for claiming that most data center generators sparking pollution fears in communities typically sit “idle.” Although Amazon emphasized that most generators only run for “roughly 10 hours per year,” Stand.Earth cited cases where “Amazon data centers ran on diesel back-up power for days at a time.”
At least one part of Amazon’s deal is promising, Stand.Earth suggested. The company ending its practice of using nondisclosure agreements when building new data centers will likely help make projects more transparent.
However, “many of the key concerns communities have are not addressed,” Stand.Earth found. For example, Amazon’s promises to replace all water used for data centers seemingly won’t address “the massive water footprint left by energy infrastructure powering its data centers” or “the potential for forever-chemical contamination from nascent cooling technologies,” Stand.Earth told Ars.
The total amount Amazon is investing also doesn’t seem like much compared to what the company has spent. In the press release, Garman said that Amazon contributed the same amount, more than $1 billion, to data center communities over the past three years.
“Compared to the $220 billion the company is investing in data centers in 2026 alone, Amazon’s commitment of $1 billion over five years for community support is a drop in the bucket,” Stand.Earth said. “It is difficult to read this statement as anything other than a plea from Amazon to continue exploiting communities at minimal cost.”

articles.title_orig: How long would it take the world to run out of clothing if production suddenly stopped?
articles.title_zh: How long would it take the world to run out of clothing if production suddenly stopped?
articles.content_orig:
One expert told Marketplace that it could take up to 20 years. People would start tapping into textile waste dumps around the world and, of course, their own closets.
This is just one of the stories from our “I’ve Always Wondered” series, where we tackle all of your questions about the world of business, no matter how big or small. Ever wondered if recycling is worth it ? Or how store brands stack up against name brands? Check out more from the series here .
Anne Crabbe from Paso Robles, California, asks:
I've always wondered how long it would take for the world to run out of clothes if all production of clothes stopped at once. There are SO many clothes out there (at least here in North America). If the entire world had to use the current supply of all the clothes existing now, when would stores run out? TJ Maxx, Nordstrom Rack, all the thrift stores. I assume (and hope), we would run out of under garments first, then socks, maybe? A ton of assumptions have to be made to answer this, but can it even be answered?
Billions and billions of items of clothing are produced each year, but if clothing production suddenly stopped, snapping up all those garments might take less time than you might think
Depending on your assumptions, it might take up to 20 years for the world to run out of clothing, said Julia DeVoy, who studies the fast-fashion industry and serves as dean of undergraduate programs and students at the Boston College Lynch School of Education and Human Development.
And yes, undergarments and socks would be the first to go, she said.
There would also be a gold rush for materials with higher-quality fiber, like cotton and denim.
"People would want that more, whether it's getting it at a thrift store, or grabbing whatever was on the shelves, or trading with other people who had closets. And there would also be a radical shift towards mending," DeVoy said.
DeVoy estimates that discount and big-box stores in the U.S. would take one month to run out of clothing. These stores operate a just-in time model, which means they only get clothing as needed.
TJX, the parent company of T.J. Maxx and Marshalls, reported its days inventory at 70 days as of mid-2026, which means that shelves would last nine to 10 weeks with zero restocking based on normal demand, DeVoy said. TJX arrives at this figure by taking the existing inventory and dividing it by the current sales rate, DeVoy explained.
But if clothing production stopped, then demand would go up.
"What happened during the pandemic with certain products? People thought they couldn't get hand sanitizer,” DeVoy said. “Basically, what would happen is all the stock on the shelves, because of the just-in-time [model] and the lean inventory that actually sits in the stores, there would be a panic, and all of the existing stock would be wiped out from the store themselves,"
During COVID-19 stockpiling, sales of household staples spiked between 70% to 170% above normal, and spending on stock-up categories ran 70% to 80% above the daily average, DeVoy said.
So if we assume that panic buying doubled demand, which is a conservative estimate, then that would halve the amount of time it would normally take for clothing to run out, leaving discount stores about four to five weeks before clothing ran out, DeVoy said.
People would also look to  thrift stores. Thrift stores are overwhelmed with donations, but they only use about 20% to 30% of the items they receive, DeVoy said. "The remaining 70% to 80% is currently exported, incinerated, or landfilled. This is not because it's all unsellable, but because the humongous volume exceeds available shelf capacity," DeVoy said.
But even if they sold their full backlog instead of incinerating it, DeVoy said they would still sell out in a matter of months.
As stores across the country ran out of clothing, people could tap into other sources that would probably become available. About 100 billion garments are produced a year, with 45 billion garments never reaching the buyer. This is referred to as  "dead stock," which means they're never sold or end up incinerated, DeVoy said.
"There would be this giant hidden reserve that we would keep probably for about the first five years," DeVoy said.
If eight billion people received a modest one to two garments per year, each, that works out to eight to 16 billion garments annually. If there are 45 billion garments, that means there would be three to five years of deadstock, DeVoy said.
There are also massive textile waste dumps around the world, which would now become a vital resource of clothing, and there's a huge surplus of clothing in people's homes, DeVoy said.
The Atacama Desert in Chile receives 131,000 tons of used textiles annually, with over 70%, or 92,000 tons, going directly into landfills or in other illegal dumps, while Ghana's Kantamanto market in Accra receives about 15 million garments a week, of which over 40% becomes direct textile waste, DeVoy said.
"Comparable sites exist all over Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America," DeVoy said.
And people normally only wear 20% of the clothing that they own, with Americans buying 68 new clothing items a year, so they could use the remaining 80% of clothing that's sitting in their closets, DeVoy said.
She estimates that both of these sources of clothing could stretch around 15 years.
One often-cited claim is that we have enough clothing on the planet to last about six generations. But the math and even the original source behind this figure is unclear, according to the BBC, which investigated the claim's origins .
Getting a solid figure is tough – some of those garments in our closet last longer than others, which is just one of the complications that arise when trying to answer this question. "Synthetic fibers tend to last longer and they don't tend to biodegrade very quickly, so we would probably end up with more polyester," said Tasha Lewis, an associate clinical professor in fashion and retail studies at Ohio State University. "We still don't have a good timeline for how long polyester will take to go away because we still have most of it."
We'd also probably think about recycling the clothing that we do have, so we'll still have clothes available to us, Lewis said.
But since clothing production probably won't come to a halt anytime soon, we still have mountains of clothing to deal with. There have been changes in social expectations on how often you should change your clothes and how much variety you should have, said Abigail Clarke-Sather, an associate professor of mechanical and industrial engineering at the University of Minnesota Duluth who's an expert on textile recycling.
"Closet sizes have gotten bigger over the last century because we store so much that we don't know what to do with," Clarke-Sather said.

articles.title_orig: Poor communication marred emergency response to deadly L.A. area fires, report finds
articles.title_zh: Poor communication marred emergency response to deadly L.A. area fires, report finds
articles.content_orig:
During last year’s fires in the Los Angeles area, police dispatchers had to temporarily route 911 calls through a single captain’s personal cellphone. So many calls came in that some firefighter units went “dark” — meaning dispatchers were no longer tracking them. As communications broke down, some firefighters began to take their cues from captains they trusted instead of the agency’s top leaders.
These are just a few examples of emergency communications failures described in a new, comprehensive review of the deadly fires. The findings paint a picture of a response marred by poor preparation, communication issues and disorganized leadership that struggled to coordinate between jurisdictions.
The 724-page report, released Friday, comes from UL Research Institutes (ULRI) , an organization that focuses on safety science. Gov. Gavin Newsom tasked the researchers with evaluating the conditions, decisions, actions and systems that influenced the conflagration. This is the second of two ULRI reports evaluating the fires.
Overall, the researchers found that Los Angeles authorities were not prepared or trained for such extreme conditions and that they struggled to work side by side as the situation deteriorated.
On the night the Eaton Fire took off, for example, “the speed and scale of the event overwhelmed the 911 system,” Derek Alconis, a senior research program manager and lead investigator at ULRI, said in a news briefing. “Calls came in faster than dispatch could manage or assign them.”
As the situation worsened, agencies struggled to communicate, and those in charge lost track of where crews were working and what they were doing.
“It was not an effective unified command,” Alconis said, adding that the confusion hampered evacuation efforts.
The report confirmed previous assessments of how the Palisades Fire started: LAFD did not fully mop up an earlier burn in the area. The department did not have standards for that kind of work, the report says.
The original burn, called the Lachman Fire, was the result of an alleged arson . The trial of the man accused of starting that fire ended in a mistrial this summer after the jury deadlocked. A second trial is scheduled for this fall.
In a statement, LAFD said it was carefully reviewing the analysis.
“While FSRI found that no single decision explains last January’s tragedy, that does not lessen LAFD’s responsibility for the decisions that were ours,” LAFD said. “The report identifies a number of areas where the LAFD must do better. They include how we confirm a fire is truly out before dangerous weather returns, how we track and direct every unit on a major fire, and how we plan and carry out evacuations with our partners. We accept those findings.”
The department said it had implemented a series of changes after its own review, including improving staffing procedures during dangerous fire weather and developing protocols to ensure fires are fully extinguished.
“This report holds the LAFD to a high standard, as it should,” the statement said. “We will carefully evaluate every recommendation that applies to us, continue to track our progress, and strengthen our ability to protect the communities we serve.”
The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s office said it had not had time to review the report but that it is updating its 38-year-old dispatch system and bringing on 80 new dispatchers. Since the fires, it has also equipped patrol vehicles with warning sirens for evacuations and strengthened its evacuation policy and training, the office said, along with upgrading emergency communications and fire protection equipment, among other measures.
The Los Angeles Police Department did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the Los Angeles County Fire Department said it is implementing recommendations from other post-fire reviews but had not had time to review the new recommendations in detail.
The fires, which started during a windstorm in January 2025, killed 31 people in the Pacific Palisades and Altadena communities. The blazes destroyed more than 16,250 homes and commercial buildings . Many residents still have not returned home and have struggled to clean up contamination left by smoke and debris. Frustration over the fire response and the rebuilding effort has become a heated election issue in the Los Angeles mayoral race.
The new report says, however, that the shortcomings it outlines did not drive the tragedy. Emergency responders were up against extreme fire behavior in windy conditions that made the homes themselves the fire’s fuel.
“The conditions in January 2025 were perfect for fire,” said Steve Kerber, a vice president at ULRI who leads its Fire Safety Research Institute. “The speed, scale and complexity of the Palisades and Eaton fires exceeded many of the capabilities of the systems designed to support suppression.”
Many of the 175 findings in the report will not come as a surprise to those who have followed the flurry of lawsuits, investigative news reports and city and county after-action reviews. But it offers a comprehensive picture of what went wrong, as well as something of a road map for the wind-driven urban firestorms that are growing more common across the West.
Among its 266 recommendations are to increase training opportunities for wildfire and incident management in California, to equip command staff with portable satellite internet kits in case of communication failures, and to train firefighters to use water from residential pools.
The report describes plenty of successes, as well. The authors said that the National Weather Service effectively communicated the extreme fire weather threat, and it credited a program of volunteers called Community Brigade with helping residents to evacuate. Private fire companies, too, helped save some structures and prevent fire spread, it says, though the report acknowledges that private firefighting is controversial.
ULRI also produced an after-action report about the 2023 Lahaina fires in Maui, an effort the authors said they were just finishing when the Palisades and Eaton fires took off. They immediately saw similarities between the events, in which fast-spreading, wind-driven fires overwhelmed fire departments.
To understand what went wrong in Los Angeles, the researchers behind the report evaluated in person more than 900 structures that burned and interviewed 200 residents and 295 people working at 22 agencies involved in the fire response. The team reviewed 911 calls, radio communications, dispatch data, evacuation maps, staffing plans and more.
However, many agencies, including LAFD and LAPD, did not provide records the report authors requested more than a year ago, they said, leaving key gaps in the assessment. For example, the authors said they did not get copies of emergency evacuation plans or records about the response to the Lachman Fire. And LAPD did not provide dispatch or radio communications or reports from officers and supervisors, they said.
Kerber said the L.A. area blazes demonstrated how fire safety no longer depends on the actions of a single homeowner or government agency.
“Risk increasingly operates at the neighborhood and regional level … future resilience depends on coordinated action across the entire system rather than on improvements made by one property owner or agency at a time,” he said.
Evan Bush is a science reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Meta Wants People To Build Their Own Muse Gadgets, Too
articles.title_zh: Meta Wants People To Build Their Own Muse Gadgets, Too
articles.content_orig:
The company created its own smart home device, the Muse Home Link
We still don't know too much about Meta's tamagotchi-like AI device, but the Muse Charm won't be the only dedicated hardware for the AI agent. The company is now encouraging developers to come up with their own Muse-powered devices with a new open source project called Muse Gadgets . It's setting an example as well, kicking things off with a smart home gadget of its own called the Muse Home Link.
According to the head of product for Meta's superintelligence labs Nat Friedman, Meta is providing the open source firmware and a Linux SDK that will enable people to bring the company's agent to hardware. Meta has made some suggestions as to what form these gadgets could take, including a dedicated E Ink display, an HDMI dongle for your TV or a small touchscreen-enabled accessory that looks a bit like the Muse Charm itself. It sounds like the platform should be pretty flexible, though, so tinkerers could hook the agent up to other kinds of devices as well. Meta has started a dedicated Discord community for the project as well.
We built a gadget of our own, too: Muse Home Link is a little usb-c powered device that allows Muse to connect to your home network to talk to smart home devices like TVs and speakers and anything else that exposes https.
We manufactured a batch of 5000 Home Links which should... pic.twitter.com/apFDZmy0kF
— Nat Friedman (@natfriedman) October 2, 2026
As for the Muse Home Link, it's basically a dongle that Meta is giving away 5,000 of to Muse subscribers. According to Friedman, it's "a little usb-c powered device that allows Muse to connect to your home network to talk to smart home devices like TVs and speakers and anything else that exposes https."
It's not clear if Meta has any bigger plans for the initiative, but seeing what hobbyists create could help inform the company's own hardware efforts. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the Muse Charm last week at Connect, saying the device could be a good alternative for people who want to talk to their agent without wearing the company's smart glasses.

articles.title_orig: DOJ will not reopen criminal probe of Powell, Blanche says
articles.title_zh: DOJ will not reopen criminal probe of Powell, Blanche says
articles.content_orig:
The Department of Justice will not reopen its criminal investigation into former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell over the central bank's overbudget multibillion-dollar headquarters renovation a department spokesperson told CNBC.
"We're not reopening a criminal investigation into him," Blanche told Bloomberg in an interview Friday.
Blanche did not rule out separate Justice Department action related to the renovation in his interview. He told the outlet the independent audit of the renovation could prompt an investigation if it uncovers evidence of criminal wrongdoing.
His comments come days after the Federal Reserve's inspector general found no reasonable grounds to believe that a federal crime had occurred requiring a referral to the attorney general, even as the watchdog faulted the central bank for major management and oversight failures that contributed to the project's soaring costs.
President Donald Trump slammed the decision, said in a Truth Social post Wednesday after the news, saying that Powell should be "forced to resign" from the central bank's Board of Governors "at a minimum."
"He can't manage a Building, and he certainly shouldn't be allowed to manage his High Interest Rate Policy (only on 'TRUMP!')," Trump said.
The Justice Department opened its investigation into the renovation in January. Prosecutors issued grand jury subpoenas seeking related records but a federal judge quashed those subpoenas in March, finding they had been issued for an improper purpose and that the government had produced essentially no evidence that Powell committed a crime. The DOJ disputed the ruling but later closed its investigation rather than appeal.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh , who succeeded Powell in May, said the central bank would bring in an independent auditor and strengthen oversight of the project. Powell remains on the Fed's Board of Governors, where his separate term runs through Jan. 31, 2028.
Trump has repeatedly pushed Powell to leave the board altogether after years of clashes over interest-rate policy.
CNBC's Ryan Ruggiero contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Hundreds gather in Mississippi to protest Republican redistricting: ‘This fight is familiar territory’
articles.title_zh: Hundreds gather in Mississippi to protest Republican redistricting: ‘This fight is familiar territory’
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of residents testify to legislature’s redistricting committee in heated hearing, the last of eight
Hundreds of people gathered across from the Mississippi state capitol building on Thursday evening to rally against the aggressive Republican efforts to draw maps that favor their own party.
Shortly after the US supreme court’s decision in Louisiana v Callais, which severely weakened section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, Tate Reeves, the Mississippi governor, moved in lockstep with other Republican governors and lawmakers to call for a special session to redraw maps. However, before that special session could occur, Reeves canceled it and wrote on X that he expected “lawmakers to redraw congressional lines BETWEEN NOW and 2027 elections!”
In August, members of the Mississippi legislature’s joint redistricting committee began a tour of eight redistricting hearings across the state . The last of those hearings took place Thursday evening in Jackson, the state’s capitol.
“This fight is familiar territory for all of us. The giants of the civil rights movement didn’t fight so that we could sit this fight out. They fought so we could stand exactly where we’re standing right now and finish what they started,” Safia Malin, policy director at One Voice, a civic organization, told the crowd before the hearing.
Malin was one of several speakers who reminded the people gathered of the history and fight for voting rights in the state, from the 1890 constitution, which disenfranchised Black voters and ushered in an era of Jim Crow, to the 1964 efforts of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic party and the work of Medgar Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer and others.
Following the rally, those gathered marched to the capitol holding signs, their chants of “Leave our maps alone” and “Whose maps? Our maps” echoing through the capitol building.
An hour before the hearing was scheduled to begin, the room was full, with some people leaning against the walls. Others sat in an overflow section outside and watched the proceedings on television screens.
Prior to the proceedings, house Democratic leader Robert Johnson, who is Black, encouraged audience members to ensure that they made the historical record.
“This is testimony,” said Johnson, one of several Democratic lawmakers who showed up to observe or speak at the proceedings. “And at some point it may be evidence. So let’s make sure we’re heard.”
The committee, handpicked by legislative leaders, is primarily made up of white men. It consists of 16 Republicans , all of whom but one are white, and four Democrats, all of whom are Black. The committee did not answer questions, provide information about how the redistricting process would look on their end or explain how citizens’ testimony would affect their decision.
And in a room full of dozens of Black men and women, six of the first 10 speakers were white. The first Black woman called to give her testimony was the 15th person to speak. Overall, 67 people spoke. Each person was given two minutes to speak. The proceedings lasted just under two hours.
State auditor Shad White, who is considering a gubernatorial run, created controversy almost as soon as he began his comments.
“The delta deserves better leadership than Bennie Thompson. It just does,” White said, as members of the audience booed. Bennie Thompson , who is Black, is Mississippi’s lone congressional Democrat. White, Reeves and other Republicans in the state have openly targeted Thompson and his district.
Through continued boos, White said that there was a “ silent majority ” of people who “want better representation for the Mississippi delta”, and not someone who is “focused on running the January 6th committee”.
Jesse Otto Smith, who was born and raised in Mississippi, said that the stakes of the redistricting hearing were personal.
“I’m 76 years old. My father was born in 1926 – he couldn’t vote. My grandfather was born in 1891 – he couldn’t vote. That’s why I’m here. My great-grandfather was born as an enslaved man, considered less than a human, in 1861 – he couldn’t vote. He was a piece of property,” he said. “That’s why I am here. My mother graduated from Rust College, grew up in Starkville, but couldn’t go to school at Mississippi State, paid taxes without representation.”
Walter Boone, who is white, called the redistricting efforts “Mississippi plan 2.0”.
“The original Mississippi plan culminated in our 1890 constitution, and we cannot ignore that history. I’m not a scholar or trained historian, and even I know that Mississippi has been here before,” he said. “Our first reconstruction ended in much the same way, through a culmination of redistricting and fraud. Our Black elected representatives were stripped of their offices, and Black constituents did not see another person represent them that looked like them for 75 years.”
Lauren Wilson, a sophomore at Tougaloo College from Tupelo, spoke in opposition to redistricting. She asked why the committee held hearings about redistricting, but not for Medicaid expansion or any of the myriad issues in the state.
“If I’ve learned one thing from history, if I’ve learned one thing from the Lord, if I’ve learned one thing from my educators and my pastors, I’ve learned no matter who holds the position, the people hold the power,” she said. “The pharaoh had the position, but Moses had the power. Woodrow Wilson had the position, but Ida B Wells had the power. Lyndon B Johnson had the position, but Martin Luther King had the power.
“We stand today before the committee who has to make a decision on redrawing the lines that seek to disenfranchise the people. So I want you to know that even though tonight you have the position, we hold the power.”
The full legislature is expected to convene in a special session later this year to redraw the state legislative maps. While those maps would not affect November’s midterm elections, lawmakers will likely target Thompson’s seat before he is up for re-election in 2028.

articles.title_orig: An Ebola treatment center was burned down as the death toll in Congo passes 4,000
articles.title_zh: An Ebola treatment center was burned down as the death toll in Congo passes 4,000
articles.content_orig:
The Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak has now killed more than 4,000 people, according to government data, making it the worst epidemic in the country’s history .
Figures released on Friday showed that the death toll has risen to 4,018, and confirmed cases had ⁠reached 8,300 across seven provinces, as the government continues to struggle to contain the outbreak.
Weak infrastructure, the remoteness of the region in eastern DRC, and ongoing conflict with armed groups near the borders with South Sudan, Uganda, and Rwanda have hindered efforts to respond to cases quickly and effectively.
The United Nations reported on Friday that an Ebola-hit camp housing a transit centre for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week as they were looking for weapons on the outskirts of Bunia, capital city of Ituri Province, which is at the epicentre of the outbreak.
The incident forced 19,000 people to flee the camp.
“The enormous challenge of halting the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) just became even harder after a key transit centre for patients requiring treatment burned down in Ituri province,” the UN said.
People’s mistrust and anger towards health workers and authorities have also contributed to the obstacles the government faces in its efforts to contain the outbreak.
A senior ‌member of DRC’s governing Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party was beaten to death days ago after taking part ⁠in a radio programme to raise awareness about the epidemic.
The attack on Marie-Celestin Karondwa, a local official with UDPS, took place last Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterwards, and he died at hospital from his injuries.
The World Health Organization has warned that the epidemic is “ far from over ” and on track to surpass the regional 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone.
Caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, the current epidemic became the largest and deadliest in the DRC after surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.
Several treatments and vaccines are being trialled against Bundibugyo, but currently, there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
The current outbreak, which is the DRC’s 17th, has spread rapidly since it was officially declared on May 15.
More than ⁠2,000 patients have recovered from the Ebola epidemic so far. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, although that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.

articles.title_orig: Apple will limit Mac disk access as AI agents ‘substantially’ increase risk
articles.title_zh: Apple will limit Mac disk access as AI agents ‘substantially’ increase risk
articles.content_orig:
Mac apps will soon need ‘very explicit user action’ to gain full disk access, according to Apple.
Mac apps will soon need ‘very explicit user action’ to gain full disk access, according to Apple.
Apple will add new limits for “full disk access” on Mac in response to risks posed by AI agents, as reported earlier by TechCrunch . In an update on Friday , Apple says it’s rolling out new controls to “ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
The change comes just weeks after Inc ’s Jason Aten found that Meta’s Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his messages , despite not giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone pushed back on this report , saying access to Messages is “entirely opt-in.” Stone added that you have to “enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector for Muse to be able to read your Messages content.”
Now Apple is addressing how developers use that sweeping access, saying:
Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding… As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially.
Full disk access is a permission on macOS that gives an app access to a user’s entire system. Apple says the feature “largely sidesteps” privacy controls offered to users “to allow backup apps to function properly on Mac.” The company doesn’t say when it plans to roll out its update for full disk access. Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge ’s request for comment.

articles.title_orig: U.S. labor market slows with midterms on the horizon
articles.title_zh: U.S. labor market slows with midterms on the horizon
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. labor market slowed during the month of September, according to new data Friday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The economy added only 29,000 jobs, fewer than expected by economists. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%.
Average hourly earnings for workers rose only 0.1% from the prior month and 3% from a year ago. Friday’s data marks the sixth straight month of wages tracking below inflation. BLS will report September inflation numbers on Oct. 14.
Additionally, 60,000 jobs were revised out of previous months’ initial readings.
“The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for July was revised down by 31,000, from +21,000 to -10,000, and the change for August was revised down by 29,000, from +162,000 to +133,000,” the BLS said in a statement.
Overall, September’s hiring was the third weakest this year — trumped only by a loss of 156,000 jobs in February, when DOGE cut tens of thousands of federal workers and the loss of 10,000 jobs in July, many from local school systems that shed teachers over the summer.
Overall, economists expected an addition of 84,000 jobs, an unchanged employment rate at 4.1% and earnings that increased by 3.1% from a year ago, according to a Dow Jones survey.
Friday’s data marks the final monthly employment report that will be issued before the U.S. midterm elections.
For months, the Republican Party and President Donald Trump have faced sagging poll numbers on the economy, as trade wars rage with close allies like Canada, the Iran and Ukraine wars drag on and tariffs continue to roil the global economy.
Democrats hope to flip majorities in both the House and the Senate by hammering the GOP over affordability, gas prices and inflation. September’s jobs report could gave them another data point to help make the case that Americans are worse off today under Trump.
On top of those issues, global bond yields have surged to levels not seen in decades. This week, the U.S. Treasury 10- and 30-year bond yields soared to their highest levels since 2002 and as a result the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped as high as 7.6%.
That came alongside gas prices that remain almost 50% higher than late February, when the U.S. and Israel launched the war against Iran, and as commercial diesel fuel prices sit 70% higher than earlier this year.
Nonetheless, hiring continued, although September’s overall figure was lower than the 133,000 additional jobs created in August, even after revisions.
Stocks jumped sharply after the release of the data, because a weaker jobs market makes it less likely that the Federal Reserve will rase interest rates when it meets later this month. The S&P 500 increased 0.74%, and the Nasdaq Composite closed higher by 1.1%.
U.S. Treasury yields initially fell sharply, but ended the day higher.
The month’s gains can be attributed largely to the healthcare sector, which added 17,000 jobs. Yet even those were at “a slower pace than the average monthly gain over the prior 12 months,” the BLS said.
Construction jobs rose by 11,000 last month, as the widespread AI data center build out continues to drive demand for skilled workers. Manufacturing added 9,000 jobs.
In many major industries, including oil and gas, professional services, and hospitality the agency said employment “showed little change.”
Economists often zero in on the leisure and hospitality sector as an early signal about consumer behaviors. Despite the muted hiring in that sector, most data show that consumer spending has remained steady.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq flirts with new record, Dow and S&P rise after soft jobs report, but Treasury yields reverse higher
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq flirts with new record, Dow and S&P rise after soft jobs report, but Treasury yields reverse higher
articles.content_orig:
Stocks rose Friday following a surprisingly weak jobs report that raised hopes the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady in October.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 250 points, or 0.5%, to close at 51,176.46. The S&P 500 gained 0.7%, rising 56.27 to 7,722.72, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.2%, adding 319.27 to 27,190.86, hitting an all-time high earlier in the day before pulling back as Treasury yields reversed course.
Despite Friday's rally, the Dow was down for the week by about 1.3%. The S&P was little changed, off 0.3%, while the Nasdaq was up 0.6% on the week, with Friday marking its third straight advance.
Treasury yields initially fell Friday following the September employment report, but later rebounded, pushing U.S. equities off their highs for the session.
Tech stocks rallied as risk-taking returned on Wall Street, with shares of Nvidia hitting an all-time high for the first time since May, though it eventually closed below its previous record close. CrowdStrike , Palo Alto Networks and AMD also all rose to all-time highs. Shares of AMD also rose nearly 3%.
Last month's nonfarm payrolls report showed the U.S. economy added 29,000 jobs last month, with unemployment rising to 4.2%. The Dow Jones consensus called for jobs growth of 84,000 and for the unemployment rate to hold steady at 4.1%.
"This is the exact kind of number the market wanted from a labor standpoint," said Phil Blancato, chief market strategist at Osaic. "Not too hot, not too cold ... not overly great, and not weakening."
That number made traders reassess the next move for the Federal Reserve. Fed funds futures trading suggests a 77% likelihood the central bank will stand pat at this month's meeting, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.
Saira Malik, chief investment officer at Nuveen, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the report may give the market support before earnings season kicks off, which she thinks will be "very strong."
"So, I think this could be the start of the Santa Claus rally that we've all been hoping for," she said.
Oil prices pulled back , supporting equities, following a report that European nation states are considering a release of strategic fuel reserves following pressure from the Trump administration.
Investors are coming off a modestly higher session Thursday, to start off the month of October. However, the Dow and the S&P 500 were headed for weekly losses amid a global bond rout, while the Nasdaq was the only major average on pace to end the week with gains.
— CNBC's Jeff Cox contributed to this report
The three major averages rose on Friday following softer-than-expected jobs data.
The S&P 500 advanced 0.49% to 7,722.93. The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.19% to end at 27,190.86, while the Dow Industrials rose 250.88 points, or 0.49%, to close at 51,177.44.
Friday's rally put the Nasdaq Composite on track for another winning week.
The technology-heavy index jumped more than 1% in Friday trading, bringing its weekly gain to 0.5%. If that holds, it would mark the Nasdaq's third positive week in a row.
The Nasdaq is the only major U.S. stock index on track to finish in the green. The Dow and S&P 500 have slid about 1.2% and 0.2%, respectively, in the period.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average on Friday was pacing to end the week in the red, despite Friday's 0.5% advance.
The blue-chip index as of late Friday trading was down more than 1% for the week. It's the Dow's fourth negative week in the last five, with its positive one in that time period coming last week when it finished up just under 0.3%.
Citi raised its price target on shares of bitcoin treasury firm Strategy to $240 per share from $136 per share, implying about 34% upside potential.
The change reflects a more bullish outlook for bitcoin over the next year and a higher valuation of Strategy's bitcoin holdings as a result, Citi analyst Peter Christiansen said in a note Friday.
The bank also maintained its buy rating on Strategy, though Christiansen noted investors should take a more cautious view of Strategy's valuation due to the company's growing but "dilutive" cash reserve, which could reduce the benefit of its bitcoin holdings.
Strategy shares were up 3% in early morning trading.
Nike shares fell 6% at the open after tanking 10% in the premarket after the global sportswear apparel giant delivered a mixed first quarter of fiscal 2027 that showed its turnaround timeline is further than expected.
The company reported weak trends in its key China market, despite growth in its core North America segment.
While Nike plans $2.5 billion in cost savings by 2031, management said it expects revenues to decline in the high single digits in 2027.
The stock is down 46% for the year.
October marks the fourth birthday of the global bull market, one where the future trajectory is still to the upside, according to UBS.
"Over the past four years, global stock markets have reached one record high after another because corporate earnings are growing faster than most analysts expected. What many initially interpreted as a short-term recovery has proved to be a structural upswing with global reach," Burkhard Varnholt, senior financial market adviser at UBS Switzerland, wrote Friday.
"We therefore see the real story of this bull market as less about prices and more about an economic revival," Varnholt added.
Tesla deliveries in the third quarter beat Wall Street's expectations on Friday, coming at 486,532 versus 461,100 expected.
Deliveries eased from 497,099 in the year-ago period but climbed up from the second quarter's 480,126 delivered vehicles.
Shares were up in morning trading on Friday.
The Grayscale Zcash ETF (ZCSH) is up more than 60% in the past month, bringing its year-to-date gain to about 253%, thanks to renewed interest in privacy as speculative capital this year has rotated into AI.
Zcash (ZEC) itself – up more than 170% this year compared to bitcoin , which is stagnant on the year – was designed to keep users' financial transactions completely private. It launched in 2016, but the privacy narrative eventually faded as privacy coins became a compliance headache for regulators and exchanges.
Crypto's mainstream investment case has become increasingly institutionalized and transparent, while AI has made large-scale financial surveillance and transaction analysis more powerful. The combination of the two has allowed the privacy narrative to gain traction and lead to the launch of the Grayscale Zcash ETF in August.
By comparison, the popular iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) is down about 1% this year and the Bitwise 10 Crypto Index ETF (BITW) , which tracks the 10 largest cryptocurrencies, is down 5%. Meanwhile, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has gained 12% and the Invesco QQQ is up nearly 22%.
Nvidia popped on Friday, briefly hitting an all-time intraday high.
Shares of the semiconductor firm rose more than 3% to as much as $237.88 on the day. At its peak, the stock traded at its highest intraday level ever.
Nvidia's shares began trading on the public market in January 1999.
Revisions in the September jobs report for July and August are making those months look weaker for job creation.
July was marked down by 31,000 to mark a net job loss of 10,000 on the month, the Labor Department reported Friday. August was marked down by 29,000 for a new total of 133,000 compared to the initial robust report of 162,000.
"Revisions made both July and August look weaker, too. Over the past 3 months, we've an average of a mere +17k per month," economist Justin Wolfers wrote on social media .
Stocks opened higher Friday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 322 points, or 0.6%. The S&P 500 gained 0.8%, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.1%.
The latest fed funds futures trading showed an 86% likelihood that the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady when it convenes for its Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. That's up from a roughly 76% chance just one day prior.
The U.S. economy added 29,000 jobs

articles.title_orig: California Sues to Block Trump From Weakening Fuel Economy Rules
articles.title_zh: California Sues to Block Trump From Weakening Fuel Economy Rules
articles.content_orig:
California, New York and two dozen other states, cities and counties sued the U.S. Transportation Department on Friday over its decision this week to finalize sharply lower vehicle fuel economy standards in a win for gasoline-powered vehicles.
The revised standards seek to reverse former President Joe Biden's push toward greater fuel efficiency and electric vehicles. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the new rules violate requirements that the standards be set at the maximum feasible level. A coalition of environmental and consumer groups also filed a separate lawsuit challenging the new rules.
The new standards will cut the cost of new vehicles but increase fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions for decades, according to the department's estimates.
The states — which also include Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Jersey, and Washington — as well as the District of Columbia, New York City, Chicago and Denver and several environmental groups, filed suits in the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.
The Transportation Department finalized rules on Monday requiring a fleetwide average of 34.9 miles per ⁠gallon (14.7 km per liter) by 2031, down from 50.4 miles per gallon (21.4 km per liter) under Biden. Environmental groups said the 2031 vehicles would be less efficient than the current fleet.
The states said the Trump administration is ignoring the presence of millions of EVs, "leading to a flawed, dramatically distorted analysis of the 'maximum feasible' fuel economy level."
U.S. drivers have paid sharply higher fuel prices since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran at the end ​of February.
The states said the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration "tries to paper over nearly $220 billion in lost fuel savings — money that drivers would have saved at the pump under the previous fuel economy standards, which will instead benefit Big Oil."
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy defended the rule, saying the agency would let "auto manufacturers produce the cars that fit families' needs at a lower price."
The Transportation Department said the ​regulation reduces manufacturers' average cost per vehicle to comply by $1,289 but increases fuel costs by more than $1,600 over the ​life of the vehicles. The department said the rule would increase U.S. gasoline consumption through 2050 by 4.6% — about 121 billion gallons — compared to the Biden rules but also boost new car sales.
In 2024, the Biden administration finalized rules to push automakers to build more EVs to meet ​rising fuel-efficiency standards.
The rules will also end credit trading among automakers in 2028, ‌which ⁠previously was a significant source of income for EV manufacturers Tesla and Rivian .
President Donald Trump has mounted a multipronged effort to make it easier to sell gasoline-powered vehicles and last year scrapped a $7,500 new EV tax credit.
