articles.title_orig: A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for now
articles.title_zh: A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for now
articles.content_orig:
As they had in the past, San Ygnacio residents banded together to stop a development threatening their town
This story was co-published and supported by the journalism non-profit the Economic Hardship Reporting Project .
Joel Ruiz pointed his cane toward a long piece of metal lying in the dirt. Unwanted construction crews had left it behind on his riverfront property where he has lived and run a small fishing business for decades in San Ygnacio, Texas .
At 90, Ruiz still tends the land. But in July, heavy machinery gouged the earth where mesquite and dense brush once grew. A steel barricade of 30ft-high bars was erected across the riverfront, including on his property just across the Rio Grande from Mexico.
For months, Ruiz and a handful of other San Ygnacio residents have been trying to halt the construction of a federal border wall in their Mexican American town of roughly 400 people . They’ve blocked bulldozers, been arrested, unearthed 75-year-old land records and filed lawsuits challenging the federal government’s authority to build here. Even though residents say nearly all the riverfront land in the county is privately owned, the government is building on it anyway, claiming a decades-old right.
While they have stopped construction on the disputed land for now – a verbal concession, not a court order – the reprieve is precarious: the lawsuits are unresolved, the federal money set aside for construction remains in place and residents know the crews could be back. But they are drawing on the memory of a town that rose up against the government once before.
“This little spot is all we have,” said Elsa Hull, who owns property downriver with her two daughters. “But [residents] fought the federal government before and won – and we can do it again.”
Founded along the Rio Grande in 1830, San Ygnacio grew from a cluster of ranches into a small border town. Today, its plaza is still lined with homes made of sandstone quarried from the riverbank. The town sits in Zapata county , where roughly 38% of residents live below the poverty line and the median household income is about $39,000. Many work in healthcare, schools, food service and ranching. The border patrol is a major regional employer : its sector in Laredo employs about 3,025 people.
The construction is part of the Trump administration’s renewed border-wall push – a roughly $46.5bn expansion funded by what is known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. San Ygnacio is located in one of the stretches where that money is now hitting the ground – and it’s going up as the number of border apprehensions is dropping drastically. Ruiz said he rarely sees anyone crossing this stretch of river any more.
The Rio Grande is also San Ygnacio’s sole source of drinking water, and the wall is being built in its floodplain. To expedite construction, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) waived 30 federal laws – among them the Clean Water Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, eliminating the environmental review that would normally accompany a project of this scale. (The DHS did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.)
To fill that gap, the Laredo-based Rio Grande International Study Center (RGISC) commissioned its own. The assessment warned that the wall and buoy system along and in the Rio Grande would worsen flooding – and, in places, fail outright.
“This is life or death for us,” said Tricia Cortez, the center’s executive director. A breach of the wall system, she warned, would be sudden and catastrophic – homes destroyed, lives endangered. “The wall will straitjacket the river, forcing flood waters to rise and move faster.”
Construction in San Ygnacio had begun without notice. Residents watched what they called a “man camp” rise at its edge and sensed something was coming. At a June community meeting to discuss other business, word began spreading through the back of the room: contractors were clearing land along the riverbank. Several residents hurried down and confronted the equipment operators, telling them they were on private property.
Hull spent 25 years as an environmental investigator for the Texas commission on environmental quality . She recalled how she would watch deer, bobcats, coyotes and sunsets over the river from a bench beneath a tree on the bluff. Border construction has since knocked the tree down and smashed the bench.
“Every part of my life is intertwined with the Rio Grande,” Hull said. “To me this river is sacred.”
When contractors arrived near Ruiz’s home and RV park in June, he invited Hull and her friend to see the damage done. Crews had razed trees and severed an irrigation line. Before leaving for an appointment, Ruiz signed a paper authorizing Hull and her friend to stay and watch the property.
Two contractor trucks slipped through the gate. Hull said one worker repeatedly flashed a card marked “CBP” – presumably Customs and Border Protection. Then she noticed Southwest Valley Constructors identification on his vest.
“You’re not CBP,” Hull recalled telling him. When another truck approached, Hull drove her car across the entrance. More trucks arrived, followed by sheriff’s deputies, state troopers and border patrol agents.
“We were just surrounded by all these men,” Hull said.
Hull pulled up the county appraisal map and argued the crews were on Ruiz’s property. A deputy insisted the land was federal. Finally, Hull put her water bottle on the hood of her car and sat down.
“Fuck it,” she said. “Arrest me.” They did.
On 14 August, Hull returned, carrying a flag that read “Keep Our River Free” on one side and “Walls and Buoys Kill” on the other. When a sheriff’s deputy called to her from across a fence, she thought he wanted to talk. Instead, she was handcuffed and arrested again.
San Ygnacio had fought the federal government for this land once before – and won. When government contractors insisted the land was federal, Frank “Chip” Briscoe, an architectural conservator, started digging through county records.
The trail led back to the early 1950s, when the government built the Falcon dam. Its reservoir submerged historic ranch communities and Indigenous sites along the river, and San Ygnacio was scheduled to be condemned and cleared for the reservoir, too. But residents refused to accept it. In 1951, more than 200 people signed a petition, organized by local veterans and civic leaders, opposing the measure. It worked: the government carved San Ygnacio out of the condemnation, the one stretch along the river bend spared from the reservoir. Seventy years later, the town is invoking that same exclusion again.
Briscoe and attorney Ricardo de Anda searched subsequent property records and still found no evidence that the federal government had later acquired the excluded land. The documents gave De Anda something concrete to act on. In mid-June, he met with the US army corps of engineers on Ruiz’s behalf, arguing the crews had no legal grounds to build on the disputed property.
When construction continued, De Anda sent a warning letter and filed two lawsuits against the federal government, alleging it took private property in violation of the fifth amendment . Two more landowners are preparing to sue, and De Anda plans to sue the contractor, Southwest Valley Constructors, in state court. Landowners filed criminal trespass complaints, while about a dozen residents pressed local officials to intervene.
About a month later, according to De Anda, the county attorney arranged a meeting with contractors and federal officials.
“They agreed to stop,” he said, and the crews pulled back – for now.
For De Anda, stopping construction is only part of the plan. “Our strategy is to affect the national consciousness,” he said. The rest is a matter of time. Every day they hold the line – with their bodies, their deeds, their lawsuits – buys more of it. They are looking toward the midterms, hoping a change in Congress could give them another opening. They are betting they can outlast

articles.title_orig: The 7-year-old Nvidia Shield TV is now $100 more expensive due to AI
articles.title_zh: The 7-year-old Nvidia Shield TV is now $100 more expensive due to AI
articles.content_orig:
The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.
The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.
Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.
When we talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project , but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that Nvidia still actively manufactures the Shield and sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.
Nvidia isn’t a victim here, though. As a key player in AI hyperscaling, the company is more responsible than most for the sky-high cost of components. It has also become one of the most valuable firms in the world thanks to its market-leading AI accelerators and GPUs. As a consequence, we’re seeing new products launch at higher prices than their predecessors, and many end up getting more expensive during their lifetimes. Game consoles have been particularly affected, with Nintendo , Microsoft , and Sony all bumping the prices of their current-gen hardware. The PS5 Pro, for example, has gone from $699.99 at launch in 2024 to $899.99 today.
Stock of the Shield TV Pro has been slim for the last few months, probably because it became too expensive to manufacture new units with component prices rising so quickly. At $300, it will make sense for Nvidia to churn out more devices. However, this higher price will cause an already niche set-top box to be even less appealing to people who just want to stream Netflix.
Unless you need the Shield’s extensive codec support or Plex server capability, it makes more sense to get a cheaper streamer. The Shield is still out of stock on Nvidia’s store , but it’s available at the new price from Best Buy .

articles.title_orig: A Different World Season 2: Sequel Series Is Officially Renewed
articles.title_zh: A Different World Season 2: Sequel Series Is Officially Renewed
articles.content_orig:
A new generation of Hillman College students arrived on campus in Season 1 of A Different World , and soon, their education will continue. The sequel series from showrunner and executive producer Felicia Pride has officially been renewed for Season 2.
“We are beyond excited to return to Hillman and continue to tell meaningful and heartfelt stories that resonate across generations. I am thrilled for our brilliant cast and our hardworking crew,” Pride exclusively tells Tudum. “It's so validating to be bolstered by our amazing audience.”
A Different World Season 1 launched on Sept. 24 with honors, making the Netflix English TV Top 10 list. “It’s because of our incredible fans that we've received such a swift Season 2 pickup! You all have watched, rewatched, posted about, created content around, and hosted events for our show. Your support, passion, and love mean the absolute world,” Pride says. “From the passionate pleas for their favorite ’ships to feeling seen by a particular character to uncovering well-laid Easter eggs , the conversations fans have been having are so rich and joyful. And I love that audiences are watching it together — parents with children, college friends, and extended family — all enjoying it in community.”
Executive producer and director Debbie Allen can’t wait for the next chapter of A Different World . “Yay! Hallelujah! The people and Netflix have spoken. A Different World brought something everybody needed: joy, romance, relevance, authenticity, and HEART,” she says. “Thank you for getting us into the Top 10 worldwide ! And now, gear up! We’re coming back at you with Season 2!”
Looking ahead, Pride promises “more Hillman, more college life, more friendship, more romance, more Black joy, and more HBCU greatness” in A Different World Season 2. You can also expect answers to some of your most burning questions following Deborah Wayne’s (Maleah Joi Moon) first year at Hillman. “Of course, we left Season 1 with quite a few cliffhangers that we must address in Season 2,” says Pride.
While you wait for classes to reconvene, study up on everything there is to know about A Different World ’s renewal and check back here for more news as it’s announced.
After transformative summers, Deborah and her Hillman classmates return to campus for sophomore year with a “new year, new me” attitude, only to find themselves faced with past decisions, uncertain futures, new loves and friendships, and deeper questions of purpose … all while, of course, getting themselves into a whole lot of new mess.
The show has only just been renewed for another school year, so there’s no release date yet. Keep checking back here for major updates coming from campus.
A lot! The sequel series follows Deborah, the youngest child of Dwayne Wayne (Kadeem Hardison) and Whitley Gilbert (Jasmine Guy), as she enters her first year at Hillman College. In the shadow of her well-meaning but sometimes overbearing parents, Deborah attempts to build her own legacy at the HBCU. As she spreads her wings as a young adult, Debo builds deep bonds with fellow Hillmanites — Rashida (Alijah Kai), Hazel (Kennedi Reece), Amir (Jordan Aaron Hall), and Kojo (Chibuikem Uche) — all of whom navigate their own academic and interpersonal struggles. Deborah also rekindles a romance with a special someone from her past, football superstar Shaquille (Cornell Young IV ), and explores a new connection with upperclassman Ellington (Vincent Jamal Hooper).
But there’s more to the sequel series than the new generation. Beloved characters from the original series return as parents, professors, administrators, and esteemed alumni to help dig Hillman out of a financial hole and prove that you never fully graduate from personal drama. For a complete breakdown of all the messiness that ensues in A Different World Season 1, including cast insights on relationship cliffhangers, check out Tudum’s ending explainer .
Of course, you could always run it back and rewatch Season 1 or return to the OG series to relive the glory days of your favorite Hillman alums. And dive deeper into all the connections between old-school and new with Pride in the 10 Nostalgic Things You Might’ve Missed in A Different World video below. You can also check out student life on other campuses with Tudum’s list of college series and movies . Or if Debo’s dating complications have left you craving more romantic turmoil, check out these movies and shows centered on love triangles .

articles.title_orig: Apple’s Flirtation With Surveillance Tech Could Put Its Reputation to the Test
articles.title_zh: Apple’s Flirtation With Surveillance Tech Could Put Its Reputation to the Test
articles.content_orig:
﻿With Apple rumored to launch a smart home hub next month, it could come with a privacy-protecting security camera too.
﻿With Apple rumored to launch a smart home hub next month, it could come with a privacy-protecting security camera too.
Apple’s rumored push into smart home tech could include a smart home security camera that only gives users text event descriptions instead of video footage. Mark Gurman said in the first episode of the Power On podcast that the camera will be part of “a new Apple smart home ecosystem,” alongside Apple’s rumored smart home hub :
They’re also building home security products, both first-party and third-party home security products. And the biggest thing is a program called J450. And this is an offshoot and a companion product to the J490 smart home display. And these are little cameras that you can put around your house. They have very low frame rate. It looks like a cylinder. It looks like a metal giant, you know, chapstick.
And what does that mean? No video recording. So it’s a sensor that cannot actually pull in real video footage. It’s analyzing your environment in your home and around your home simply using AI.
Gurman also mentions that the camera uses “a very similar technology” to what Apple’s reportedly developing for a pair of AirPods with cameras that leaked earlier this year .
Instead of using something like mmWave for presence sensing, using an image sensor with AI embedded that processes everything on-device, like these Sony IMX500 sensors , could work without passing images that would need to be stored and secured. Apple Home currently has a “Detect Activity” setting for HomeKit Secure Video cameras that stops video streaming and recording, but continues tracking motion, similar to what Gurman describes.
He goes on to add that the smart home camera will have facial recognition for things like detecting when someone enters a room, but, “You’re not getting anything but text descriptions. There’s nothing you can do with it. There’s no video recording.”

articles.title_orig: Pixel 10a gets a $100 price hike, now starting at $599
articles.title_zh: Pixel 10a gets a $100 price hike, now starting at $599
articles.content_orig:
Google has quietly raised the price of its mid-range Pixel 10a by $100, giving the device a starting price of $599.
Effective as of today at the Google Store, Pixel 10a has jumped from $499 to $599. The reason is obvious, of course, with the current skyrocketing costs of components such as memory. Google has not officially commented on the price hike yet, though.
This follows Google issuing a price increas e to each of its new Pixel 11 devices compared to the prior generation.
When Google confirmed the Pixel 11 would be more expensive, the company said that this would eventually impact “in-market Pixel phones” which, at the time, we speculated could include Pixel 10a.
The 128GB base Pixel 10a is $599 as of today, with the 256GB model at $699. The updated prices have already kicked in at Amazon and Best Buy , and Google Store now shows Pixel 10a at $849 in Canada, £599 in the UK, and €649 in Europe.
However, this could be fine IF it means the 11a will come at the same $599 price and with Tensor G6 and PixelSnap magnets.
Hopefully street price for those wanting to buy a 10a soon won't change much.
In our review of Pixel 10a , we called the device a “well-rounded experience” for its $499 price, but a $100 jump certainly makes that a tougher conversation, especially considering Google’s mid-ranger is at this point using a two-generation-old chipset in its Tensor G4. But, of course, Google is far from alone here. Just this week, Samsung also issued price hikes across the Galaxy lineup including flagship and mid-range devices alike.
AI is just great isn’t it?

articles.title_orig: The Endhó Dam: One of the World’s Least Known Sacrifice Zones
articles.title_zh: The Endhó Dam: One of the World’s Least Known Sacrifice Zones
articles.content_orig:
Environmental Law and Climate Policy Insights
Last week, about halfway down the New York Times’ Monday morning newsletter, there was a video titled “ Living Next to Mexico’s Toxic Reservoir .”  I watched it, appalled not only by the dangerous conditions described in the video and accompanying article , but also by the fact that I had never heard of this enormous environmental justice disaster.  I worried that if I—someone who inevitably spends some part of everyday thinking about environmental injustices—was previously unaware that over 20,000 people have been forced to live around a toxic reservoir for approximately five decades , then it was unlikely that these communities had been receiving much, if any, attention and support from environmental organizations outside of the region.  It turns out that, unfortunately, my concern was well-founded.  In 2023, Judges for the Society of Environmental Journalists’ 22nd Annual Awards for Reporting on the Environment awarded “ Los Olvidados de Hidalgo ” [English transcript here ]—a N+ Focus feature story about the Endhó Dam—third place, in part because of how “shockingly unknown” the story was.
The Endhó Dam was built in the 1950s as a freshwater reservoir, and for about 20 years, it served as such.  There was plenty of clean water to irrigate the crops in the otherwise arid Mezquital Valley, and the dam provided locals with an enjoyable and clean natural environment .  In the 1970s, however, as the population of Mexico City continued to grow, federal officials decided to begin diverting the capital’s storm runoff and wastewater into the dam.  This means that for the past 50 years, all of the wastewater from a metropolitan area of around 20 million people has been dumped into the Endhó Dam.  Every year, the dam receives around 326 million cubic meters of largely untreated wastewater—that’s enough wastewater to fill over 130,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Approximately 60% of the wastewater does pass through a treatment plant, but before the treated water can make it to the reservoir, it mixes with discharge and waste from a nearby oil refinery, thermopower plant, and the rest of the massive industrial corridor that surrounds the dam.  The result is an environmental and public health nightmare, referred to by locals as “ Mexico’s toilet bowl ,” and “the world’s largest cesspool.”
Yury Uribe, a lifelong resident of the region and activist with El Movimiento Social por la Tierra, has been organizing her community in an attempt to get the Mexican government to recognize the Endhó Dam as an environmental emergency, but through no fault of her own, she has seen little success.  Although the area was declared an ecological restoration zone in 2024, the declaration did not allocate any funding to cleaning up the area.  Accordingly, Endhó Dam residents continue to suffer from seemingly endless environmental and health problems.  Cancer rates in the area tripled between 2007­–2018, and today,
communities surrounding the dam report rates of cancer and kidney failures that are sometimes double the national average ; the dam contaminates the surrounding towns’ wells —the main source of drinking water for those towns’ residents; and the hyacinth that grows on top of the dam has become a breeding ground for mosquitos , endangering locals’ livestock and forcing residents to “ lock themselves inside ” every evening.  Emiliano Rodríguez Mega, a long-time science reporter covering Latin America and the NYT reporter who covered this story, said that even he “ had never quite seen something like the Endhó Dam .”
The big question that normally follows learning about an injustice like this is, “how is this allowed to happen?”  Unfortunately, the answer this time is the same as it almost always is:  some communities—low-income, marginalized communities—are seen as expendable.  As explained by the legendary environmental justice advocates Dr. Robert Bullard and Beverly Wright, the people and communities who are viewed as being expendable suffer from having “ the wrong complexion for protection .”
Areas like the Endhó Dam are often referred to as “ sacrifice zones ” because “the health and safety of people in these communities is being effectively sacrificed for the economic gains and prosperity of others.”  In this instance, the low-income farming communities living around the dam ( a substantial percentage of whom are Indigenous , primarily from the Otomí Nation ) are being sacrificed to protect Mexico City from flooding and to keep the profitable agricultural area surrounding the Tula River rich with nutrients.  Similar cases of environmental injustice and racism exist around the world:  the risk of cancer to the primarily Black residents of “Cancer Alley” in Louisiana is over 50 times higher than the national average; 95% of children in Kabwe, Zambia , largely from poor families, have dangerously elevated levels of lead in their blood caused by the nearby lead mining; nearly every Aamjiwnaang First Nation household living in Canada’s “Chemical Valley” suffers from high rates of miscarriages, asthma, and cancer.  The examples, unfortunately, abound.  Recognizing that these areas “illustrat[e] egregious human rights violations, particularly of poor, vulnerable and marginalized communities,” former United Nations Special Rapporteur on Human Rights and the Environment, David Boyd, described sacrifice zones as “ the worst imaginable dereliction of a State’s obligation to respect, protect, and fulfil[l] the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment.”
How do we finally rid the world of a system in which, as Naomi Klein put it in This Changes Everything , “poisoning [whole subsets of humanity] in the name of progress [is] somehow acceptable”?  Like most things worth doing, it’s somewhat complicated.  But as the Climate Justice Alliance—an alliance of over 100 frontline communities in the climate justice movement— has noted , it is critically necessary not only because everyone has a right to drink clean water and breathe clean air, but also because “[o]ur society cannot build a more just and healthy economy if communities continue to be seen as expendable.”  Eliminating sacrifice zones can be distilled into a three-stage process:  (1) prioritize protecting the communities living in sacrifice zones from further harm; (2) allocate resources to repairing the harm that has already been done and passing strong regulations; and (3) invest in the communities that have historically been viewed as expendable, and ensure that they have power over their own futures.  Let’s get to work.

articles.title_orig: Taylor T-Shirts Impact Lives Through Partnership with World Orphans
articles.title_zh: Taylor T-Shirts Impact Lives Through Partnership with World Orphans
articles.content_orig:
Lydia Wilhelm 02 October 2026
Would it really be a prospective student visit without a free t-shirt? If you see a student walking backwards across campus giving a Taylor tour, you’re bound to see some visitors with classic Taylor purple t-shirts hanging over their arms. However, you might not know that this common prospective student gift is creating uncommon change in the lives of Guatemalan families through Taylor’s partnership with World Orphans .
World Orphans is a non-profit organization with a vision of relational healing and financial independence for families who have been separated due to poverty or abuse. One of the ministry arms within the organization is the World Orphans Market , an economic empowerment program. This program equips women with sewing skills, and these women are then employed as artisans to return to them the dignity of meaningful work and financial freedom. All of World Orphans’ work is grounded in a Christ-centered philosophy of human worth: everyone is created with intrinsic dignity and with a God-given purpose. Additionally, World Orphans works through local churches, ensuring that these women are supported by Christ-centered communities as they work their way out of poverty and towards better lives for their families.
Like so many Taylor stories, Taylor’s journey to partnering with World Orphans is a story of community. When the Admissions team connected with World Orphans, they saw an opportunity—an opportunity for Taylor as an organization to model the same mission it seeks to foster in its student body. Taylor always has a need for t-shirts—particularly in Admissions. Here, Taylor’s tangible need for shirts meets these Guatemalan women’s tangible need for living-wage work, creating a true, mutually beneficial partnership.
As the Admissions team collaborated with World Orphans’ Guatemalan team, they encountered some community connections that made one thing clear—God had already been opening doors for this partnership. One of these connections was Lily Sachsenmeier ’26, who finished her Orphaned & Vulnerable Children degree interning at World Orphans in Guatemala, where "a highlight was getting to talk with social workers at World Orphans who support local families, empowering parents with education and resources to care for their children. I was really moved by the personal experiences they shared and by their passion for their work."
During her time in Guatemala, Sachsenmeier also had the opportunity to meet some of the artisans making the t-shirts for Taylor Admissions, bringing this community story full circle.
Reflecting on Taylor’s choosing World Orphans to supply their next batch of Admissions t-shirts, Sachsenmeier said, "I’m deeply touched that Taylor is partnering with World Orphans. As a student, I got many free t-shirts for events and programs, and I’m so glad that Taylor is being intentional about where they source some of these t-shirts. I’m incredibly proud that Taylor is investing in t-shirts made by these women in Guatemala as part of World Orphans’ economic empowerment program!"
At Taylor, a t-shirt is so much more than a clothing item—it’s a walking billboard for who we are. It says, "I believe in what goes on here." Now, Taylor purple has additional purpose. These t-shirts are a physical manifestation of our mission to "minister Christ’s redemptive love, grace, and truth to a world in need." They are a reminder of a God who opens doors. And a reminder of what a true partnership can look like.
Learn more about how Taylor equips students to break cycles of vulnerability through our Orphaned & Vulnerable Children major.

articles.title_orig: McMinnville siblings earn karate medals around the world
articles.title_zh: McMinnville siblings earn karate medals around the world
articles.content_orig:
MCMINNVILLE, Ore. (KPTV) - Logan and Kenzie Mendonca, a brother and sister from McMinnville, are competing in karate tournaments around the world.
“We are more stressed watching each other fight than when we are competing ourselves,” Kenzie said.
The siblings have traveled to multiple countries to compete.
“Canada, Mexico, Chile, Brazil, Paraguay, Costa Rica,” Logan said.
“I think Africa, just to make one,” Logan said, referring to places they haven’t competed.
Logan and Kenzie recently returned from Guadalajara, Mexico, with Youth League Karate gold medals. Their medals hang in the family dojo, the Mendonca Academy of Martial Arts in McMinnville.
“It’s a place of calm. I come in here and my problems are outside,” Logan said.
The siblings have competed in karate since they were three years old. Their father, Tony, leads their training routine.
“You learn time management, you learn how to get your things done because the dojo isn’t something that you can skip. It is a mandatory part of your routine,” Kenzie said.
“Just traveling and seeing crazy stuff but also winning and losing together is something really special to me,” Logan said.
Logan and Kenzie competed at the Junior Pan American Karate Championships in San Jose, Costa Rica. Logan won the Junior Male title in his fifth appearance at the event.
“I went bronze, silver, silver, then I took fifth and this year I won, so this year was my first year winning, pulling it out. It was my third year in the finals,” Logan said.
Logan is ranked No. 1 in the U.S. and is a senior at McMinnville High School. Kenzie, a sophomore, won Pan American Cadet Female silver for a third straight year.
“I think the most-cocky part of it for me is being in three finals before Logan,” Kenzie said.
“Yeah, I mean her record is better than mine,” Logan said.
“On paper if you look at like our ages my stuff looks cooler than his,” Kenzie said. “Because I’m better earlier.”
Both Logan and Kenzie were named team captains for the United States. They will next compete at the Junior World Championships in Poland.
“He’s Spiderman but when he comes home, he’s Peter Parker,” Kenzie said.
Logan is a National Merit Scholar semifinalist with aspirations of attending college in France to study physics.
“Right now Peter Parker has national merit, but nobody knows he’s Spiderman and nobody cares,” Kenzie said.
Logan and Kenzie will miss about nine days of school for the trip to Poland. They are completing tests during lunch breaks and will bring homework with them.

articles.title_orig: Vape store clerks face federal drug charges after tracing purchases made by dead Ole Miss students
articles.title_zh: Vape store clerks face federal drug charges after tracing purchases made by dead Ole Miss students
articles.content_orig:
OXFORD, Miss. – Two Oxford, Mississippi vape store clerks are facing federal drug charges after investigators say they traced purchases made by two University of Mississippi students before their deaths , according to court documents detailing.
Yahya Mohamed Mosleh and Islam Yahya Mosleh are each charged with possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance, the documents show.
According to a DEA affidavit, bank records linked Aidan Hamilton to purchases at Puffs Vape Tobacco & Beer and Robert Strang to Express Mart #7 before investigators recovered similar suspected kratom products at both death scenes.
Authorities also described undercover purchases and the seizure of more than 500 suspected kratom-related products from the Oxford vape shop.
In a statement Wednesday, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics, a department in the sheriff’s office, stopped short of declaring that investigators found kratom itself near either student.
“During the investigations, packaging associated with kratom-related products was discovered at both locations,” part of the statement read.
The Sept. 25 affidavit reported toxicology results from the medical examiner were still pending.
American Kratom Association Senior Fellow on Public Policy Mac Haddow said Wednesday during a press conference that the specific drug found near both students is illegal.
Haddow pointed out the sale and possession of kratom has been illegal federally as of August and illegal to sell or possess in Oxford, Mississippi since 2019, and illegal in Lafayette County, where Oxford is located, since 2021.
The affidavit dated Sept. 25 says investigators were still awaiting toxicology results from the medical examiner at the time.
The charges come as officials await the toxicology results from the deaths of Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
Both students were found dead with similar packages of synthetic kratom found to be in their possession, court documents say.
The Moslehs aren’t accused in either death.
Packaging on the kratom items found near both men was labeled “Smax, Pseudo-DHM” tablets, which is a “Kratom-like substance at gas stations or tobacco shops” that people buy for the “narcotic-like effect,” according to the court documents.
In September, Hamilton made multiple purchases at Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford, where employees Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Mohamed, 18, were arrested Friday on a state-level charge of possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute, according to officials.
Court documents did not establish that the kratom discovered near Hamilton at the time of his death originated from that store.
One of those purchases occurred the day before Hamilton was found dead.
According to court records, a confidential law enforcement informant visited Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store and inquired whether the store carried “7 O Kratom based pills.”
A store clerk responded “yes,” then opened a drawer beneath the register and produced a package of kratom.
Mosleh allegedly told the informant to “be quiet” about the pills and to be careful taking them because “people were dying from them.”
Over 500 units of kratom were seized from the vape store along with THC cartridges, gummies, pre rolls, and other suspected THC substances.

articles.title_orig: France student protests spread from Paris, with violent clashes forcing hundreds of high schools to close
articles.title_zh: France student protests spread from Paris, with violent clashes forcing hundreds of high schools to close
articles.content_orig:
Paris — French high school students lit fires outside schools and faced off with police on Friday as a protest movement that has forced the closure or disrupted education at more than 560 establishments showed no sign of abating.
The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils in their final years of high school block access to buildings and clash with police.
The students say their school hours are excessively long, conditions inadequate including overheated classrooms and dilapidated buildings, and that there are too many staff absences.
"For a whole year, we didn't have a science teacher. We don't have any textbooks," said Simon, a 15-year-old who declined to give his surname outside the Turgot high school in central Paris. "And still, we're the lucky ones. It's even worse in the suburbs."
The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it calls "urban violence."
Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing tear gas canisters to disperse the protests.
In Paris on Friday, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools, with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes, an AFP photographer said.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said "the high school student movement is being held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups."
His ministry said Friday that education had been disrupted at more than 560 high schools out of the 3,700 in the country. More than 1,000 high schools were affected Thursday, the interior ministry has said.
Many high schools have planned to conduct classes remotely, particularly in the southern city of Marseille.
At least 65 staff members have been injured, including 40 high school principals, since the start of the movement, Geffray told BFMTV, while about 170 students have been wounded and over 100 high schools have suffered "severe damage."
"Parents must clearly step up and tell their children not to go" to the protests, he said. "What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger."
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said he has asked prosecutors to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children during the protests and "pay for repairs."
Since the start of the movement, around 2,000 people have been taken into police custody "90% of whom were minors," Darmanin told RTL.
In the western city of Rennes, the tension was already palpable outside the Jean-Mace high school with students dressed in black and wearing balaclavas standing not far from a heavy police presence.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won — our school is closed this morning," said Lola, 16, who declined to give her last name.
She condemned what she said was police violence.
"It makes us even angrier —   the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she said.
Police used tear gas at the Kerichen high school in Brest, in western France, an AFP photographer said.
The protests have also made a strong political echo just over half a year before presidential elections, with the government accusing the hard left France Unbowed (LFI) —   whose firebrand leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is again standing for the presidency - of being behind the movement.
But senior LFI official Manuel Bompard accused the government of "descending into conspiracy theories."

articles.title_orig: Nike stock misery continues after another dreadful quarter and outlook: Wall Street reacts
articles.title_zh: Nike stock misery continues after another dreadful quarter and outlook: Wall Street reacts
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nike ( NKE ) reminded investors why the stock is trading at record lows on its earnings day.
Shares of the fallen sportswear giant dropped 6% in early trading on Friday, extending the plunge in a stock that had already dropped 76% in the past five years alone.
Nike's quarter and earnings call were littered with red flags about how far the business has fallen and how difficult the road to recovery still is:
🛑 Nike Brand sales: down 4% 🛑 Online sales: down 13% 🛑 Converse sales: down 28% 🛑 China sales: down 26% 🛑 Inventory: down only 3% 🛑 Signaled a major round of layoffs (again) 🛑 Sales seen dropping by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal year 2027 🛑 Earnings guidance well below consensus ($1.15 to $1.35 vs. estimates of $1.66)
"Overall, there's a lack of energy in the lifestyle space right now, which is impacting traffic. Yes, the consumer is cautious. But as the leader in the industry, it's on us to bring more creativity to sportswear," Nike CEO Elliott Hill said on the earnings call.
Here is the vibe on the quarter and outlook from Wall Street.
"We are not ready to call a bottom yet with shares trading at 28x P/E at the midpoint of FY27E guidance. The new Pace cost savings plan helps, and we expect it to be increased at the November investor day, helping paint a path towards a more tangible margin structure vs. the MSD% EBIT margin in FY27E. We recommend the challenger athletic footwear brands while NKE is off its game (DECK, ONON, WWW)." -Stifel analyst Peter McGoldrick
"NKE's F'1Q reinforced that the turnaround is progressing, with Performance continuing to scale while NA trends improve and profitability showing signs of stabilization. While China, Jordan, and Sportswear continue to weigh on results, mgmt's deliberate actions and revised FY27 framework suggest greater focus on rebuilding long-term brand and marketplace health." -Jefferies analyst Randy Konik
"With yet another downward revision, the questions remain when guidance cuts will represent the band-aid rip versus slow bleed as they continue to debate the path potential stabilization ahead. With the November analyst day ahead, we would assume management likely preferred to get the 'bad news' out of the way to offer up a more positive tone in person, but clearly there has been plenty of "bad news" to spare. Recognizing ongoing noise, we lower our Price Target to $50 (from $60). And though it certainly is not easy (and certainly has not been correct), we maintain our BUY rating amid increasingly negative sentiment and a potentially emerging catalyst path (potentially troughing estimates, new CFO, November Analyst Day)." -Guggenheim analyst Simeon Siegel

articles.title_orig: Respiratory virus season has arrived. Flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines are available
articles.title_zh: Respiratory virus season has arrived. Flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines are available
articles.content_orig:
SEATTLE — There's a bit of a chill in the air, pumpkin spice in your coffee, and children back to school — which means the threat of respiratory viruses like COVID-19, influenza and RSV is looming.
Some respiratory illnesses have arrived already. Seasonal influenza activity is still low at the national level, data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show.
But certain flu metrics are inching up – especially in the West . Health officials in Washington state's King County note that since mid-August there has been an increase in people with flu visiting emergency departments in the area.
Vaccines that help prevent illness and reduce the risk of serious infections and hospitalization are now available, and for some people, this is the right time to roll up their sleeves.
Typically, the CDC launches a fall campaign around this time of year, recommending seasonal immunizations such as the flu shot and COVID-19 vaccines. But after sweeping changes to the agency's vaccine advisory committee during the second Trump administration and ongoing lawsuits, the CDC recently posted guidance online to follow last year's recommendations for flu and COVID-19.
Meanwhile, the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota's Vaccine Integrity Project launched their own independent reviews of this fall's vaccines – including those for flu , COVID and RSV – which was published in September in the medical journal JAMA.
The review papers helped inform 2026-27 respiratory virus immunization recommendations released by several medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.
"For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP," Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a news briefing.
"Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter," Gellin said.
"Clinicians will still have patients to care for. Parents will still have decisions to make for their children, and older Americans, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions will still need to know how best to protect themselves," he said. "We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance."
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has not responded to CNN's request for comment on the groups' recommendations.
Flu, COVID-19 and RSV immunizations are now available at most major pharmacies.
"And really reassuringly, insurers have indicated to the major groups that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations," Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in a news briefing.
Ordering through Vaccines for Children , the federal program that provides routine immunizations at no cost to children who are uninsured or underinsured or whose families may not otherwise be able to afford them, has also started. About half of U.S. children are eligible for the program.
"Vaccines are one of medicine's greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives," Nosal said in a news release. "As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients."
Groups eligible for RSV immunizations include older adults, pregnant people and infants.
"People age 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75 years old, should get one dose," Nosal said. "This is not an annual vaccine. If you got one before, you do not need a new one this year. Getting one should protect you throughout the entire season."
During pregnancy, RSV vaccination is recommended in the third trimester, between weeks 32 and 36.
Children younger than 8 months should be immunized against RSV using a monoclonal antibody unless their mother got an RSV vaccination during pregnancy, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.
And a single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for adults who have weakened immune systems.
For older adults, RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall.
The advice slightly changed this year for pregnant people.
For infants, the RSV monoclonal antibody is typically recommended around virus season, from October through March.
Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu shot.
"On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to go to the doctor by 30% to 60%," Nosal said.
"Adults 65 years and older should get an enhanced flu vaccine, one that is high-dose, adjuvanted or recombinant, when it's available," she said. "But do not delay your vaccination if that one's not available."
And for the first time, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for use in adults 50 and older.
October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, Nolan said, because "protection wanes throughout the season."
Some providers use the slogan "flu before boo" to remind people to get a flu shot before Halloween.
Getting an updated COVID-19 vaccine is recommended for all adults.
"If you're older than 19, we recommend getting the COVID-19 vaccine," Nosal said.
"This is especially important for people who are 65 years and older, at increased risk for severe COVID infection and those who've never received a COVID-19 vaccine," she said. "For those adults 65 years and older, they should receive a second dose of the updated COVID-19 vaccine six months after that season's initial dose to help maintain protection as immunity wanes over time."
The vaccine is also recommended for infants between six months and 23 months of age, and children in certain high-risk groups or those whose families request vaccination.
It's recommended to get the updated vaccine now, but if you have been recently infected with Covid, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the vaccine.
The updated COVID-19 vaccine "targets the most recent strain that's been circulating, and so if you want to update your protection, that's the best way to do it," Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, president-elect of the American Medical Association, said in a news briefing.

articles.title_orig: World Jewish Congress Commemorates Third Anniversary of October 7
articles.title_zh: World Jewish Congress Commemorates Third Anniversary of October 7
articles.content_orig:
Cookies allow us to understand how you use this site and improve your experience. Our detailed Cookie Policy can be found here . By continuing to use this website you accept our use of cookies.
Mandatory cookies help make this website usable by enabling basic functions like page navigation and access to secure areas of the website. Our website cannot function properly without these cookies.
Statistic cookies help us understand how visitors interact with this website, for example seeing which pages are most popular. This information is collected anonymously and helps us improve the site by making the most sought after information easy to find.
Marketing cookies are used to track visitors across websites allowing the display of ads that are relevant and engaging for the visitor. Whilst we do not display any advertising on the WJC website, allowing marketing cooking may allow other sites to see that you have visited our site.
Start time 09:00 AM (New York) / 15:00 (Brussels) / 16:00 (Jerusalem)
As we approach the third anniversary of October 7, we invite you to join the World Jewish Congress for a special online commemoration on Tuesday, October 6, with Rabbi Doron Perez , President of the World Zionist Organization and Executive Chairman of World Mizrachi.
For Rabbi Perez, October 7 is both a national tragedy and an intensely personal one. His son, Captain Daniel Perez, was killed while defending Nahal Oz on October 7, 2023, and his body was taken hostage into Gaza. For 163 days, his family held on to the hope that Daniel might still be alive. After learning of his death, they waited another year and a half until he was finally returned to Israel and laid to rest.
In this deeply personal conversation with our communities, Rabbi Perez will share Daniel’s story and his family’s journey through hope, devastating loss and remembrance. He will reflect on the faith and resilience that carried them through these unimaginable years and on the strength and hope that continue to sustain the Jewish people.
Three years after October 7, its impact continues to be deeply felt in Israel and throughout Jewish communities worldwide. This gathering is an opportunity for us to remember together, to acknowledge all that our communities have endured, and to reaffirm the connection and solidarity that bind us across borders.
We warmly invite you, your leadership and members of your community to join us and encourage you to share this invitation widely.
Registration: Webinar Registration - Zoom
We hope you will join us in remembrance, as we come together to mark the darkest day for the Jewish people since the Shoah. May the memory of those we lost forever be a blessing.

articles.title_orig: 2026 Right Livelihood laureates challenge autocracy, patriarchy, and AI bias
articles.title_zh: 2026 Right Livelihood laureates challenge autocracy, patriarchy, and AI bias
articles.content_orig:
The 2026 Right Livelihood Award is honoring women and women-led organisations confronting the world ’ s most entrenched power structures: authoritarian rule, patriarchal violence, and unchecked AI development.
Their common thread is resistance to systems that push people to the margins, and a shared insistence on putting people back at the centre.
The 2026 Right Livelihood Award, also known as the “ Alternative Nobel Prize, ” has been awarded to Jalila Haider from Pakistan “ for breaking barriers, as the first female lawyer from her Hazara community, to challenge ethnic, state and patriarchal persecution, guided by the conviction that no human being is illegal,” the Rural Women ’ s Assembly “ for organising rural women across Southern Africa into a united force defending land, seed, and bodily autonomy against corporate and patriarchal dispossession,” the Georgian Young Lawyers ’ Association “ for building and safeguarding Georgian democracy and sustaining civic power in the face of an autocratic crackdown,” and Timnit Gebru from the US “ for challenging concentrated power in artificial intelligence and pioneering digital technology rooted in justice, lived experience and human agency.”
World Council of Churches general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay commended the women honored. “ These Right Livelihood laureates exemplify the kind of empowerment that is life-flourishing, deep-rooted, and of the people,” he said, adding a special congratulations to the Rural Women ’ s Assembly from his home country of South Africa. “ I have seen firsthand the power of volunteers who can put the region ’ s food systems back into the hands of resilient people and communities.”
For over 45 years, the Right Livelihood Award has honoured and supported people leading the way to a just, peaceful, and sustainable world for all.
The 2026 awardees were chosen from 200 nominees from 72 countries. They will be honoured during a televised award presentation in Stockholm on 1 December.
